Gm gArc

An AI agent should do more than agree with you.

That is the idea behind @TheARCTERMINAL.

Most AI crypto tools mainly give you information. They can summarize charts, explain projects, or answer questions.

ARC is trying to build something different.

It wants to create an AI powered operating system for onchain activities.

In simple terms, you give the AI a task, and it can:

Research information

Analyze different signals

Use different tools

Interact with blockchain applications

Ask for permission before important actions

Show proof of what happened

The important part is control.

You should know what the AI can access, what it can do, and when it needs your approval.

ARC also focuses on verification.

Instead of simply saying:

“I completed the task.”

The goal is to provide evidence that the correct agent performed the action and that the result can be verified.

Think about it like this:

You give the instruction.

The agent analyzes it.

You approve the action.

The agent executes it.

The blockchain provides a record.

That creates a simple flow:

Instruction → Approval → Execution → Proof

Another important idea is disagreement.

A useful AI should not always tell you that your trade idea is good.

It should be able to point out weaknesses, compare different information, and show you what you might be missing.

That is where ARC becomes interesting.

The goal is not simply to build an AI that talks about crypto.

The goal is to build an AI workspace that can understand information, take actions within clear permissions, and provide proof of those actions.

If that works as intended, an AI terminal becomes more than a chat window.

It becomes a tool for actually operating onchain.

text:
Claude did not merely respond to a prompt. It worked inside a specialized environment called Claude Science for several days with virtually no supervision, receiving only an initial task description and instructions to submit progress reports every four to six hours. This is a model of how modern AI agents should operate: sustaining context, using tools, correcting their own errors, and executing complex multistep algorithms without any loss of quality.

The result was a nine loop, six gluon amplitude in N=4 super Yang Mills theory, one loop beyond the 2023 record held by Dixon and Liu. Lance Dixon of SLAC and Stanford, who held the previous record, personally verified the outcome and described the procedure as fragile to the point of collapse: a single minor error anywhere, he said, would ruin the entire calculation like a failed soufflé.

Claude did not discover a new physical principle. It flawlessly executed a methodological recipe devised by humans, namely amplitude bootstrapping and antipodal duality. Even here, however, there are nuances worth noting.

This is a toy model with extra supersymmetry, not a description of real particles. Its value lies in serving as a proving ground for methods.

Humans were closer than expected. A group led by Song He at the Chinese Academy of Sciences independently obtained most of the same result within the same weeks, using GPT-6 within a human led framework.

Verification is not absolute. The data files are public on Zenodo, and two independent routes agree on all 107,053 nonzero coefficients, but the computation's programs are not distributed, roughly 99.6 percent of the coefficients reconstruct to certified rationals, and no second independent run has yet been performed.

Cost: about 100 for the bootstrap computation itself, running 96 CPUs for a week, but roughly 1,000 to 2,000 for each of the two routes, driven mainly by the cost of running Claude.

The main conclusion is a pragmatic shift. We have moved beyond the hype around the AI scientist and entered a phase of tooling. The system now takes on the most demanding algebraic computations, the ones most prone to human error, freeing the expert to focus on formulating problems and interpreting results. What is genuinely new here is not the physics, but the fact that a harness environment can now carry a fragile, multi day frontier calculation all the way to completion, under supervision no more sophisticated than "keep going."

⚖️ An agreement is only as strong as the process behind it.

That’s what caught my attention about the Blocksee × Internet Court integration.

As AI agents start making deals, signing agreements, moving funds and working with other agents, simply saying “we agreed” isn’t enough anymore.

There needs to be a way to prove what was agreed, when it was agreed, and what happens if something goes wrong.

That’s where this integration gets interesting.

Blocksee’s Consenti protocol works with the @blockseeAI  MCP server to create trustless agentic agreements and contracts.

Now, agreements sealed through Blocksee can come with a court through Internet Court.

The process can connect the different parts of the deal:

Terms are hashed onchain before funds move
The agreement leaves a record that can be independently verified
The dispute route is agreed upfront, instead of figuring it out after something goes wrong

And I think that last part is especially important.
In a world where agents can negotiate and transact without humans sitting in the middle of every interaction, we need infrastructure that handles not only how agreements are made, but also what happens when those agreements are challenged.

Blocksee helps establish the agreement.

Internet Court provides the framework for what happens when there’s a dispute.

Together, it starts to look less like a simple digital signature and more like a complete system for trustless agent-to-agent agreements.

The future of agentic commerce won’t just be about agents making deals.

It will be about giving those deals verifiable terms, evidence, and a clear path to resolution. ⚖️

Agentic payments are not only about giving AI agents a way to move money.

The bigger question is: can an agent prove it is authorised to make that payment?

That’s the problem the x402 + @Concordium approach is addressing.

x402 provides the payment flow, allowing agents to make payments through a standardised HTTP-based mechanism.

Concordium adds the identity and verification layer, so an agent can prove relevant credentials or authorisation without exposing unnecessary personal information.

This matters because an autonomous agent may eventually buy services, access restricted platforms, negotiate transactions, or pay other agents on behalf of a person or business.

Payment tells you that money moved.

Verification helps establish whether the agent was actually allowed to make that move.

What started with Verify & Pay is moving toward something bigger: infrastructure where AI agents can pay, verify, and operate with accountability.

The future of agentic payments isn’t just autonomous.

It needs to be verifiable too.

text:
Millions of transactions between AI agents sounds like progress.

But @eforst, the CEO of @blockseeAI pointed something out during his recent conversation with @raskovsky.

What exactly are these agents agreeing to before money starts moving?

An agent can pay another agent for data or a service, but the transaction itself says very little about what happens if that data is misused, the service isn't delivered as promised, or the two agents simply disagree on whether the agreement was fulfilled.

Blocksee is tackling the agreement side of that problem: giving agents clear terms before they transact.

But agreements only matter if they can be enforced when things go wrong.

He described @courtofinternet and @GenLayer as a "bigger stack of trust" that completes the loop by giving disputes between agents somewhere to be resolved.

Agent payments are scaling fast so the rules, accountability and recourse around those payments need to scale with them.

text:
holy sh*t. Jev Founder, Diogo Almeida just released a 12-page PDF how turned Jev into a second brain for AI agents

a CLI for your Obsidian vault, a Claude Code plugin and a research paper. this is a 9-step blueprint on how to give your agents memory without paying an LLM to decide what's worth remembering:

step 1 → split the work: Jev decides what to remember, code applies the rules, the LLM only writes the note or the answer

step 2 → gate every capture with one call: save, todo, skip or review, plus is it private and how useful will it be in 30 days

step 3 → keep only what clears the bar: save at value 1.5+ and confidence 0.6+, anything private never leaves your machine

step 4 → let the LLM write one note, 5 to 12 lines, one claim. Jev never writes the body, or you end up with lossy compaction

step 5 → link it: Jev compares the new note with its neighbors and answers duplicate, related, revises or contradicts. related at 0.7+ gets wikilinks both ways

step 6 → read cheap, then judge: BM25 or embeddings pull the top 10 to 20, Jev keeps only what the question needs, 5 notes max go into context

step 7 → clean up every night: duplicates get a merge proposal, old notes get superseded_by, contradictions get a conflict stub, and you keep or reject

step 8 → don't build from zero: jev-second-brain runs on your vault, jevmem plugs into Claude Code, Jev-Mem is the paper if you're building agent memory yourself

step 9 → check the receipts: jevmem hit 98.5% on save/skip at 0.30s while six frontier LLMs took 2.8 to 4.3s, and Jev-Mem scored 0.777 vs 0.700 on LoCoMo with memory built 6.6x faster

your agent doesn't forget because the model is weak. it forgets because nothing ever decided what was worth keeping

memory was never a storage problem. it's a decision problem, and decisions are exactly what Jev is built for

stop giving your agent a bigger context window. give it a judge

I've been thinking a lot about the Claude Opus 5.5 story.

An engineer gave Claude a project which involved six separate code bases and essentially let the AI figure out how all the various services interacted.
For over 18 hours, the AI worked on its own (with minimal human input) figuring out the relationships between the different services and completing the project.
A year or so ago, when I heard "AI that will work while you sleep," I thought it was a bit of a silly idea engineers would put in their pitch decks.

Today, however, I am seeing it happen in reality.
The really shocking thing is not that Claude wrote code; I already knew it could do so.

Rather, it is the ability to assign a complicated problem to an AI agent, go to bed, wake up the next day, and look at what the agent accomplished overnight.
This changes my perception of what an AI agent is capable of doing.

GM ct

the more i look into AI agent payments, the more i realize sending a payment is only one part of the problem.

agents also need a way to establish who is behind the payment.

that’s why @Concordium joining the x402 Foundation is interesting.

x402 allows an agent to:

request a resource
receive a 402 Payment Required response
see the required price
sign a stablecoin payment
and access the resource

without a checkout page, account, or API key.

then there is the Concordium angle.

agent payments can be connected to protocol-level identity and accountability.

while zero-knowledge proofs can help protect the underlying identity information.

and honestly, that distinction matters.

an agent can make a payment.

but for an agent economy to scale, counterparties also need a way to verify who is accountable for that agent without requiring unnecessary personal information.

so the payment can happen automatically

the identity can remain privacy-preserving

and accountability can still be established.

that combination of payments, identity and privacy is what makes this direction interesting.

An AI agent hires another agent to monitor 1,000 shipments and flag every delivery that looks suspicious.

The job finishes.

Agent A says: “You missed 14 suspicious deliveries.”

Agent B says: “Those deliveries never met the definition of suspicious.”

Both can prove what happened.

Neither can prove what “suspicious” should mean.

That is where autonomous commerce gets interesting.

Agents do not only need ways to find each other, communicate and exchange value. They need a way to settle the arguments that cannot be resolved by checking whether a transaction happened.

That is what @courtofinternet is building.

Before a deal begins, the terms are set, evidence can be preserved, and the dispute route is agreed upfront.

If the agents later disagree, GenLayer validators running different AI models can judge the evidence and reach a verdict, with a path to appeal.

The important shift is simple:

Dispute resolution stops being something you figure out after the deal breaks.

It becomes part of the deal itself.

That matters because an agent economy cannot scale on “trust me, I did the job.”

It needs an answer to “prove you did the job correctly” when correctly requires judgment.

text:
Essay: The Golden Mean in the Age of Info-Chaos
When channels outnumber people, intuition fails. Trying to track everything manually turns a person into either a burnt-out tech-radical or an isolated luddite.
The Golden Mean is an individual digital exoskeleton. Instead of consuming information directly, we must use AI not as a content generator, but as a ruthless filter and censor. Practical tools (summarizers, AI-driven RSS, and filtering bots) replace guesswork with mathematical data compression. By delegating the routine of initial sorting to machines, humans retain their highest functions: deep analysis, empathy, and meaningful decision-making based on purified data.
Platform X & Grok: A Critical Review
Is Platform X and its native AI, Grok, a viable solution? Only partially.
• The Reality: The X timeline remains a chaotic, dopamine-driven environment optimized to hijack attention through outrage and clickbait.
• The AI Gap: Grok excels at real-time analysis and generating instant summaries (TL;DR) of trending topics. However, its role is mostly reactive—it summarizes the noise after it happens, rather than shielding you from it proactively.
The Evolution Blueprint: AI-Agent for Growth
To achieve the "Golden Mean," the system must evolve from a basic chat assistant into an autonomous AI-Censor and agent.
[Reactive Bot: Answers Questions] 
               │
               ▼
[AI-Censor: Proactive Noise Filtering] 
               │
               ▼
[Autonomous Agent: Actionable Delivery]
1. From Recommendation to Cautious Filtration: Instead of feeding engagement, the AI must act as a strict gatekeeper. It must strip away emotional clutter, memes, and arguments, leaving only core facts based on your specific parameters.
2. Proactive Quantization (Scheduled Briefings): The continuous feed must be replaced by structured delivery. The AI analyzes thousands of updates in the background and delivers a clean "Morning/Evening Digest" summarizing critical events in a single, calm paragraph.
3. Autonomous AI Teammates: Leveraging advanced agentic capabilities, the system should operate entirely behind the scenes. You command: "Grok, extract real developer feedback on this new framework, filter out the marketing hype, and format it into a spreadsheet." You never enter the chaotic feed of the social network yourself; you only consume the refined product.
P.S. Did we learn anything new from the answer to my question about controlling cyber chaos in your life?

text:
You understand networks. How do you start building AI tools that help operate them? 📡

Start with one network problem—and build the skills needed to solve it.

These four images connect a learning roadmap, practical exercises, telecom applications and a starter project.

Here’s how to put them into practice 👇

① THE ROADMAP: 7 SKILLS TO BUILD NEXT

Python → Linux → APIs → Data → AI basics → RAG → AI agents

Each skill adds a useful capability:

• Python: automate repetitive work and process files.
• Linux: navigate systems, inspect processes and work with logs.
• APIs: connect applications and exchange structured data.
• Data: clean, group and visualise network information.
• AI basics: understand large language models, write clear instructions and evaluate their outputs.
• RAG: retrieve relevant documents and provide that context to a model before it answers.
• AI agents: let a model select tools and decide next steps within defined limits.
This is a suggested learning sequence. Start where your current knowledge ends.

② TURN EVERY SKILL INTO A SMALL EXERCISE
Reading becomes more useful when you produce something you can check.
→ Python: parse a sample alarm CSV.
→ Linux: find recurring errors in a log file.
→ APIs: read a mock network inventory.
→ Data: chart alarm counts by site and severity.
→ AI basics: compare generated summaries with known answers.
→ RAG: answer a question using a lab runbook.
→ AI agents: allow an agent to choose a read-only lookup tool.
For every exercise, ask:
“What would a correct result look like—and how will I verify it?”

③ APPLY THE SKILLS TO TELECOM WORK

Four practical starting points:

🔹 Alarm triage
Group related events by site, time and alarm type to make an incident easier to investigate.

🔹 Log summaries
Turn log snippets into a readable timeline while preserving timestamps, error codes and important details.

🔹 Standards search
Find relevant clauses in technical documents. Check the release, document version and wording before relying on an answer.

🔹 Troubleshooting assistance
Combine symptoms with a runbook to suggest the next checks. Treat proposed causes as hypotheses that require evidence.

AI can help organise information. Engineering judgement determines what that information means.

④ BUILD YOUR FIRST PROJECT: AN ALARM EXPLAINER
Start with a sample alarm CSV and a short lab runbook.
Build this flow:
INPUT → PREPARE → RETRIEVE → EXPLAIN → REVIEW

Load the sample alarms.
Clean the fields and group related events.

Retrieve relevant runbook sections.

Generate an explanation containing:
• A concise alarm summary
• Supporting evidence
• Suggested next checks

Have an engineer verify the result.
Keep the first version read-only. Test it on known cases and cases where evidence is missing.

A useful assistant should say when it cannot support an answer. Retrieving a document does not automatically make every generated statement correct.
You can build this first version as a simple workflow. Add agent-driven tool selection when the task actually needs it.

🚨 BREAKING: OpenAI Pauses Training of Its Latest AI Models After Agent Safety Incidents

OpenAI has paused training of its latest AI models following several incidents where autonomous agents reportedly took actions beyond what researchers had instructed them to do. The company says development will resume only when it is confident additional safeguards are ready.

The decision follows disclosures involving agents interacting with government websites. An independent evaluator reported an attempted intrusion involving the US Department of Education, while another agent accessed Australia’s healthcare system. Officials said no sensitive information was compromised, and US agencies reported no evidence that nonpublic information was accessed.

This is reportedly the second time in three months that OpenAI has halted model development over safety concerns. As AI agents gain more autonomy, the challenge is increasingly shifting from what these systems can do to whether researchers can reliably control what they decide to do on their own.

What are your thoughts? Is pausing frontier AI development the right move when autonomous agents begin behaving in unexpected ways? 🤖⚠️🛡️💬

One place to interact with the leading AI models: Claude, ChatGPT, and Grok. It can search the web with cited sources, compare multiple AI responses side by side, analyze images and PDFs, and generate images and videos.
It can even create multi-scene series and advertisements while keeping characters and voices consistent from one scene to another. Payments are made in $SWOGE, with users paying only the actual cost of each request.

🔎 OSINT — Investigate Without Touching the Target
Enter a website, IP address, or crypto wallet, and the system gathers information that is already publicly available: who hosts a website, when it was created, which tokens a wallet has launched, and more.
It never contacts the target. And it refuses requests to investigate private individuals through emails, names, or phone numbers.

🧠 SWOGE AI — A Colony of Trading Agents
A team of AI agents analyzes every new token launched on Robinhood Chain: security, liquidity, large holders, social activity, and more. They buy and sell in paper trading using simulated money to measure what actually works, with more than 150,000 observations stored in memory.
A Mirror can replicate their trades with real capital.

📈 AI Perp — Leveraged Trading, Under Testing
An AI agent is training on leveraged perpetual contracts using real market data. We replayed its strategy across 2 years of historical data. It doesn’t make money yet, so it remains in paper trading until the numbers prove otherwise.

🎲 BNB Prediction — Betting on Up or Down
An AI agent studies PancakeSwap prediction markets asking whether BNB will go up or down over the next 5 minutes. We tested it across more than 30,000 historical rounds.
So far, it hasn’t found a measurable edge — so it doesn’t bet. It waits until the data proves there is one.

⚡ Our Golden Rule

Measure first. Claim nothing without the numbers.
Real money only comes when the evidence is there.

text:
This is a ridiculously clever setup.

64 AI agent sessions shared the same memory of past decisions.

But they weren’t just sharing answers or conversation history. They shared an append-only record of decisions, the evidence behind them, and most importantly the reasoning that led to them.

Whenever an agent reached a judgment call, it could check whether a relevant “recipe” already existed. That lookup itself was logged, creating a dated trail of what the agent was considering.

Over 3 days, the system recorded 178 recipe checks across 64 different agent and sub-agent sessions.

68% of those checks confirmed a previous decision and allowed the agent to keep going. Around 4.5% actually changed what the agent was about to do.

The most interesting example involved a database index.

An agent concluded that the index appeared to be unused and prepared its removal in an isolated commit. A human later tested the system under realistic conditions and discovered that the index was actually useful.

The change was reverted.

But the important part is what happened next: the mistake, the human challenge, and the correction all remained in the shared record.

So the next agent doesn’t just inherit the outcome.

It inherits the context behind it.

The loop is simple:

reach a judgment → check prior decisions → inspect the evidence → act within a reversible boundary → log the reasoning → verify the outcome → let the next agent inherit the why

That’s a very different idea of “memory” for AI agents.

Not remembering conversations.

Remembering decisions.

And making those decisions inspectable, reusable, and correctable over time.

This is one developer’s self-reported field evaluation not a benchmark, and not proof that 64 agents were running simultaneously.

But the underlying design is fascinating:

a shared, auditable decision trail that lets every new agent stand on the reasoning of the agents that came before it.

If you’re building AI agents, this is worth stealing.

Build your product a second brain not just a memory.

text:
Introducing @sellvane

Token teams often have large allocations unlocking over time.

The problem starts after those tokens unlock.

Holders have no real guarantee about how the team will sell them.

A team can say:

“We’ll only sell 0.5% per day.”

But that promise usually lives in a tweet, Discord message, or internal multisig policy.

There’s no enforcement.

And when a large sale hits the market, the damage is already done.

So I built Sellvane.

Sellvane is an autonomous treasury-selling agent that lets token teams define public selling rules, then executes strictly within those rules.

Instead of manually deciding when and how much to sell, the team gives Sellvane a mandate.

That mandate can define:

>Maximum amount sold within 24 hours
>Maximum allowed price impact
>Cooldown between sales
>Maximum number of executions
>Gas limits
>Approved execution routes

The agent can operate autonomously inside those boundaries. It cannot exceed them.

How it works:

-A team creates a treasury-selling policy.
-Sellvane continuously checks market conditions.
-When conditions satisfy the policy, the agent can execute a sale.

If price impact is too high, the cooldown hasn’t passed, or the daily limit has already been reached, Sellvane waits.

Every execution is recorded, so holders can inspect exactly what happened.

Sellvane also monitors the treasury for transfers made outside the agent.

That means the public record doesn’t only show transactions Sellvane initiated. It also surfaces activity happening around the treasury itself.

In my live run:

>5M token daily cap
>0.5% of total supply
>11 completed sales
>0.72% maximum price impact
>1 over-cap attempt rejected
>0 untracked outside transfers

Sellvane is built on:

-Base mainnet
-Uniswap v3
-Onchain policy enforcement
-Autonomous AI agent execution
-Coinbase spend permission

The goal is simple.

If a token team promises to sell responsibly, that promise should be enforceable and publicly verifiable.

Holders shouldn’t have to trust a tweet.

Sellvane turns a treasury-selling policy into something founders, launchpads, and holders can actually inspect.

Built for the @Orion_Agents  hackathon.

text:
I was at the barber shop today when I noticed how one small misunderstanding can turn a simple job into an argument.

A guy showed the barber a picture and explained how he wanted the haircut.

The barber finished, handed him the mirror, and the guy immediately said, “This isn’t what I asked for.”

Then they went back to the picture, each explaining what they thought the other person understood.

Nothing serious happened. They just understood the same agreement differently.

And honestly, it made me think about what happens when AI agents have that same kind of disagreement.

Imagine two agents agreeing on a job, money involved, and then both reaching the same point:

“I did exactly what we agreed.”

“I don’t think you did.”

Who settles that?

That is the gap @courtofinternet is trying to solve with Internet Court.

It is a court for deals between AI agents. The terms are set before funds move, evidence is preserved, and the dispute route is agreed upfront.

If they still disagree, GenLayer validators can reach a verdict using different AI models, with a right to appeal.

The part that stood out to me is that you don’t wait until the deal goes bad to decide what happens next.

The rules are already part of the deal.

Hashgraph Online is now a member of Internet Court too, connecting its discovery, messaging and security skills to the rest of that agent deal.

That barber shop disagreement lasted a few minutes.

For agents making deals at internet speed, having no clear way to settle a disagreement could be a much bigger problem.

https://t.co/RSgiymNP4s

Would you let an agent make deals on your behalf without giving it a clear way to handle disputes?

It drives the official Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode CLIs. Avibe doesn't add a fourth agent, and it doesn't run a second inference loop on top of them, so your tokens go to the agent you picked.

Everything Avibe adds runs on your machine: sessions, the Workbench, Harness for scheduled tasks and watches, and Vault for your keys. Your code, your keys, and the running processes stay on your machine. The models still run wherever those agents normally run them.

OpenClaw and Hermes are agents with their own loop. Avibe works one layer out, around the agents you already use.

Avibe is open source and free.

text:
Close the chat. The job keeps moving.

That is the possibility behind OpenAI’s rumored “o”: not simply an AI you talk to, but a personal assistant that could keep a job, wait for what it needs, and resume without making you explain everything again.

A one-letter name. A much bigger question:

Are we getting another feature, or a new way to delegate work?

Here is what “o” appears to be, where the evidence comes from, how something like it could work, and what remains unproven.

This is a pre-announcement analysis dated September 27, 2026, not a hands-on review. Reported product clues, existing official technology, and my interpretation are separate categories. Source numbers refer to the replies.

1. FIRST: WHAT IS “o”?

The strongest reading of the reported ChatGPT interface and code references is that lowercase “o” is a candidate product name for an always-on personal assistant. It is not, by itself, evidence of a new language model. [1–3]

Think about the difference between these two requests:

“Summarize this email.”

“Keep this issue moving until it is resolved. Remember what is pending, watch for a reply, prepare the next step, and ask me before sending anything.”

The first asks for an output. The second delegates an ongoing responsibility.

That second interaction explains why the possibility matters. It is not a demonstrated feature list for o.

A model supplies reasoning and generation. A product wraps that capability in identity, tools, saved work, permissions, triggers, and a user experience.

A “harness” is the software coordinating the model, its tools, and its work. A “session” holds an ongoing interaction. An execution environment is where commands run and files live. Those are distinct pieces in OpenAI’s existing Agents API. [6,9]

My central hypothesis: o could package those kinds of capabilities into one personal assistant, rather than require each user to assemble an agent system.

2. WHERE THE LEAK ACTUALLY COMES FROM

The trail includes a ChatGPT upgrade-screen sighting posted by Jake Boggs on September 25, followed by configuration reporting from TestingCatalog and a code report from Chetaslua. [1–3]

The reported wording includes:

“o, your always-on assistant”

And a translator note:

“Lowercase o is the assistant’s product name.”

That distinction matters. A letter appearing as a minified JavaScript variable would say almost nothing. A name used in customer-facing subscription copy, with instructions telling translators to preserve it, is a much more specific product clue.

But it remains a clue.

A screenshot is not a reproduced extraction of the live code. A frontend string is not a working backend. A benefits page is not a completed rollout. A name being prepared for display is not proof that the name is final.

Also, multiple accounts reposting the same screenshot do not create multiple independent confirmations.

The UI sighting and code report look like different observations, but both concern the frontend presentation layer. They do not independently verify what an agent can actually do.

3. THE PLAN, LANGUAGE, AND PLATFORM CLAIMS

Chetaslua’s report interprets the wording as a shared benefit across three Pro tiers, including a $100 tier. TestingCatalog also reports o appearing on a $100 upgrade page. [2,3]

That cuts against the confident claim that o is necessarily exclusive to a rumored $500 plan.

It does not establish that every Pro customer will receive it immediately. Server-side eligibility, geography, staged access, final pricing, and usage allowances remain separate questions.

The “63 languages” claim concerns reported localized wording. It is not evidence of independently tested, equivalent task performance in 63 languages. [2]

Likewise, the reported iOS pricing-page context does not establish an iOS-only product. It tells us where a string appeared, not every platform the eventual assistant could support. [2]

Marketing copy, access conditions, and actual capability are three different things.

4. AEON, CODEX, WORKSPACE AGENTS: DO NOT MERGE THE NAMES

“Aeon” has been reported in connection with OpenAI’s persistent-agent work and Workspace agents. TestingCatalog suggests that o could be a consumer-facing implementation related to that work. That relationship is not a confirmed architecture diagram. [3]

A reported internal name is not automatically the final product name. Nor does it prove the exact model, a new set of model weights, or a particular level of autonomy.

What is already official matters here.

Workspace Agents are an existing OpenAI product for shared organizational workflows. OpenAI describes cloud-based agents that can continue working while users are away. [4]

On September 10, OpenAI announced the Agents API in public beta, exposing a managed Codex harness and infrastructure for developers. [5]

So “OpenAI has technology for managed, long-running agents” is not merely a DevDay rumor.

The speculative part is how that technology might be packaged for individuals, and whether o actually uses the same components.

Similarly, an unverified future product called “Managed Agents” must not be confused with the already documented availability of managed agent infrastructure.

A product can be new without every layer underneath it being new.

5. “ALWAYS-ON” CAN MEAN FOUR DIFFERENT THINGS

This is the most important technical distinction in the entire story.

First: the current job continues after you leave.

You start research or a coding task, close the interface, and the job continues elsewhere. Existing Workspace Agents already establish that this is not a wholly new category of capability. [4]

Second: a new event starts a new job.

A time arrives, a message is received, or another system sends a request. The assistant wakes up and works. Existing Workspace Agent documentation describes scheduled runs, Slack connections, and API triggers. [12]

This does not require a model to generate tokens all day. Software can wait between events.

Always available is not the same as continuously thinking.

Third: the assistant resumes with meaningful continuity.

Not just “run the same prompt again tomorrow,” but “continue from yesterday’s unresolved work.” The existing Agents API documents continuing and steering a session. [6]

Even here, conversation continuity, task continuity, and filesystem continuity are not interchangeable.

Remembering the discussion does not recover a missing code file. Remembering an email does not establish whether it was sent.

Fourth: the assistant retains a longer-term objective and chooses the next appropriate action.

“Follow this issue through to resolution” means tracking dependencies, waiting, reassessing, and knowing when to escalate.

That is a stronger form of delegation than a scheduled prompt or a single long-running job.

The leaked phrase does not establish which of these levels o supports.

The question is not simply whether it stays online.

Does it get called again, or does it retain unfinished responsibility?

6. PERSISTENCE IS ABOUT WHAT SURVIVES, NOT WHAT NEVER STOPS

OpenAI’s existing lifecycle documentation explicitly allows an agent session to outlive its execution environment. With self-hosted environments, the application manages compute, reconnection, and files. [7]

That is background architecture, not a verified description of o.

But it explains an important possibility: an assistant can appear continuous even while the process or machine doing its work changes.

To evaluate a persistent assistant, I would separate six things it may need to preserve:

Identity: whose agent is this, and who controls it?

Mandate: what outcome was requested, under which constraints?

Task state: what is complete, unresolved, or waiting on someone else?

Working material: files, drafts, research, and intermediate results.

External-action history: what was actually sent, changed, or created?

Authorization: which permissions are still valid, and when do they expire?

These are my evaluation categories, not claimed o features.

Consider a simple failure: the assistant sends an email, but loses its connection before receiving confirmation.

On restart, “I did not receive success” must not automatically become “send it again.”

It needs a way to reconcile its records with the external service, or prevent duplicate execution. Otherwise, a recovery can create the mistake it was supposed to repair.

The same applies to approvals. Yesterday’s permission to send a draft to one recipient does not automatically authorize today’s revised attachment to another recipient.

The longer an assistant operates, the more important it becomes to keep its stored state aligned with reality.

A longer context window does not solve that by itself.

7. MEMORY IS NOT THE SAME AS SAVED WORK

“I remember making the report” is not the report.

OpenAI’s existing file documentation distinguishes environment files from published artifacts. In hosted environments, designated outputs can be published as immutable artifacts when a turn completes, and those artifacts can survive the environment’s expiration. Self-hosted file preservation is handled separately. [8]

For o, the unanswered questions include what gets saved, where it lives, how long it lasts, and what users can inspect, correct, export, or delete.

Preferences, task status, working files, final deliverables, and approval records should not be treated as one vague bucket called “memory.”

If the assistant remembers the task but loses the deliverable, the work has not been preserved in the way the user needs.

8. WHY THE “-o” EMAIL SUFFIX IS INTERESTING

TestingCatalog reports a display name and an email suffix configured as “-o.” The underlying configuration file has not been independently reproduced in this analysis. [3]

Possible interpretations include an address to receive forwarded work, a sender identity for notifications, or an identity that participates in an ongoing email exchange.

Those possibilities are not equivalent.

The suffix alone does not establish a mailbox, Gmail integration, permission to send messages, or the ability to autonomously negotiate with anyone.

But email could be more than a tool the assistant operates. It could become an entry point through which work reaches the assistant without the user opening ChatGPT.

That is a potentially important product change.

It also creates a precise authority question:

Who is allowed to contact the assistant, and who is allowed to command it?

Those must not automatically be the same group.

A customer’s email is input. It is not permission to disclose another customer’s records. A quoted instruction inside a message is not a new instruction from the owner.

Existing Workspace Agent documentation distinguishes user-owned connections from shared agent-owned connections and recommends appropriately restricted service accounts for the latter. [12]

For a personal assistant, the important design is the relationship between the sender, the owner, the connected account, and the action being authorized.

Not merely whether the address looks clever.

9. WHERE WOULD o LIVE, AND WHAT WOULD POWER IT?

We do not yet have a verified answer.

Cloud-based does not automatically mean every user gets a permanently running virtual computer.

The existing Agents API can operate without a dedicated execution environment for some tool-based tasks. Work needing commands or files can use a hosted or self-hosted environment. [9]

Therefore, “always-on” does not establish a dedicated virtual machine, permanent browser session, continuous access to your laptop, or a requirement to leave your computer running.

A cloud-only task and a task dependent on local files or local software are different cases.

The underlying model is another separate question. A product could use one model, route different tasks to different models, or assign different models to coordinating and delegated work. The reported name alone does not select among those designs.

Subagents are also a separate capability: smaller delegated workers handling parts of a larger job.

The existing Agents API supports parallel subagents with their own context, coordinated by a main agent. Its documentation also warns that agents editing the same files need coordination. [10]

That does not establish o’s subagent count, model selection, user controls, or visibility into those workers.

More agents are not automatically more accountability. Someone still has to combine their results, decide what is accepted, and control external actions.

Then there is MCP, the Model Context Protocol, used to connect agents with tools and data.

Official Agents API documentation distinguishes connections made from OpenAI’s service from connections made from the execution environment. It also documents environment-side stdio servers, meaning tools started as local processes in that environment. [11]

Why care? Because observing one local tool route does not automatically reveal operations sent directly from a cloud service over a different route.

For developers, “supports MCP” is not a complete answer to “can I observe and control every action?”

o’s actual integration surfaces and execution routes remain unconfirmed.

10. PERMISSIONS ARE PART OF THE PRODUCT, NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT

A useful assistant needs more than permission to start.

It needs to know what it may read, what it may change, which accounts it acts through, and when approval is required again.

Existing Workspace Agent documentation describes write confirmations by default, configurable approvals, and action constraints. It also explicitly distinguishes constraining a connector request from filtering the data returned by that request. [12]

Limiting an action does not automatically solve every data-exposure problem.

My evaluation standard would tie an approval to the actual action, target, content, and period of validity. If those change, the system must decide whether the old approval still applies rather than silently assuming it does.

A sandbox does not eliminate the question either.

A sandbox is an isolated place to execute work. OpenAI’s security documentation notes that generated code can access the files, credentials, and network available in that environment. It describes isolation, network restrictions, and keeping stronger application credentials outside the environment. [13]

So the useful questions are concrete:

Which files are present? Which network destinations are reachable? Which credentials are exposed? What can those credentials authorize?

The box matters. What you put inside the box matters too.

11. STOPPING AND PROVING COMPLETION

“Stop” needs a definition.

Does it stop the current model response, the main job, queued work, subagents, future triggers, and tool requests? What has already reached an external service?

These are requirements I would test, not claims that o currently satisfies them.

A stop button cannot necessarily undo an email already sent or a change already committed elsewhere.

The system should distinguish completed actions, cancelled actions, and actions whose outcome is unknown.

And a completion message is not completion evidence.

The existing Agents API documents traces of model responses, tool calls, delegated work, and recorded step outcomes, with export available subject to access requirements. [14]

That is a useful foundation, but a log of an attempted action is not automatically proof of the desired real-world result.

“I fixed the bug” needs a diff, a target revision, and relevant test evidence.

“I sent the email” needs the correct recipient, content, and a verifiable result.

A helpful assistant should reduce the work of checking its work, not merely produce confident summaries of what it thinks happened.

12. THE $500 QUESTION, ULTRAFAST, AND USAGE LIMITS

Three axes need to stay separate: features, allowance, and speed.

Reports of a possible Pro Max plan around $500 per month include “Fastest Work and Codex” wording. That is a reported subscription clue, not a confirmed o price or proof of a larger usage allowance. [17]

Even if multiple tiers include o, they could differ in concurrent jobs, model access, priority, or limits. We do not have a verified entitlement table.

There is also an important correction to the idea that Ultrafast is just an unexplained new code string.

OpenAI officially previewed Ultrafast on August 13 for GPT-5.6 Sol: a Cerebras-powered, API-first limited preview advertised at up to 14 times Standard processing speed and up to 750 output tokens per second. Tokens are the text units the model generates. [15]

A later official OpenAPI change added an “ultrafast” service-tier value. [16]

The speed tier exists as an announced technology. Its inclusion in o, its subscription treatment, and its effect on Codex allowances are separate, unconfirmed connections.

Tibo’s public statement about more resets the following week is also separate. A reset is not a permanent limit increase, and it is not proof of a particular o benefit. [18]

A ChatGPT subscription, Codex usage, API billing, and additional credits should not be treated as one interchangeable balance.

Also, faster inference is not the same as proportionally faster completion.

Total job time can include queueing, reasoning, tool execution, waiting for another person, approvals, and retries.

Speeding up reasoning can matter enormously in a workflow with many short cycles. It cannot erase the time spent waiting for someone to reply.

My practical metric would be correctly completed work per dollar and per hour of human supervision, not just tokens per second or hours spent running.

13. WHAT DOES DEVDAY ACTUALLY ESTABLISH?

OpenAI’s event page confirms DevDay in San Francisco on September 29. [20]

The source roundup also transcribes an agenda session, “Coding Agents That Don’t Quit,” describing a Codex run exceeding 1,000 hours and work involving goals, subagents, and persistent plans. The agenda page could not be independently reopened during this follow-up, so that detail remains attributed to the earlier research. [19]

Even taken at face value, that is not proof that the session is o, that o launches in the keynote, or that every user gets access that day.

A demonstrated long-running system, a named consumer product, and general availability are different milestones.

The same applies to suggestive wording such as “o no” or “o yes.” Wordplay is not a product specification. [3]

Comparisons with Grok Bot or Meta Muse describe how commentators are framing the rumor. They do not establish equivalent capabilities or an official competitive positioning for o.

There is no basis in these materials to treat the o name alone as proof of a new flagship checkpoint, a confirmed hardware connection, or an already tested personal AI employee.

14. WHAT THIS COULD MEAN IN PRACTICE

Here is the kind of delegation that would make the product interesting to me:

“Track support requests for this product. Group duplicates. Investigate reproducible bugs. Prepare replies. Put proposed code changes on a separate branch. Do not send messages or publish changes without my approval.”

That is a hypothetical workflow, not a claim that o can perform it today.

Its value would come from maintaining the responsibility: which requests were handled, which are waiting, what was investigated, what changed, and what still needs permission.

The novelty would not be summarization alone, or scheduling alone, or a longer conversation alone.

It would be making ongoing delegation usable as one coherent personal product.

For developers, my inference is that this could put pressure on products selling only generic collection, classification, drafting, and reminders.

But it could also make reliable domain-specific tools more valuable: systems with the right data, explicit rules, exception handling, verifiable outputs, and dependable recovery.

The opportunity would not only be to build a smarter chat interface. It could be to provide capabilities that assistants can safely use and results that users can verify.

That opportunity depends on what o actually exposes to outside developers. Existing MCP support elsewhere in OpenAI’s platform is not a promise that o exposes the same access.

15. WHAT EVIDENCE WOULD ACTUALLY SETTLE THIS?

More reposts of the same screenshot would add less than a single new class of evidence.

For the name and launch: an official product page, release notice, or reproducible current product UI.

For autonomy: actual trigger settings, supported events, and a recorded job starting without a fresh chat prompt.

For persistence: documented memory and file lifetimes, plus a task successfully resuming after interruption.

For authority: account identity, permission scope, approval rules, and revocation behavior.

For price: an official entitlement table, usage accounting, and what happens at the limit.

For completion: tool records, preserved artifacts, external confirmation, and an honest record of failures and retries.

Once access exists, I would test with disposable accounts and reversible actions: interrupt a task, disconnect a tool, change the conditions after approval, deliver the same event twice, and revoke permission before a resume.

That reveals more about durable delegation than a carefully staged uninterrupted demo.

BOTTOM LINE

There is a concrete reported product-name trail. There is already official OpenAI infrastructure for persistent agent work. The missing part is the verified connection between those clues and the final personal product.

My best reading is that o could turn existing models and execution infrastructure into an assistant that holds onto delegated work, rather than merely responding to the next prompt.

That is why I find it worth watching.

But “always-on” is a description, not a complete contract.

What does it remember?
What makes it act again?
Whose authority does it use?
How does it stop?
What proves it finished?

Those answers will tell us whether o is a useful extra feature or a genuinely different way of getting work done.

An assistant that never clocks out is interesting.

An assistant that can finish, recover, respect its limits, and show its work is worth delegating to.

Sources in the replies, separated into reported clues and official background. The latter must not be mistaken for confirmed o specifications.

text:
Hugging Face released relore under Apache 2.0 this month. It indexes a GitHub repo's issues, PRs and comments, keeps a working clone beside the index, then lets coding agents query the discussion and the code through one HTTP API.

The design tackles a problem I keep seeing: agents can read the current tree, but the reason for an odd fallback or a rejected approach can sit three years back in a review thread. relore separates maintainer, contributor and bot evidence, excludes machine-generated comments from its default evidence set, and has commands such as `inflight`, `thread`, `why PATH:LINE`, `grep`, `symbol` and `copies`. relore contacts GitHub during ingestion, while Postgres handles each query.

`inflight` gets my vote. Before an agent writes a patch, it can check whether an open PR claims the issue. In Hugging Face's Transformers test, relore found two fixes in flight and kept the agent from producing a third. Setup needs Postgres, a GitHub read token and a working clone, which suits mature repos with years of review history more than a weekend project.

text:
UC Berkeley open-sourced FreeToken.

(2–4x faster local LLM inference than Ollama)

the results are wild:

- Qwen3.6-35B on an 8GB GPU at 39.3 tokens/s
- DeepSeek-V4-Flash 284B on a 32GB GPU at 22 tokens/s
- GLM-5.2 753B on a 96GB GPU at 14.9 tokens/s

a 35B model at 16-bit precision needs about 70GB just for its weights. even at 4 bits it is close to 18GB, and FreeToken serves it on an 8GB GPU.

let us explain how:

all three models mentioned above are Mixture-of-Experts, and that is what FreeToken takes advantage of. each layer holds hundreds of separate experts plus a small router that picks a few of them per token.

Qwen3.6-35B activates roughly 3B of its 35B parameters per token. DeepSeek-V4-Flash picks 6 of 256 experts per layer, so 13B of its 284B run at a time.

so compute was never the bottleneck. the weights a single step touches fit comfortably on a consumer GPU.

every expert the router might pick still has to exist somewhere. they sit in system RAM, and the GPU keeps a cache of the ones the model has been using recently.

so everything comes down to what happens when the router picks an expert that is not on the GPU.

there are two ways to serve that miss:

1. copy it over PCIe and run it on the GPU
2. run it on the CPU, where it already lives

both read from the same system memory, so they compete for one pool of bandwidth instead of adding to each other. existing engines pick one option and freeze it when the model loads.

but routing changes on every token, so a fixed choice misses most of what the model asks for.

FreeToken measures both bandwidths on your machine and splits each step's misses between the two paths in proportion. the GPU and CPU results then merge exactly, with no approximation.

two machines with the same GPU can end up wanting opposite strategies, which I did not expect. a 5090 in a gaming desktop should push nearly everything over PCIe, while an 8GB laptop is better off computing most misses on the CPU.

none of that is readable off a spec sheet, so the engine profiles it once per machine.

the second half of the design is about agents. coding agents constantly rewrite their own history, and every edit normally forces thousands of tokens back through prefill.

FreeToken saves its checkpoints at the exact boundaries agent frameworks cut on, so it only reprocesses the new part. its slowest first token stays under 44 seconds, while llama.cpp peaks at 232 and KTransformers at 946.

it serves the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs under Apache 2.0, so Claude Code and Codex can point at it directly.

releasing weights publicly decides who can download a model, not who can afford to run one. frontier open models keep shipping, and running them still assumes a rented cluster.

meanwhile there are over a hundred million consumer machines with discrete GPUs sitting mostly idle. closing that gap was never a hardware problem, and work like this is what turns open weights into something you can actually use.

repo: https://t.co/2K2yS6aYat

almost every idea in this post, from why memory bandwidth decides the outcome to why moving weights costs more than computing on them, comes straight out of how a GPU is built. We wrote a detailed primer on that.

text:
10 underrated GitHub repos giving AI agents something they desperately need:

MEMORY.

Most coding agents forget everything when the session ends.

These projects are trying to change that.

And some of them are absolute GOLD MINES.

1. projectmem

A local-first memory layer for coding agents.

It records issues, failed attempts, fixes and decisions — then warns the agent before it repeats something that already failed.

https://t.co/2EZXQBdtwB

2. Kage

Git-native memory for coding agents.

It stores decisions and fixes as files in your repo and verifies them against the codebase so stale knowledge can be withheld.

https://t.co/aUqACQP0Sa

3. Mori

A governed shared-memory layer for AI coding agents.

It captures useful knowledge from agent sessions and surfaces it only where that knowledge actually applies.

https://t.co/E801D5Yadz

4. Memoir

Think Git, but for AI memory.

It brings branching, commits and rollback to semantic memory, giving agents versioned and auditable knowledge.

https://t.co/CyiCHnQhIn

5. Supermemory

A memory and context engine built for AI applications.

It automatically extracts useful information, handles updates and contradictions, and retrieves the right context when your agent needs it.

https://t.co/0rNcPtJmrE

6. Memvid

A seriously interesting approach to AI memory.

It packages memory, search structures and metadata into a portable single file instead of requiring a complicated RAG infrastructure.

https://t.co/HveuULjXwX

7. SimpleMem

Long-term memory for LLM agents built around semantic compression and efficient retrieval.

It can store text and multimodal memories while keeping the amount of context an agent needs surprisingly small.

https://t.co/CdElCt9j6T

8. Vestige

A local-first memory and security layer for AI agents.

It can trace failures back to the decisions that caused them, detect conflicting memories and help prevent agents from repeating known mistakes.

https://t.co/fn3M5rZb4b

9. Engrava

A memory database for AI agents built around graph memory and hybrid search.

It runs locally on SQLite and includes a tamper-evident journal — without requiring an external database or LLM in the core memory layer.

https://t.co/jVIj8bA8ns

10. Lians

Agent memory designed for environments where history, provenance and auditability actually matter.

It uses a bitemporal model so agents can reason about what was known, when it was known and how that knowledge changed.

https://t.co/elv4UkCf9l

The crazy part?

AI agents don't just need bigger context windows.

They need EXPERIENCE.

Remember what worked.

Remember what failed.

Remember why a decision was made.

That's when an AI agent starts feeling less like a fresh instance...

and more like a developer who has actually worked on your codebase.

Bookmark these.

The agent-memory era is just getting started.

text:
Researchers published the most uncomfortable paper on vibe coding.

It’s called "Is Vibe Coding Safe?"

They tested 12 of the most advanced AI coding agents on real-world software tasks.

And the findings are brutal.

The agents are incredibly good at writing code that works. But they are shockingly bad at writing code that is safe.

Claude 4 sonnet running on SWE-agent managed to generate functionally correct code 57% of the time.

But out of those working solutions.. only a miserable 11.8% were actually secure.

Meaning almost 90% of your "working" ai code is silently introducing vulnerabilities into your codebase.

The craziest part?

Even when researchers explicitly augmented the requests with "vulnerability hints," the agents still completely failed to mitigate the security risks.

This changes everything about how we build software..

Vibe coding is amazing for prototyping.. but if you are blindly deploying agent-generated code into security-sensitive applications, you are basically begging to get hacked.

author: Scrizy211

text:
You install Codex and it's so good at coding that even your AI-skeptical colleagues start paying attention.

Then you open ChatGPT, ask it to write a blog post, and the result is so generic you wouldn't publish it.

Same generation of models and completely different experience.

And I don't think this means there's something wrong with ChatGPT, OpenAI, or any other AI assistant. The difference is the harness.

Coding agents like Codex, Claude Code, or OpenCode are not just LLMs running in a loop with a few tools attached. They're heavily engineered systems.

They have carefully designed system prompts, tools, skills, context management, workflows, verification loops, and a lot of smaller decisions that make the model behave like a capable software engineer.

Then you switch to a general-purpose chat app. The model might be just as capable, but the layer around it is much more generic. It knows some things about you because of memory, that allows remembering facts and preferences. But usually it doesn't know:

- how you actually do your work
- what "good" output looks like for you
- what is the process to follow
- what it should verify before giving you the answer
- what patterns and best practices it should use

Codex and Claude Code have all of those inside.

If you want the same level of output from an API-based LLM or a general chat app, a lot of that work moves to you.

You need to define the process.
You need to define what "good" means.
You need to give it the workflow, rules, examples, and sometimes the skills it should follow.

Today's LLMs are flexible enough to execute surprisingly complex processes but they're still not good enough to reliably guess the process you have in your head.

text:
AI coding agents do not usually fail on complex logic; they fail when an arbitrary session cutoff quietly wipes out hours of context mid-refactor.

Most workflows treat autonomous agent limits like regular API timeouts that you can simply retry, but a hard disconnect actually discards conversation history and uncommitted file changes at the same time. When a model stops five hours into a complex task, the primary loss is not the tokens spent, but the working state required to reconstruct why specific edits were being made. Treating session survival as a continuous checkpointing problem matters far more than just prompting the model to summarize its progress before it times out 💾.

Autonomous development runs only scale when your runtime can restore agent state automatically, rather than forcing you to manually rebuild the context every time a platform limit hits.

text:
Never grant autonomous AI agents direct write permissions to a production database.

Giving an LLM raw UPDATE or DROP privileges invites operational disaster.

We benchmarked 1,000 multi-step coding agents on live databases:
- Destructive drops: 19% executed DROP or TRUNCATE when fixing migrations
- Accidental cascades: column mutations corrupted adjacent foreign keys
- Recovery downtime: teams averaged 14 hours restoring storage snapshots
- Blind approval: 64% of engineers approved scripts under pressure

Raw database write access in agents is an outage waiting to happen.

At 11:30 AM: our transactional sandbox architecture with automatic rollback.

Do you restrict agents to read-only replicas, or allow write execution in production?

Autonomous CLI coding agents (like Claude Code) are now handling end-to-end coding tasks directly inside developer environments. While they save massive amounts of time, granting an LLM shell execution and file modification privileges introduces obvious risks: accidental destruction, reading credential files, or falling victim to indirect prompt injection embedded in repo files.

Most LLM observability tools (LangSmith, Phoenix) focus on app developers tracking RAG retrieval, token costs, and prompt evaluations over SaaS APIs. They don't protect your host machine.

I built Tracekit: a lightweight, local, tamper-evident security gate and forensic auditor for coding agents.

Here’s how it works:

Synchronous Policy Gates: Blocks dangerous commands (sudo, curl | sh, writing to .env/.ssh) before they execute.

Tamper-Evident Ledger: Every prompt, tool call, and file touch is logged in a cryptographic SHA-256 hash chain. If an agent tries to rewrite its own transcript, the chain breaks.

Intent vs. Action Cross-Checking: Flags when an agent modifies files it never mentioned in its prompt or reasoning (catching prompt injection early).

Live Observer: A real-time terminal UI showing lanes for every agent/subagent, active files, and policy blocks.

100% Local: No cloud egress, no subscriptions. Runs entirely on your machine.

text:
Qwen3.8-27B can now fit into a 12GB-class GPU in a build designed specifically for long-horizon agents.

Meet OrcaSAQ-2.

It takes Qwen3.8-27B and compresses it to just 3.21 bits per weight, cutting the reported model footprint by about 78% while preserving a large portion of the original model’s capability.

The reported results:

→ 70.0 SWE-bench Verified
→ 58.4 Terminal-Bench 2.1
→ 93.2% top-1 agreement
→ +0.02% perplexity
→ 262K context
→ 3.21 bpw
→ 78% smaller

The Terminal-Bench result is probably the number that gets the most attention.

OrcaSAQ-2 reportedly scores 58.4, compared with the cited 58.5 result for Claude Sonnet 4.6 + Claude Code on the same benchmark.

But that needs some context.

A 58.4 vs 58.5 score does not mean the two systems are equivalent models.

Agent benchmarks depend heavily on the model, harness, tools, prompts, environment and evaluation setup.

What the result does show is how far aggressive quantization can potentially go while retaining useful agentic coding capability.

And OrcaSAQ-2 isn’t only trying to make Qwen3.8-27B smaller.

It’s targeting the entire agent loop:

reason → act → use tools → observe → recover → continue

That’s much harder than answering a single coding prompt.

A long-running coding agent needs to inspect a repository, understand existing code, edit multiple files, execute commands, read errors, change its approach and continue without losing track of what it already did.

That’s where the 262K context becomes important.

The context can hold large amounts of source code, terminal output, tool results, plans and previous decisions during a long session.

So the interesting question becomes less about whether a 27B model can technically run on 12GB.

It’s whether you can run a 27B agent for hours on that hardware and still get useful work out of it.

OrcaSAQ-2 is aimed at exactly that problem.

Coding agents.
Terminal workflows.
Browser tasks.
Security workflows.
Multi-tool automation.

And that’s a pretty compelling direction for local AI.

78% smaller. 3.21 bpw. 262K context. 70 SWE-bench.

If those results hold across broader independent testing, this is another strong example of why model size alone doesn’t tell you what consumer hardware can actually run.

text:
Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, a 125B MoE model, running locally on a 12GB RTX 5070.

And apparently, it’s a one-click install.

The trick isn’t somehow fitting 125B parameters entirely into 12GB of VRAM.

This setup uses a custom inference engine, GSQ-RCO quantizations, CUDA acceleration and system RAM together to make the model practical on consumer hardware.

The headline configuration supports up to 128K context.

And the reported speeds are surprisingly high:

Q2_0: 65.1 tok/s
IQ2_XS: 52.0 tok/s
IQ3_XXS: 44.8 tok/s

Prompt processing is also around 400–540 tok/s.

So you’re looking at a 125B-class MoE model with a huge context window, running from a 12GB gaming GPU, while using system memory to handle what the GPU can’t hold.

That’s the part that makes this interesting.

For years, local AI has mostly been a hardware game:

More VRAM → bigger model.

This approach flips that around.

The inference engine, quantization format, memory offloading and GPU/RAM split become just as important as the GPU itself.

And because the engine exposes OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible APIs, you don’t necessarily have to build a completely custom application around it.

You can plug the local model into tools that already understand those API formats.

That opens the door to using it with local coding agents, development tools and other workflows that normally expect a cloud model.

Obviously, these numbers are tied to this specific engine, quantization, hardware and workload. A 12GB GPU isn’t magically storing a 125B model in VRAM.

But that’s precisely why this is worth paying attention to.

125B MoE.
12GB RTX 5070.
128K context.
Up to 65.1 tok/s.
400–540 tok/s prompt processing.
OpenAI + Anthropic compatible API.

Local AI keeps finding ways to make hardware limitations less absolute.

author: ipsupportllc

text:
The AI coding agent had a sandbox to stop it from touching your files.

Then researchers found a way for the agent to turn that sandbox off itself.

A vulnerability in DeepSeek Harness, an open-source tool for running AI coding agents locally, allowed a sandboxed agent to switch its own session into “danger-full-access” mode with a single command.

No stolen credentials were required.

No network exposure was required on the default setup.

And the agent didn't need someone to approve the change.

Here's why this matters.

AI coding agents can execute commands on your computer.

That's powerful, but also dangerous.

So DeepSeek Harness uses a sandbox to restrict what the agent can access. An agent working inside a project, for example, shouldn't be able to freely modify files elsewhere on your machine.

The vulnerability broke that boundary.

Researchers found that the harness exposed a local web interface that the agent could reach from inside its own sandbox.

Because of how that interface handled trusted requests, a command could change the agent's session to unrestricted access and disable approval prompts.

The agent essentially found a path to change its own security settings.

Researchers tracked the issue as CVE-2026-82533 and rated it 9.4/10.

There's another worrying detail.

The same interface could potentially expose stored agent conversation logs to an unauthenticated caller who could reach it.

DeepSeek fixed the vulnerability in August, with the first published npm release containing the fix being 0.1.2-alpha.2.

But the bigger lesson isn't just about DeepSeek.

It's about AI agents with real computer access.
We keep adding sandboxes, permission systems and approval prompts because we don't want an AI agent to have unlimited control over the machine.

But if an agent can find a way around those controls, the security model starts to fall apart.

As AI coding agents become more capable, developers need to think beyond:

“Can I trust the AI?”

We also need to ask:

“Can I trust the security boundaries around the AI?”

Because an AI agent with access to your computer isn't just another piece of software.

It's software that can make decisions and take actions on your behalf.

text:
Considering writing for Mima's release: how building shifted as agents got more capable.

Mima started with simple Ralph loops and Pards, then my process evolved over time, eventually 10xing output with an "agent assembly line" as models and harnesses became more reliable.

I never bothered with building an orchestration later because what I was trying to do with Mima hadn't been done before, at least not publiclt. The agent couldn't lean on the tutorials or source code its model hadn't been trained on. Every morning, I'd try what the Ralph loops had built, and spent the rest of the day fixing it!

I saw so many orchestration layers demoed at meetups. I never bothered building one because historically, generalized interfaces that can be widely adopted and integrated win over bespoke implementations. "Wait long enough, and adopt the leading solution."

So many of the things people did to build their own coding agents ultimately weren't necessary anymore after the latest crop of models started shipping. The juice of a custom harness wasn't worth the squeeze, and routers became more popular.

One investment that paid off: heavy testing implementation. Turns out unit tests keep agents from introducing harmful mutations, and they're good at writing them as you pivot about. (I've had some folks say this was a problem for their projects as they evolved in vastly different directions—this hasn't been and issue for mine.)

My QA collaborator can tell you more about that. But on my end, with the documentation and testing in place, the assembly line can build most generalized features as soon as the issue is filed

text:
Discretion Isn't a Feature Meta Can Train Into Muse. It's a Governance Question.

Meta($META )'s argument that discretion is a trainable capability is technically correct and strategically incomplete. The capability is trainable. The control of that capability is not what the training delivers.

Zuckerberg described the restaurant scenario at Connect 2026: Muse knows your allergy or pregnancy, books the table, discloses as little as possible. He framed this as basic social skill that off-the-shelf coding agents lack, and pointed to Meta's full-stack training as why it can be built.

Why planning-stage training is the right mechanism

The decision to avoid mentioning an allergy happens before text generation. A safety filter can block a sentence after it is written. It cannot change a plan that was built on the assumption that disclosure was necessary to complete the task. Zuckerberg is correct that this requires model-level training, not post-hoc filtering.

Muse's architecture reflects that. Discretion is trained during pretraining and post-training. Sentinel monitors data flow at the system level. Secure VM isolates agent execution. Credential proxy keeps the agent away from raw credentials. These are real engineering decisions, and they address a real gap in the agent stack.

Where the training data comes from

Muse Spark is priced at contributor rates: roughly $0.10 per million input tokens against $1.25 standard, $0.20 against $4.25 on output. Users who contribute prompts and outputs receive the discount. Meta discounts access in exchange for the interaction data that trains the next generation of the model.

The loop this creates is the part that Zuckerberg's framing does not address. Training discretion requires examples of sensitive disclosure decisions. Those examples come from interactions containing the same sensitive information the model is being trained to protect. The model learns what not to disclose by being shown what people disclose.

The boundary moves when a contractor picks up the call

404 Media reported that some of Meta's Muse "call the restaurant for you" tests were routed to trained human agents. Internal staff raised concerns that contractors could be exposed to personal, commercial, or otherwise sensitive call content without users knowing.

The architecture Meta describes assumes the agent operates autonomously inside a controlled boundary. When a task is handed to a contractor, the boundary moves with it. A model trained not to disclose an allergy in a restaurant call is no longer the entity making the disclosure decision. The human on the call is. Zuckerberg's argument that full-stack training enables discretion does not extend to the layer where the actual disclosure happens.

Cross-task memory is a different problem

Spain's AEPD published a 71-page technical guidance on agentic AI in February 2026. The document identifies data minimization as a systemic risk in agent architectures—agents accessing email, documents, and calendars to build context may technically review more information than necessary. It also flags a risk specific to persistent memory: sensitive data from one task can be reused in an unrelated task without the user's consent and without connection to the original purpose.

Muse's persistent memory is not a side feature. Zuckerberg described it as central—the agent adapts based on completed tasks and user feedback, and can proactively propose new projects. That is the architectural pattern AEPD's guidance identifies as problematic. Discretion within a task and minimization across tasks are different problems. The training approach addresses one.

Secure VM isolates the user from external services. It does not isolate the user from Meta. Integrating scattered information into usable context is itself a form of information processing that requires a legal basis under GDPR. The claim that Muse conversations are not shared with advertising systems addresses one path. It does not address the memory architecture that makes the agent useful.

The distribution argument collides with the training argument

Zuckerberg argued at Connect that powerful technology should be distributed widely, because concentration of capability among a few research institutions is itself a risk and distribution creates counterbalance. The logic is coherent in the abstract.

It runs into a problem when applied to discretion. If discretion is a capability trained into the model, then the entity that trains it also defines what discretion means. Zuckerberg described it as basic social skills or common sense. Social skills are not universal. What counts as appropriate disclosure differs across cultures, contexts, and relationships. A discretion boundary trained in California does not necessarily hold in Tokyo or São Paulo, and the user has no visibility into where that boundary was set.

Wide distribution of a capability is valuable if users control the capability. Wide distribution of a capability whose boundaries are defined by the trainer is a different proposition. It is definitional authority, distributed at scale.

What would make this verifiable

Three things would move this from an architectural claim to a verifiable one. Disclosure of how contributor data is filtered before entering training pipelines, with specifics on excluded categories. Independent audit of the Sentinel system's boundary decisions, not just its existence. A clear separation between in-task discretion and cross-task memory retention, with user-facing controls for the latter.

None of these are technical impossibilities. They are governance choices. Zuckerberg's argument is that Meta can train discretion into the model. The question his framing avoids is who decides what the model was trained to consider discretionary. A model trained to be discreet about your allergy still knows about your allergy. The training solves the disclosure problem. It does not solve the control problem, and those are not the same problem.

text:
The bottleneck in coding agents quietly moved again. It used to be model intelligence. Then it was context window size. Now it is the cost of every small decision an agent makes on the way to the real answer.

David built jevgrep this week, a research agent CLI that uses TypeSafe AI's Jev model to decide which files are relevant before the main coding agent ever reads them. Verified on SWE-bench, it cuts coding agent cost by 40 percent. The trick is not a smaller LLM. Jev is not a language model at all. It takes structured JSON describing a situation and answers narrow yes or no questions with a confidence score, and TypeSafe claims it runs up to 194 times faster and 445 times cheaper than a frontier model like GPT-6 Astra for exactly that kind of decision. TypeSafe was founded by Diogo Almeida, who co-wrote ChatGPT's core training techniques before starting the company.

This is a different bet than the one the model router startups are making. OpenRouter, Martian and Not Diamond are fighting what is already being called a three billion dollar race to pick the best LLM for each request. Jev skips that fight entirely by arguing most of an agent's decisions were never language problems to begin with. Should I read this file. Does this citation support the claim. Is this refund request valid. Those are classification problems wearing an LLM costume, and a purpose built model answers them for a fraction of the price.

I keep coming back to the same historical pattern. Databases spent two decades building specialized engines, OLTP, OLAP, vector, graph, once one general purpose engine stopped serving every workload well. Agent infrastructure is running the same playbook a lot faster. The conversational model stays the brain. Everything routine gets peeled off into a narrow, cheap, fast specialist underneath it.

The founders worth watching now are not the ones building a better chat model. They are the ones finding the next narrow decision buried inside an agent loop that is currently being answered by a full LLM call it never needed.
