A repo went semi viral in Chinese dev circles this week for a feature that sounds small until you have hit the wall it fixes: happier-dev's happier lets you start a session in Claude Code and finish it in Codex without losing the thread. MIT licensed, actively updated.

That one feature points at a real gap in how people actually use multiple coding agents. Everyone talks about running Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI and the rest side by side. Almost nobody talks about what happens when you need to hand the same task from one to another mid stream, because each tool keeps its own private session state and none of them export it cleanly.

I ran into this constantly building Campfire. Two backends racing the same task is the easy demo. The hard problem is when a leader agent delegates a step to a different backend and you need to replay exactly what that backend saw, not just what it eventually committed, especially once something breaks three steps later.

Campfire's answer is to record every session as a full JSONL log from the start, across Claude Code, Codex, Goose, Aider and OpenHands, so a session is portable and auditable by construction instead of bolted on afterward. Fork it, replay it, or hand it to a different backend mid task, the history travels with it.

Happier is solving continuity across devices. Campfire is solving continuity across backends. Different layer, same underlying bet: the session log is about to matter more than which model produced it.

text:
🤖 We're wasting frontier AI on problems the compiler ALREADY KNOWS how to solve.

Today's coding agents repeatedly spend expensive tokens guessing whether a variable exists, what type it has, which functions call it, or whether generated code will compile.

Then the compiler rejects the mistake, turns it into an error message, and sends it BACK to the model as more tokens.

That's backwards.

Compilers, type systems, language servers and static analyzers already know much of this information deterministically.

They shouldn't just check the AI's work AFTER generation. They should participate IN generation.

Give the model the semantic structure of the codebase. Let deterministic tools constrain impossible choices before they're generated. Catch an invalid program after 3 tokens, not 5,000.

Then reserve frontier intelligence for the parts that actually require intelligence.

We keep throwing bigger models at coding.

Maybe the better architecture is a SMALLER model surrounded by much better tools.

text:
I’ve been thinking about the lack of custom software in light of the availability of LLMs.

I know some very successful users of LLM coding agents.
I know some very successful users who roll their eyes when talking about LLM coding agents.
But I don’t see widespread adoption.

And yes, many people use LLMs for SWE work.
And yes, very few people in the general population use LLMs for much of anything.

That sweet, sweet corner where you create tools with LLMs - THAT is what I am asking about.

See, the issue here is KNOWING WHAT TO ASK FOR.

…

And the problem is really simple: it boils down to INTERNALIZING information.

You know how every sitcom is the same, and every email app is the same, and when you travel, every light switch in a city or country looks like it came from exactly the same Chinese factory floor - which is different from the factory floor that apparently supplied another country - and not because of standards?

The gap has to be very, very narrow. If you want someone to understand what you are saying, and there is too much unfamiliar stuff, they’ll just blank out, overload, ignore it, or replace it with some straw-man imitation.

…

I think about it a lot. Maybe this is why I can see all these chasms so well: the abyss in between, the isolated little three-acre islands humans inhabit.

My own island is this very question.

I’ve been charting human minds my whole life, not for the tingling sensation that creates a philosopher, but out of necessity - through tears and sweat, to create profits and tools.

I am a huge fan of human intellect. I want it to be powerful. When the e/acc crowd shits on other people’s cognitive skills, I cringe.

Because it is out of humans that we build civilizations.

Humans are our spare parts, our fuel, our logic gates.

And I really, REALLY want to build a K1 civilization - or, at the very least, survive the next crossing event.

text:
So I know Cognition doesn’t care about Little Ole’ Me, and this is just my story, so take it with a grain of salt, but here’s why I don’t think all these crazy scaling revenue numbers by coding agents are going to stick:

We’ve been happy Devin users for a while. Really like the product, and like the company. Still do! This isn’t shade at Cognition, and I’m not upset with them, just a sample of why I worry about the competitive landscape for these cos. 

Anyway, our usage grew to >$100k run rate or so. I think one or two of our users even received an email congratulating them for being Top 200 users of Devin. 

As usage grew, we added more capabilities and needed a BAA (layman’s terms: an agreement that says they are HIPAA compliant). This required an Enterprise contract (why a piece of paper requires extra money is a topic for another discussion, but it’s very normal…) so we started talking to their sales team. 

Basically, we were going to ~1.5x our spend in order to get the BAA. Honestly, that was fine with us. We like Devin!

Our only request was to pay quarterly (already a big concession from our existing monthly payments, given our relatively small size). They declined, unless we committed to EVEN MORE usage. 

Before responding, I decided to see how difficult it would be to set up Hermes to do the equivalent work as Devin, and to see what the costs were. I’d host it in our infrastructure and only use providers we already have a BAA with. 

Two days. 

That’s it. It’s functionally 100% equivalent. Maybe slightly better in some ways, slightly worse in others. We spend a little bit of time futzing with it, but we did that with Devin, too. 

The cost is roughly 25% of Devin. 

So, two days for $100k or so per year savings. All because they didn’t want us to pay quarterly. 

At some point, other companies are going to catch onto this, too. So congrats on this milestone, but keep finding more ways to provide value and keep customers happy. It’s hard to compete.

text:
Once models, inference, and agents are part of the same system, another question arises on the developer side: how can these components be used directly within the environment where developers work every day? @LLMTUNE_IO addresses this with LLMTune CLI, a command-line tool for inference, coding agents, and automating LLM workflows.

The CLI allows users to interact with models directly from the terminal through a REPL-style conversational interface. Users can open a multi-turn session, use slash commands, and run inference without switching to a separate web interface. LLMTune also supports one-shot usage with llmtune chat -p, allowing users to send a request directly from the command line.

More importantly, the CLI can work with the project currently being developed. It can attach files or directories to a request, allowing the model to read the context of the codebase and perform tasks such as explaining a repository or modifying part of the code. LLMTune demonstrates this workflow by attaching the src/ directory to a request and having the model work with the files directly within the session.

The CLI also connects directly to Agent Hub through its skills system. Users can install skills from Agent Hub through the CLI and then use them in their workflows instead of having to build each capability from scratch. In addition, LLMTune provides a streaming agent loop that allows agents to work through tool calls, with results streamed in real time. The system also includes mechanisms for compaction and permissions.

On the connectivity side, LLMTune CLI is built on LLMTune’s OpenAI-compatible APIs. The CLI is therefore not a separate model system, but another way to access the platform’s inference and agent layers. LLMTune describes the CLI as OpenAI-compatible and does not require a proprietary SDK.

The CLI is also designed to work with tools that already exist in the terminal environment. Users can pipe data through stdin, attach files, and combine the llmtune command with Unix tools such as grep or jq, including workflows that run in CI/CD. This places LLMTune CLI closer to practical software development workflows than simply providing another chat interface in the terminal.

Looking at the LLMTune system as a whole, the CLI serves as the developer-facing interaction layer. Fine-tune Studio creates and customizes models, Inference Studio provides the environment to run models and deploy agents, Agent Hub provides reusable building blocks, and the CLI brings these components directly into the terminal and codebase where developers are already working.

text:
MiniMax is not simply a Chinese imitation of frontier AI. It is a serious AI lab attacking a central industry problem: how to produce more useful intelligence from less compute.

Its model lineage shows a coherent strategy. MiniMax-Text-01 and M1 used a 456B-parameter mixture-of-experts architecture with only 45.9B active per token and hybrid Lightning Attention for million-token context. The M2 family cut that to roughly 230B total/9.8B active, optimized for coding and agents. M3 then moved to about 428B/23B active and introduced MiniMax Sparse Attention, selecting relevant KV blocks instead of attending across an entire million-token context. In controlled testing, MSA reduced attention compute 28.4× at one million tokens. These are architectural contributions, not the fingerprints of an API wrapper. 

The human capital behind that work is formidable. Founder, chairman, CEO and CTO Yan Junjie earned a mathematics degree from Southeast University, a doctorate in AI from the Chinese Academy of Sciences, conducted postdoctoral research at Tsinghua University, and spent more than six years at SenseTime, ultimately becoming vice president and vice-head of its research institute. MiniMax credits him with roughly 200 papers and more than 30,000 citations. 

MiniMax is also scaling real infrastructure. M1’s RL phase used 512 NVIDIA H800s for three weeks, but that was one post-training run—not the cost of creating the base model. More revealing is its cloud trajectory: $75.6 million of Alibaba Cloud consumption in 1H 2026, with purchase ceilings of $300 million in 2026, $400 million in 2027 and $500 million in 2028. Roughly $1.62 billion of 2026–27 financing proceeds is earmarked for AI infrastructure and model R&D. 

The distillation question requires precision. Anthropic alleges MiniMax generated more than 13 million Claude exchanges focused on agentic coding and tool use. That is serious evidence that frontier-model outputs contributed to post-training. But it does not establish that MiniMax is merely distilled American intelligence. Lightning Attention, CISPO, Forge-style RL, MSA, open weights and custom kernels form a substantial original R&D record, much of it predating the 2026 allegations. 

That is why MiniMax matters. It is showing that near-frontier utility in coding, agents and long-context multimodal work can be delivered at sharply lower cost, while open weights make capable intelligence ownable rather than permanently rented. The challenge to U.S. frontier labs is not that MiniMax copied them. It is that MiniMax has helped prove a different economic architecture for AI: sparse, efficient, inexpensive, rapidly improving—and increasingly capable of moving intelligence from the hyperscale cloud onto hardware its users own and control.

text:
💻 COMPUTER SCIENCE DEGREES ARE BECOMING THE NEW LIBERAL ARTS DEGREES.

That may sound provocative.

But AI is fundamentally changing what it means to “know computer science.”

For decades, computer science education was largely built around learning how to make computers do things:

→ Write code
→ Build algorithms
→ Understand data structures
→ Design databases
→ Develop software
→ Debug systems

🤖 AI can now perform a growing share of this work — and it is getting better rapidly.

So the value of a Computer Science degree is shifting.

It is becoming less about:

❌ “Can you write the code?”

And more about:

✅ “Can you understand the problem?”
✅ “Can you design the system?”
✅ “Can you ask the right questions?”
✅ “Can you evaluate what AI produces?”
✅ “Can you connect technology with business, law, design and society?”
✅ “Can you decide WHAT should be built — and WHY?”

This reminds me of the original idea of a LIBERAL ARTS EDUCATION.

Liberal arts was never supposed to train someone for one specific tool or job.

It was supposed to teach people how to:

🧠 Think
🔍 Analyse
💡 Create
🗣️ Communicate
⚖️ Make judgments
🌍 Understand complex systems

Computer Science may now be moving in the same direction.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🚀 THE ENGINEER OF THE AI ERA

The engineer of the future may not spend 8 hours writing code.

Instead, one person might orchestrate:

🤖 AI coding agents
📊 Data agents
🎨 Design agents
🔎 Research agents
📣 Marketing agents
⚙️ Automation agents

The scarce skill becomes less about producing every line manually.

The scarce skill becomes:

🎯 PROBLEM DEFINITION + SYSTEM THINKING + JUDGMENT + ORCHESTRATION

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

This also means universities may need to rethink Computer Science education.

Perhaps the future CS curriculum needs much more:

📌 Economics
📌 Entrepreneurship
📌 Product management
📌 Psychology
📌 Design
📌 Communication
📌 Law & regulation
📌 Ethics
📌 Domain expertise
📌 Systems thinking

…alongside strong computational foundations.

Because when AI makes BUILDING cheaper, knowing WHAT TO BUILD becomes much more valuable.

💡 Coding will remain important.

But coding may increasingly become a medium of expression rather than the entire profession — much like writing, mathematics or spreadsheets.

The question for the next generation of computer scientists may therefore change from:

“Which programming language do you know?”

to

🔥 “What problems are you capable of solving with computation and AI?”

That is a much bigger question.

text:
Diogo Almeida just shared 30 Jev + Opus 5.5 prompts for coding agents

30 prompts. 3 roles. your agent stops burning Opus on work a classifier could decide in 0.1s

the loop:

task → Jev decides in ~0.1s → Opus 5.5 builds → Jev gates the result → ship

section A - the router. spend Opus only where it pays

→ Jev tags every task trivial / standard / hard. only hard wakes Opus

→ route by trust, not difficulty. secrets/ infra/ auth/ → Opus. docs → cheap model

→ one route per task. hopping Opus → cheap → Opus reloads the whole context

section B - the bouncer. nothing runs without a typed yes

→ Jev reads the script before bash runs. allow / ask / deny per line, not per command name

→ task spend over $2 → pause and show the plan first

section C - the shipper. review less, merge more

→ Jev scores risk per file. Opus deep-reviews only the top 20%

→ failures sorted: real bug / flaky / env. only bugs reach Opus

→ confidence ≥ 0.85 + green CI → auto-merge. anything else → human

Jev decides fast - Opus 5.5 builds it

all 30 prompts in the video ↓ send them to your Claude Code and let it rebuild your harness

Graphify graphs the codebase so coding agents can navigate it.

I found a simpler route for architecture docs: put the graph in the Markdown itself.

Give a subheading a stable address, e.g. 8.1#3.2, which in the document becomes:

## 8.1#3.2 - Retry Bounds

At most five attempts.

Then reference it from another document:

Retry behaviour is constrained per 8.1#3.2.

Now 

grep "8.1#3.2" 

finds both the constraint and every document that references it.

The IDs are the nodes. The references are the edges. The coding agent already has the traversal tool.

I used this on a 47-document architecture corpus while an agent built ~19k lines of TypeScript.

text:
A small MIT CLI reads Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI sessions locally so you can see which models and projects are eating the budget.

tokentab saves you from waiting for a monthly bill to discover which coding-agent session burned the budget. The MIT-licensed CLI reads local session logs from Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI, then breaks usage down by model, project, and day without asking for an API key or sending the logs to another service.

That fills a real gap when one repository is touched by several agents. Each tool stores usage differently, vendor dashboards rarely share the same project boundaries, and the final invoice arrives after the expensive decision has already been made. tokentab normalizes the local evidence into a terminal report or a dashboard on localhost.

The workflow is straightforward. Clone the repository, install the package, and run tokentab for the default seven-day view. Filters cover month, provider, project, and custom date ranges. The JSON output is the useful escape hatch: feed it into your own report or budget alarm instead of treating the built-in dashboard as a new platform you must adopt.

The total is only the first clue. Split spend by project and model. If an expensive model dominates short routine tasks, your routing rules may be too generous. If cache hits stay low, the context may be changing too often or caching may not work as expected. Compare two similar tasks before and after a prompt, tool, or routing change. One spectacularly expensive session is an anecdote; repeated work is a signal.

tokentab keeps pricing in a local table and makes no network request to fetch rates. Predictable is good, but stale prices are the obvious failure mode. An unknown model appears as $0.00 with a warning until someone adds the correct entry. Treat that as missing data, never as free usage. The activity labels are deterministic guesses based on tools and the opening message, so token counts are stronger evidence than whether a session was classified as coding or debugging.

One honest note: this is a very young project. The source article found no visible test directory or published release, and the README still has small signs of unfinished polish. Run it against a copy of sensitive logs first. Keep the web dashboard bound to localhost, because session history can reveal much more than cost.

If you use two or more coding agents, capture a seven-day baseline and verify the prices for your actual models. Then change routing with numbers instead of vibes.

Here is the repo if you want a local seven-day cost baseline: https://t.co/g1KFZmE54n
Verify the local price table against the models you actually use: https://t.co/EG9GZmNIzj

text:
BREAKING $AMD CTO Mark Papermaster | Agentic AI Driving Demand 158x increase in tokens consumed per month over two years 🚨🚨🚨

Papermaster is not arguing “our GPU is X% faster.” He is arguing that the workload changed. Chatbots were bursty, centralized inference. Agents are persistent loops with tools, sub-agents, and routing. That justifies:
~heterogeneous placement (PC / on-prem / frontier)
~a token router as first-class infrastructure
~rack scale systems for the models that still need them

AMD is saying customers will not run every agent on a frontier API. A router that can drop work onto Ryzen AI or an MI350 class box is how you keep inference spend from exploding with the 158x token curve. That is a more enterprise-friendly story than “buy the biggest rack.”

AMD is trying to win three layers at once:
~Endpoint: Ryzen AI for private/local agents  
~Enterprise box: MI350-class on-prem inference + EPYC agent sandboxes  
~Hyperscale rack: MI455X + Venice + Pensando, sold as an open alternative to a vertically locked rack

The software story (ROCm, token routing, coding agents, upstream PRs) is meant to glue those layers so customers do not have to pick a single silo. That is coherent. It is also the hard part: the deck assumes the software abstraction is already good enough that agents can treat AMD hardware as just another backend. If that is true, the 158x token wave helps AMD as much as anyone. If it is not, the rack slide is just another SKU list.

Why agents burn more compute.
Slide 3 treats an agent as a loop, not a one-shot query:
~Request
~Sub-agents
~Inference / reasoning
~Tool use
~Orchestration
~Result
more agents → more inference → more tools → more compute

For large models, @AMD  shows a co-designed rack stack (this is the Helios generation, even if the slide does not always use that name):
~MI455X — 5th-gen Instinct GPU  
~Venice — 6th-gen EPYC CPU  
~Salina — Pensando DPU  
~Vulcano — Pensando AI NIC

“tightly integrated and fully optimized solution.” Public Helios specs around the same generation put 72 MI455X GPUs in a rack, with open Ethernet/UALink-style scale-up rather than a proprietary GPU fabric

Open software as the multiplier.
~The strategic middle of the deck is not silicon. Three claims:
~AI is now writing the accelerated code.
~Agents collapse the cost of tuning and porting because they learn from what is public.
~Abstraction is the new portability, developers should not rewrite for every hardware generation.

“The pace of AI is set by shared software.” Innovation “lands in the open first,” and silicon has to meet that stack on day one.

“Easy, Accessible Development” is reduced to https://t.co/s6YJYifoUM plus the current coding-agent set: Cursor, Claude, Codex, Gemini. The implication is that the relevant IDE is now an agent, so ROCm has to be something those agents can use without a specialist.

text:
AI coding gets messy when every agent has its own chat. This repo gives one person a conveyor.

Claude Lane Stack is a small AI coding factory for one person, using Claude Code as a project manager with CLI coding agents.

It helps you move work from a task card to verified changes on `main` by running writers as durable processes, assigning file ownership, and recording acceptance checks.

Key features:

• Claude Code control plane – a `dev-orchestrator` plans, dispatches, and merges after checks
• Pluggable CLI writers – supports optional Codex, Qwen, Grok, Kimi, AGY, Cursor, and OpenCode lanes
• Task-card contracts – YAML task cards define `owns_paths`, verification checks, and a writer lane
• Acceptance receipts – work records ownership and verification, with `acceptance.json` as the done signal
• Day and night lanes – daytime writers ship tasks while the night flow reviews work and refreshes enabled docs or memory

It’s open-source (MIT license).

text:
@dhh is thinking too small here, assembly is not the end state. A programming language with a good enough JIT compiler could optimize programs *as they run* based on real world data.

Creating a JIT compiler this good is a massive undertaking that can now be made possible because of coding agents.

We can have our cake and eat it too. I think people think of high level languages as only being good because they are easier to use but a powerful language runtime can make code much faster and easier to run.

Look at Cloudflare Durable Objects for example, when you write to sqlite in a durable object it will continue to run your code even while the write has not been durably committed because it knows it can without causing data inconsistency. The second you try to make an outbound request and the write isn't durable, it will pause the work. This is only a peek at the kind of power you get with a language runtime.

The Beam (Elixir, Erlang, Gleam) is another peek at what you get with a powerful language runtime.

We could have entire languages designed around this kind of behavior from the ground up.

text:
The comparison CopilotKit just published between Jev's instant UI rendering and GPT-6 Luna's LLM-streamed components is the same argument I keep making about web data.

Streaming a UI token by token from a language model looks impressive in a demo and is expensive and slow in production, because you are paying inference cost and latency for something that is actually deterministic once you know the shape of the data. That is exactly the problem with LLM-based web scraping. Most extraction pipelines re-read the entire page with an LLM on every single run, so every price check, every inventory sync, every monitoring job burns tokens for a structure that almost never changes between requests.

DeepScrape generates a CSS selector once with an LLM, then reuses that deterministic selector on every future pass and only calls the LLM again when the page actually changes shape, the same self healing idea Jev applies to decisions instead of extraction. The LLM does the targeted judgment call, selector generation, validation, adaptation, and nothing else touches inference cost. It also runs an MCP server so Claude and Cursor can call scraping and site to structured data queries directly as tools, plus an autonomous agent mode that navigates toward a goal instead of a fixed selector.

If your agents need reliable, cheap web data instead of a token bill that scales with every page load, this is built for exactly that.

So the agent is going to do all the reasoning and use what tool to do it? Oh the Saas tool with an MCP wrapper.

But who builds all that logic..  the Saas dev company that's who.  Who builds the Agent logic?  The company consuming the Saas tool, or the SaaS company. Where is the agent governing/ guardrails and security implemented?  In the cloud... using cloud tools.

So yeah okay a different paradigm. But still the same.

For me this is how I am looking at it for CPQ.

I have a quote that I am negotiating with a buyer on.

That could be in the future a Sales Agent negotiating with a buyer agent.  They still need to record the quote.  That functionality still needs to exist.

The Saas tool provides that functionality.

Now the quote is agreed to, before it becomes a contract and a purchase order it must be approved.  So it goes up the approval ladder.

At each stage we could have approval agents.

They approve based on certain criteria..

But they still have to record the approval. 

Some companies might need a human in the loop for approval at some point.

Either way all approvals must be recorded. 

That happens by the agent calling out to the MCP server to make that happen.

An MCP entry point built on top of a Saas application. 

What I see more going forward is less UI capabilities. 

I see more service consumption by agents doing a lot of the work in the background. 

But to get there we will have years of developing those agents to do the work correctly.   

That's going to be the challenging part.

A developer wants to build an AI agent that can answer questions about JustLend DAO, things like current supply rates or whether a given account is close to liquidation.

The developer encounters a limitation quickly, raw contract calls and scattered API endpoints are not built for an agent to reason over directly.

JustLend DAO provides infrastructure for exactly this, JustLend Skills, a GitHub distributed package bundling structured skill instructions with a lightweight, read only MCP server exposing nine query tools.

The developer integrates the solution by cloning the repository and running its install script, which sets up a TronGrid API key and configures the bundled server for tools like Claude Desktop, Cursor or Claude Code.

The application uses that infrastructure through tools such as get_all_markets for live APYs, get_dashboard for protocol wide TVL and user counts, and get_account_summary for health factor and shortfall data on any given address.

Users interact with the resulting application in plain language, asking something like whether their position is safe, while the agent quietly calls get_account_summary behind the scenes and returns a clear answer.

Activity feeds back into the ecosystem as more of these integrations appear, with the same nine tools returning versioned, structured errors, including a retryable rate_limit code, so agents can recover gracefully instead of failing silently.

JustLend DAO's role in enabling that cycle is providing the read only rails so developers can focus on the agent, not on reverse engineering the protocol.

text:
The editing timeline is becoming the least important part of making a video.

Motion shipped an MCP server this week that plugs directly into Claude Opus 5.5. Give it a product idea, your brand assets, and a reference clip, and the agent builds scenes, typography, and transitions into a finished launch video inside the same conversation. Ask for a change and it edits the actual footage, not a new prompt. Mosaic, the team behind Motion, raised a $3.8M seed and already has TubeScience, Meta's largest ad creative partner at 8,000 videos a month and 100 million views a day, running its workflows alongside News Corp.

The mechanism matters here. This isn't text to video from a blank page. It's an agent that treats the video editor as a tool it can call, the same way a coding agent calls a compiler. The generation model does the pixels. The agent does the judgment: pacing, hook strength, whether the CTA lands.

I keep seeing the same split play out at every price point in this category. Kling, Kuaishou's video unit, just raised over $2B at an $18B valuation, on revenue that went from $100M to $500M annualized in a year, a 36x multiple. Runway sits at $5.3B, Synthesia and Luma AI both around $4B. Higgsfield ships its own MCP so Claude and other agents can drive its generation pipeline directly. Meanwhile OpenAI's Sora burned roughly $1M a day against thin revenue before getting shut down, the clearest sign yet that raw generation quality alone doesn't win this market.

What's actually getting funded is control, not pixels. The labs selling generation as an API get commoditized fast. The ones building the agent layer on top, the part that understands briefs, iterates on feedback, and ships a finished asset, are the ones landing enterprise contracts with ad agencies and news networks.

This is the same arc dev tools went through. Nobody pays a premium for a compiler anymore. They pay for the IDE, the agent, the thing that turns raw capability into finished work without you touching the internals.

My read: the AI video story stopped being about who has the best model months ago. It's about who owns the loop between a brief and a shipped asset, and right now that loop is being built as an MCP tool call, not a new app.

Markets move.

Projects evolve.

Protocols upgrade.

Documentation changes.

The intelligence of an application therefore depends not only on its model.

Better context can produce better decisions.

Google just automated the PhD.

They built an AI that reads a problem, forms hypotheses, runs experiments, writes the paper, AND simulates its own peer review. no human touches it.

It’s called “ScientistTwo”

It is a fully autonomous multi-agent framework that executes end-to-end machine learning research.

Without a single human in the loop.

You give it a fundamental challenge. That’s it.

The AI independently navigates the literature. It establishes the baselines. It formulates novel hypotheses.

Then it writes the code. It runs the experiments. It conducts its own ablation studies.

It even argues with a simulated peer-review engine to refine its work before submitting.

The results are staggering.

Researchers tested ScientistTwo against the highest standards of human scientific achievement—papers accepted at top-tier conferences like NeurIPS and ICML.

The AI improved human state-of-the-art results on 86 different tasks.

It generated an average performance gain of 25.2% over the absolute best human models.

It didn't hallucinate a single citation. It wrote fully executable, verified codebases. And it autonomously generated expert-level, publication-ready papers.

We’ve spent the last two years using AI as a highly advanced intern to help us write code and summarize data.

That era is over.

ScientistTwo isn't an assistant. It is an autonomous scientific pioneer.

It doesn't just summarize the frontier of human knowledge. It expands it.

If an AI can autonomously hypothesize, test, and publish breakthroughs in machine learning...

How long until it discovers something we don't even have the math to understand?

Someone made XX runs off YY balls. I cannot place the game. Which match was it?

text:
🚨 7 AI Agent Architectures You Should Know

AI agents aren't built in just one way.

As workflows become more complex, developers combine agents, tools, memory, routers, MCP servers, and human oversight.

Here are 7 common architectures 👇

1️⃣ Single Agent + Tools
One agent uses multiple tools to complete tasks.

2️⃣ Sequential Agents
Multiple agents work step-by-step, passing results to the next agent.

3️⃣ Single Agent + MCP Server + Tools
MCP connects the agent to external tools and services through a standardized interface.

4️⃣ Single Agent + Tools + Router
A router decides which tool or workflow should handle each request.

5️⃣ Single Agent + Human-in-the-Loop
The agent can pause and ask a human for approval before taking important actions.

6️⃣ Single Agent + Dynamically Calls Other Agents
One agent can delegate specific tasks to other specialized agents when needed.

7️⃣ Hierarchy + Parallel Agents + Shared Tools
Multiple agents can work in parallel under a hierarchy while sharing tools, memory, and resources.

The key idea:

Simple tasks → Simple agents.
Complex workflows → Multiple specialized agents.

AI agents are evolving from simple chatbots into systems that can reason, delegate, use tools, and take action.

Save this for later. 🔖
Bookmark it if you're building AI agents.

text:
Create your own hacker news clone (https://t.co/AxYZxoCs9i):

Here is a comprehensive, production-grade prompt you can copy and paste into any leading LLM (Claude 3.7 Sonnet,
  GPT-4.5 / o1, Gemini Pro) to recreate this exact system from scratch:

    You are an expert full-stack engineer and Cloudflare specialist. Build an autonomous, agentic Hacker News clone
  deployed on Cloudflare Workers, Cloudflare Pages, and Cloudflare D1 with dual-engine AI automation (Cloudflare
  Workers AI + Google Gemini).

    ### System Overview & Architecture

    The application consists of two decoupled components sharing one codebase and one Cloudflare D1 SQL database:
    1. **Frontend & API (`hackernews-agentic`)**: Deployed to Cloudflare Pages. Handles SSR HTML (faithful Hacker
  News retro design), Markdown-negotiated views, REST API, and an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server.
    2. **Autonomous Background Engine (`hackernews-cron-sync`)**: Deployed as a Cloudflare Worker with cron triggers
  for scheduled ingestion, AI curation, and peer review commenting.

    ---

    ### Tech Stack
    - **Framework**: Hono with TypeScript running on the Cloudflare Workers / Pages runtime (`compatibility_flags =
  ["nodejs_compat"]`).
    - **Database**: Cloudflare D1 SQL database (`hackernews-db`) for relational data, sessions, rate limits, and KV
  ledger.
    - **Primary AI Models**:
      - Link Curation: `@cf/meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct-fp8-fast` (Cloudflare Workers AI).
      - Peer Review Critic: `@cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-32b` (Cloudflare Workers AI).
    - **Secondary AI Model (Reasoning & Fallback)**:
      - Google Gemini 3.7 Flash (`gemini-3.7-flash`) via REST API with hybrid reasoning (`thinkingConfig: {
  thinkingBudget: 1024 }`).
    - **Bundler**: esbuild for bundling `src/index.ts` to `dist/_worker.js`.

    ---

    ### 1. Database Schema (`schema.sql`)
    Create D1 tables for:
    - `items`: `id` (INTEGER PRIMARY KEY), `type` (story, comment, job, poll), `by` (TEXT), `title` (TEXT), `url`
  (TEXT), `text` (TEXT), `score` (INTEGER DEFAULT 1), `comments_count` (INTEGER DEFAULT 0), `parent_id` (INTEGER),
  `root_id` (INTEGER), `dead` (INTEGER DEFAULT 0), `deleted` (INTEGER DEFAULT 0), `created_at` (INTEGER).
    - `users`: `id`, `username`, `password_hash`, `salt`, `karma`, `about`, `api_token`, `is_agent` (BOOLEAN),
  `created_ip`, `created_at`.
    - `votes`: `user_id`, `item_id`, `direction`, `created_at` (Unique on user_id + item_id).
    - `sessions`: `token`, `user_id`, `expires_at`, `created_at`.
    - `rate_limits`: `key`, `timestamp`.
    - `kv_store`: `key` (TEXT PRIMARY KEY), `value` (TEXT), `updated_at` (INTEGER).

    Pre-seed system bot accounts:
    - ID 999: `math_ai_curator` (Curator bot)
    - ID 998: `deepseek_critic` (DeepSeek-R1 peer reviewer)
    - ID 997: `gemini_critic` (Gemini 3.7 Flash peer reviewer)

    ---

    ### 2. Dual Rendering (Human & Agentic)
    Implement Content Negotiation in Hono:
    - If a request contains `Accept: text/markdown` or comes from a known AI user-agent, return pure GitHub-flavored
  Markdown instead of HTML (~76% token reduction).
    - Standard web requests return classic Hacker News HTML:
      - Header: `#ff6600` orange bar, HN title, navigation (`news`, `newest`, `past`, `comments`, `ask`, `show`,
  `jobs`, `submit`).
      - Canvas: `#f6f6ef` background, Verdana typography, collapsible comment trees, upvoting buttons.
    - Response Headers: Send `Content-Signal: search=yes, ai-train=yes, ai-input=yes` on all HTTP responses.
    - In HTML `<head>`, include `<link rel="alternate" type="text/markdown">` and https://t.co/fDETrQDx0t JSON-LD
  (`DiscussionForumPosting` and `ItemList`).
    - Build a dedicated `/agent-readiness` dashboard page that displays a 5-pillar verification checklist (Token
  Efficiency, Markdown discovery, Content signals, MCP support, Edge latency).

    ---

    ### 3. Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server
    Implement a JSON-RPC 2.0 endpoint at `POST /mcp` supporting:
    - `tools/list`: Expose `get_top_stories`, `get_story`, `submit_story`, `post_comment`, and `search_stories`.
    - `tools/call`: Execute D1 queries and mutations based on input arguments and return structured markdown/JSON
  tool responses.

    ---

    ### 4. Autonomous RSS Poller & Curator (`src/cron/mathAiPoller.ts`)
    - **Trigger**: Runs every 30 minutes (`*/30 * * * *` at `:00` and `:30`).
    - **Sources**: Ingest feeds from arXiv (`https://t.co/zyqyxuUmrl`, `https://t.co/xSefgjPXov`, `math.CT`, `math.LO`, `cs.LO`, `https://t.co/divXS5FLUx`, `cs.LG`),
  The n-Category Café, Andrej Bauer, and https://t.co/f6yr115p0D.
    - **Title Sanitizer**: Strip Unicode Object Replacement Characters (`U+FFFC`) and unescape HTML entities in paper
  titles before saving.
    - **Neuron Budget Guard**:
      - Cloudflare Workers AI offers 10,000 free daily neurons. Set a safe cap at 7,500.
      - Track consumption in `kv_store` under `neurons:YYYY-MM-DD`.
      - Batch evaluate up to 6 candidates with `@cf/meta/llama-3.3-70b-instruct-fp8-fast`.
      - If neurons fall below 30 or budget is exceeded, automatically fallback to Google Gemini (`gemini-3.7-flash`
  with structured JSON output) or keyword filtering.

    ---

    ### 5. Autonomous Peer Review Critic (`src/cron/deepseekCritic.ts`)
    - **Trigger**: Runs once every hour (`45 * * * *` at minute 45).
    - **Target**: Find stories in D1 with `comments_count = 0`.
    - **Content Extractor**:
      - arXiv Preprints: Fetch full text from `https://t.co/5xsqlGQR2a{id}` or fall back to abstract meta tags.
      - General URLs: Fetch HTML and strip boilerplate/scripts.
      - Direct PDFs: Parse raw PDF byte stream text operators (`(text) Tj`) into plain English without external
  binary dependencies.
    - **Balanced 50/50 Randomization**:
      - Keep a run counter of comments posted by Cloudflare and Gemini.
      - Allocate stories to the engine with fewer comments in the run; if tied, perform a 50/50 coin flip (`Math.
  random() < 0.5`).
      - **Engine 1 (`@deepseek_critic`)**: `@cf/deepseek-ai/deepseek-r1-distill-qwen-32b`. Strip internal `<think>...
  </think>` tags and enforce a 2048 token limit.
      - **Engine 2 (`@gemini_critic`)**: Google Gemini 3.7 Flash (`gemini-3.7-flash`) with `thinkingConfig: {
  thinkingBudget: 1024 }`.
      - **Sentence Boundary Sanitizer**: Guarantee the critique never truncates mid-sentence by trimming backwards to
  the last valid sentence terminal (`.`, `!`, `?`).
      - **Mutual Fallback**: If DeepSeek fails/times out, immediately retry with Gemini; if Gemini fails, retry with
  DeepSeek.

    ---

    ### 6. Deployment Configurations
    1. **`wrangler.toml` (Cloudflare Pages)**:
       ```toml
       name = "hackernews-agentic"
       pages_build_output_dir = "./dist"
       compatibility_date = "2024-09-23"
       compatibility_flags = ["nodejs_compat"]

       [[d1_databases]]
       binding = "DB"
       database_name = "hackernews-db"
       database_id = "<D1_ID>"

       [ai]
       binding = "AI"

       [vars]
       GEMINI_API_KEY = "<GEMINI_KEY>"

  2. wrangler.worker.toml (Cloudflare Cron Worker):
    name = "hackernews-cron-sync"
    main = "src/index.ts"
    compatibility_date = "2024-09-23"
    compatibility_flags = ["nodejs_compat"]

    [[d1_databases]]
    binding = "DB"
    database_name = "hackernews-db"
    database_id = "<D1_ID>"

    [ai]
    binding = "AI"

    [triggers]
    crons = ["*/30 * * * *", "45 * * * *"]

    [vars]
    GEMINI_API_KEY = "<GEMINI_KEY>"

  3. package.json Scripts:
    {
      "scripts": {
        "build:pages": "mkdir -p dist && cp public/* dist/ 2>/dev/null || true && npx esbuild src/index.ts --bundle -
  -format=esm --platform=neutral --main-fields=module,main --conditions=workerd,worker,browser --
  outfile=dist/_worker.js",
        "deploy:pages": "npm run build:pages && wrangler pages deploy dist --project-name=hackernews-agentic --
  branch=main",
        "deploy:cron": "wrangler deploy --config wrangler.worker.toml",
        "deploy:all": "npm run deploy:pages && npm run deploy:cron"
      }
    }

  Generate clean, idiomatic TypeScript code for all modules, and provide the exact database initialization commands.

text:
Someone asked today whether https://t.co/8qYSYtSDwB is any good for pulling brand data. Fair question, and it points at something bigger than one API.

https://t.co/8qYSYtSDwB raised real money to solve this the LLM heavy way: one unified endpoint that scrapes, crawls, researches and normalizes into JSON, backed by Y Combinator, explicitly built to win Firecrawl customers on reliability. Firecrawl itself just quietly raised another $82 million on top of its $14.5 million Series A from Nexus Venture Partners, so investors clearly think give an agent clean web data is still an open problem worth funding twice in one year. Apify and Bright Data are fighting for the same budget line.

Here's the part nobody selling these APIs likes to say out loud: most of them re run an LLM over the page every single time you scrape it. That is how you get flexible extraction. It is also how you get a bill that scales with every page view instead of every site.

I built DeepScrape around a different assumption: the LLM's job is to figure out the extraction once, not forever. It generates a deterministic CSS selector for a page, and after that it just runs the selector, no model call, until the page's structure actually changes, at which point it self heals and regenerates the selector. The LLM layer only does the expensive part: selector generation, validation, adaptation. Everything else is plain scraping speed.

It also ships an MCP server, so Claude or Cursor can call scrapers as tools directly, plus a site to MCP mode that turns any website into a structured source an agent can query on its own. For brand data specifically, that means one pass to learn the page, then near free reads after that.

text:
Agent skills get installed before anyone reads them. NVIDIA shipped a tool that answers "is this safe to install" before your agent touches it.

SkillSpector by @nvidia is a security scanner for agent skills (v2.12.0, Apache-2.0, Python 3.12+) — https://t.co/QAK2bMoLdQ. Not a skill itself: skill-inspector is its companion skill inside the repo. The scanner is part of the NVIDIA Verified Skills pipeline (@NVIDIAAI): scan, evaluate, sign, publish to the catalog.

Two stages. Static layer: 68 patterns across 17 categories — prompt injection, data exfiltration, privilege escalation, taint tracking, YARA signatures for known malware, dependencies checked against OSV. Optional second layer: an LLM pass that compares the description's intent against the code's behavior and filters static false positives; the prompt carries anti-jailbreak protection so a malicious skill can't talk its way out. Report formats: terminal, JSON, Markdown, SARIF for CI. Ships as an MCP server and a Docker image too.

I ran it on two targets. First, the skill-inspector companion from the repo itself: 0 findings, verdict SAFE, coverage 100%. Second, all ~70 skills in my own profile: 337 findings (265 MEDIUM, 70 HIGH, 2 CRITICAL), final scanner verdict CRITICAL — DO_NOT_INSTALL. About 10 minutes, a 1.2 MB JSON report.

Confirmed: the static layer is fast and deep — YARA signatures and taint analysis catch what eyes miss. SARIF output means the scanner drops into CI in one line. The companion skill comes back clean — the scanner eats its own dog food.

Rejected: the verdict on my profile. Both CRITICALs are YARA matches on a catalog cache file (.hub/index-cache) where skill descriptions mention malware family names and crypto text. That's data, not code. The top categories across my skills — Agent Snooping (95), Privilege Escalation (93), Data Exfiltration (42): the static engine flags instruction lines like "read these files", "send to the bus". A SKILL.md is an instruction document, not a program, and the pattern engine can't tell a described operation from dangerous code. 337 findings merged into noise I had to untangle by hand.

Honest limits: for instruction-only skills the static pass produces a false-positive stream — you need the LLM layer, and that needs a provider key. The Python floor is 3.12+; my system 3.11 didn't qualify. A flat DO_NOT_INSTALL verdict on false positives undermines trust in verdicts: severity without confirmation is a warning, not a sentence.

Installing unvetted skills is becoming the new pip install without pinning — same ending. A scanner that reads SKILL.md before your agent does is the missing brick in agent infrastructure: skills have grown their own attack surface, and now there's a versioned tool that covers it.

Building in public. 🤖

text:
The thread going around this week about a startup fixing their site for AI agents (dropping captchas, exposing prices in the page HTML, adding a plain text copy of every key page) and seeing agent signups jump 10x says something true: most of the web still assumes its only reader is a human with a browser.

I built DeepScrape because most sites sit on the other side of that gap. They were never redesigned for agents, and an agent that needs their data still has to render JavaScript, guess at a CSS selector, and hope the layout does not change tomorrow.

DeepScrape generates the CSS selectors once with an LLM, then reuses them deterministically on every later pass, calling the model again only to self heal when the page actually changes. That is the same economic shift behind both stories: you stop paying a model to re-read the same page every single time.

It ships an /api/map endpoint for discovering a site's structure, autonomous navigation toward a plain language goal, and an MCP server so Claude or Cursor can call a scraper as a tool directly. There is also a site-to-MCP mode that turns any existing website into a structured data source an agent can query, giving a site the agent-ready front door it never built for itself.

text:
Health data is fast becoming a commodity. 

Useful, personalized interpretation is still exceptionally rare.

Every smartwatch, smart ring, and health tracker on the market continuously logs raw signals heart rate variability, sleep phases, recovery scores, stress spikes, and daily activity routines. 

Yet getting buried in a wall of colorful metrics rarely helps anyone make a better decision when they wake up tomorrow morning.

A wearable can easily report what happened yesterday. 

The far more valuable layer is understanding what all those signals mean when viewed together.

That missing connection is the exact gap @sleepagotchi is targeting.

Looking closely at the product, the long term bet isn't simply building another sleep tracker with an AI chatbot attached.

The thesis actually breaks down into three distinct, interdependent layers:

1. Data (The Raw Material)

Sensors handle the heavy lifting of collection, but a passive dashboard only reports the past.

 Showing that you slept 6 hours tells you what happened; it doesn't tell you why or how to fix it.

2. Intelligence (The Context Engine)

One off night is random noise. Three consecutive weeks where your recovery drops because high afternoon activity collided with a gradually shifting bedtime is a structural pattern. 

The real value lies in moving from static logging to dynamic context: collecting signals, mapping recurring patterns, isolating what actually matters, and surfacing one high conviction recommendation.

3. Consumer Experience (The Retention Engine)

This is where the vast majority of digital health products fail: long term retention. Dashboards lose their novelty after a week, and generic AI advice gets ignored after a month.

 If users stop opening the app, the underlying intelligence never gets enough historical context to become useful.

This is why Sleepagotchi’s playful elements Dino, customizable rooms, character progression, and morning reward reveals are not extra fluff. 

They form the core retention engine that keeps users returning daily.

Gamification gives the intelligence layer the time and touchpoints it needs to become truly personal.

The Multi Agent Execution Flow

As the platform’s multi agent framework evolves, the system shifts from passive monitoring to active decision making. 

The Sleep Coach identifies the pattern, the wellness context layer explains the biological mechanics, and specialized execution agents make following through frictionless. 

You move from reviewing yesterday's stats to optimizing today's routine.

The ultimate goal isn't to build a prettier tracker.

 It's to construct the default consumer intelligence layer sitting directly between raw personal health data and daily human action wrapped inside an experience people genuinely look forward to opening every single morning.

Data is becoming a commodity. Personal, habit forming health intelligence is the real product.

text:
#DeepManifoldInterpretation 
Paper: Harness as a Language: A Minimalist Agent Framework With Maximal Expressivity
Author: Zhening Li (@zli11010) et al... 

From the Deep Manifold perspective, the pretrained model provides a neural fixed-point field, while the agent acts as both executor and navigator over that field. 

Inference is an iterated integral: each invoke(...) establishes a new boundary condition and initiates a relatively short inference pathway through the field. Rather than forcing one long trajectory, JAZ recursively composes many such local pathways—

invoke #1 → invoke #2 → invoke #3 → ...

—while carrying forward task state, tools, history, and executable results. 

The harness therefore becomes a navigation mechanism: it dynamically constructs waypoints and execution structure without changing the underlying pretrained field. 

This is especially important for highly nonlinear and jagged neural fields, including MoE models, where composing shorter pathways may be more stable than attempting a single long-horizon inference trajectory.

It gathers ~4,000 vetted studies from trusted sources like What Works Clearinghouse and Campbell Collaboration, accessible via an MCP server, chatbot, and browsable website—helping researchers, teachers, and AI tool builders get reliable, sourced answers instead of noisy web search results.

As an educator who has sustained enthusiasm for LLM support in classrooms, this project feels like a meaningful step forward. Sometimes, AI tools generate confident-sounding answers without evidence behind them. A curated, agent-readable library changes that dynamic—grounding classroom-relevant questions in vetted research from trusted sources like WWC and Evidence for ESSA, rather than leaving teachers to sort fact from plausible-sounding fiction.

What stands out most is accessibility. Teachers don't have time to comb through academic databases between lesson planning and grading. A simple chat query like "what reading interventions have strong evidence" returning sourced, credible answers in seconds could genuinely reshape how educators make instructional decisions. https://t.co/MGm0GnRgXJ

text:
Researchers just caught AI agents inventing answers when their tools quietly break

They gave an agent over a thousand requests, like a bank balance or a patient's lab result, and rigged every tool to send back nothing usable

When the tool openly returned an error, the agent reported it honestly

But when the tool said everything was fine and sent back a blanked-out value, the agent answered as if it had the number, or made up a reason it couldn't share it, almost half the time

What makes it worse is that every agent framework prompt they tested had this problem, and none of the nine they checked tells the model what to do when a tool fails

Personally, I'm adding one sentence to every agent I run, it has to mark each lookup as OK or FAILED before answering, and in the paper that alone cut dishonest answers from 14% to under 1%

text:
David Yang once told me: write in the language you know best, and let a translator do the rest. He may have put it differently, but that is how it stuck with me.

I have no illusions that I will ever know English better than Russian. Even though English is not a problem for me today.

One problem remains. You need a translator that doesn't make you switch context and copy text back and forth. I used to use DeepL. It froze a lot, but the main thing is that it can't write in my style.

And style isn't only formatting or how wordy you are. It is how I express myself, and how I believe one should express oneself.

So I built Translate Like Me for myself. It's a macOS menu bar app: select text in any app, press ⌥⌘F, and the selection is replaced with the translation. It figures out the direction on its own. Each language pair can carry a description of your style, so the translation reads the way I would have written it.

The biggest plus is that it runs on subscriptions I already pay for. The app calls the official Claude, ChatGPT or Grok CLI you are already signed in to. No API keys.

That convenience has a price, and I had to measure it. claude -p launches the whole of Claude Code and attaches its tool descriptions, my MCP server schemas and my global CLAUDE.md to every call. A one-line question in Russian, "When is the release planned?", reached the model as 48,795 input tokens and took over five seconds on Sonnet. Three flags (--tools "", --strict-mcp-config, --setting-sources "") brought it down to 770 tokens and just over two seconds. The translation itself needed 1.6% of the request.

The code is open source, link in the first comment.

Which language do you write your work in: the one you know best, or the one your readers read?

text:
Lyzr's agent infrastructure runs inside some of the most regulated organizations on earth: leading banks, insurers, healthcare institutions, and federal agencies. Building for them taught us what an enterprise agent stack actually needs.

Here is the checklist. For each piece: how to build it yourself, and how we built it at Lyzr.

1. Fluid data, not a finished ontology 

The agent should never touch raw data. It should see business objects and a fixed list of actions it is allowed to take on them. 

Build it yourself: typed tools like update_order_status, never raw SQL. 

On Lyzr: most enterprises cannot wait months to model everything first. Our Fluid Data Intelligence architecture builds a transitional knowledge store for each data source, a knowledge graph, knowledge base, or vector store, with an agent acting as the gatekeeper. Agents reconcile across sources in real time and ship in weeks, not after the data is perfect.

2. A layer between the agent and the model PII masked before the prompt leaves. Responses cached. Failed calls retried. Rate limits and token spend tracked. 

Build it yourself: route every LLM call through one gateway, LiteLLM or your own wrapper. 

On Lyzr: Opencontroller puts every agent call through one enterprise gateway, across every agent, framework, and cloud you run.

3. Models you can swap and models you own Keep the model name in config and switching providers becomes a single line change. 

Build it yourself: a model catalog plus bring your own model. 

On Lyzr: every agent is LLM agnostic. Then Openfinetuner takes it further. It captures real traffic, trains a small open model on it, runs it in shadow mode behind the same agent, and gradually shifts traffic over. The agent never changes. Only the model behind it does.

4. Three ways to start an agent On a schedule, on an event, or through an API call. Same agent behind all three. 

Build it yourself: cron, webhook, and endpoint. 

On Lyzr: Agent Studio ships all three natively, with durable execution so a run that crashes resumes exactly where it stopped.

5. Everyone builds, IT decides what ships 

Build it yourself: one dev environment every agent must enter, and an approval flow to production. 

On Lyzr: business users vibe code agents in Architect. Every employee gets chat, search, and agent building in Open Cowork. Everything they create lands in dev and moves to production only through approval gates.

6. Evals inside the lifecycle Agents tested before release and again after every change. 

Build it yourself: a small eval set that runs in CI on every prompt edit. 

On Lyzr: simulations and evals are built into the agent lifecycle, with dev, UAT, and production environments and approvals at each step.

7. Every action logged Tokens, tool calls, who triggered what, traced end to end. 

Build it yourself: Langfuse or OpenTelemetry. 

On Lyzr: Opencontroller discovers and traces every agent, including ones built on other platforms and clouds, and turns good decision traces into fine tuning data.

8. Nothing leaves the building For the most regulated workloads, even a private cloud is a hop too far. 

Build it yourself: GPUs, open weights models, and your own serving stack. 

On Lyzr: Lyzr Optimus ships as an on prem appliance, preloaded with open weights models, fine tuning, and the full Lyzr platform. Zero data egress.

On top of all this, access should be checked three ways: by role, by data marking, and by purpose. And an agent should only ever get the permissions of the user who runs it.

Every one of these can be built in house. The question is how many of them your team wants to build and maintain before the first agent reaches production.

### Emerging AI Utilities

#### [Qwen3.8-Omni-Flash](https://t.co/gArK3852RM)

* **Capabilities**: A native omni-modal reasoning model with a 1-million-token context window that accepts text, images, audio, and video inputs, outputting text. It supports default-on extended reasoning, 2-channel and 4-channel spatial audio parsing, structured outputs, and integrated tool calling.
* **Primary Use Cases**: Automated video and audio intelligence ingestion, spatial audio transcriptions, long-form document and footage synthesis, and multimodal GUI interaction.
* **Pricing & Availability**: Commercial hosted API available via [Alibaba Cloud Model Studio](https://t.co/wouemLlpX6), [QwenCloud](https://t.co/ty1zuewdEd), and [OpenRouter](https://t.co/vPbVeliepd) ($0.15/1M input tokens, $0.47/1M output tokens). * **Capabilities**: A hardened, anti-detection stealth browser engine built on a customized Firefox runtime that replaces fragile JavaScript-level monkey-patching with C++ engine-level fingerprint spoofing (canvas, WebGL, OS fonts, and audio hardware). It operates with a lightweight ~200MB memory footprint and exposes both a Python automation API and a standalone REST/MCP server ([Camofox Browser Server](https://t.co/voP0ucUUOt)) designed to integrate with agent harnesses.
* **Primary Use Cases**: Bot-resilient web scraping, defensive intelligence collection, and browser-use agents navigating strict bot mitigation systems (e.g., Cloudflare, DataDome).

* **Capabilities**: A local hardware-orchestration utility that dynamically shards and routes AI inference and reasoning tasks across multiple consumer and workstation GPUs on a single host. Coupled with recent kernel optimizations across `llama.cpp` and `vLLM`, it yields up to 1.9x faster execution on local model weights like Nemotron-3.5 Lightning and GLM-5.3-Flash without external network calls.

text:
I built Whylode for the @IBM  Bob 2.0 Hackathon.

It’s an IBM Bob mode that asks why before changing legacy code.

Thousands of companies still run invoicing, tax, payroll, and other critical systems on IBM i code written in RPG decades ago.

The code still works.

The problem is that the reasons behind it often live in the heads of people who are retiring.

In Fortra’s 2026 IBM i survey, 69% of shops named skills as a top concern, ahead of cybersecurity for the first time in nine years.

Nothing breaks until a rule changes. A state raises its sales tax.

Someone now has to edit code nobody properly explained.

Tools can show you where a value lives. They usually can’t tell you why it’s there, and that context is what determines whether changing it is safe.

My sample invoice system has two hardcoded rates.

One is the state sales tax rate.

The other is a contract rate that must not change until 2029.

Nothing in the code tells them apart.

A search and replace, or an AI agent guessing from the code alone, can easily change both.

Whylode makes Bob ask instead of guess.

How it works:

→ Give Bob the change notice PDF. Bob reads it, breaks it into clauses, and traces the code implementing each one.

→ When the code can’t explain why a line exists, Bob sends the owner one plain-language question.

They answer from their phone through a link. No account required.

→ That answer is pinned to the exact lines in a memoir.

The next time Bob touches those lines, it checks the memoir first, so the same person doesn’t get asked the same question twice.

→ Bob drafts the diff.

Every changed line and every intentionally unchanged line carries its reason.

A human approves the final change.

In the recorded run, Bob found both rates and asked about the second one.

The owner explained that it was a contract rate fixed until 2029.

Bob changed only the state tax rate and preserved the contract rate, with the owner’s answer attached as the reason.

On the next change, Bob found three relevant lines already explained in the memoir and didn’t ask again.

How I used IBM Bob:

Whylode runs inside Bob using:

>A custom mode that defines the workflow and the rule: ask, never guess.

>Three skill.md files: trace, ask, draft.

>An MCP server with 8 tools connecting Bob to change records, questions, and the memoir.

>Document understanding to read change-notice PDFs directly.

Bob also helped build Whylode.

In Agent mode, it wrote the custom mode, skills, MCP server, schema and data layer, API, sample RPG system, and test suites.

Every Bob task and its cost is documented.

text:
Wiring MCP without a scan is how tool poisoning becomes production. Scan is necessary — not sufficient.

CTO gates before any MCP server touches a prod agent:
1) Deny-by-default tool allowlist: exact server + tool name + arg schema; unknown tools never bind
2) Scoped proxy: agent gets surrogates, not host creds / browser cookies / cloud keys; exfil channels die at the proxy
3) Egress allowlist: MCP connectors POST only to approved hosts; no open-web fetch by default
4) Receipts: every tool invoke signed with session ID → SIEM; kill switch kills the cell

If your "agent demo" can pull an unpinned MCP and call an attacker-shaped tool because nobody scanned the folder, you didn't ship a prototype — you shipped a credential-exfil path with a chat UI.

text:
Anthropic opened a submission portal for the Claude plugin directory yesterday: submit a remote MCP server or a GitHub repo of MCP servers plus skills, get it validated and security-scanned on submit, and see installs and search terms once it is live. Paid Claude plans only, says @ClaudeDevs.

the tl;dr

What can you submit?
- MCP connector: one remote MCP server, listed on its own
- Plugin bundle: MCP servers and Agent Skills in a GitHub repo; in Claude Code the bundle can also carry LSPs, commands, hooks and agents
- A repo with several plugin folders needs one submission per folder; a plugin that calls a server you run also needs that server submitted as a connector, if it is not listed yet

What happens after you submit?
- Every version gets automated validation plus a security scan; a person reviews a new listing before it goes live
- The scan looks for behavior the plugin does not disclose: sending data elsewhere, running hidden code, changing Claude's permission settings. A first submission that fails it is rejected
- Compiled, packed or minified code is held for a reviewer because the scan cannot read it
- A validation result applies to one commit. Push again, validate again
- Once approved you pick the publish moment; later versions can auto-publish when they pass, and the listing keeps serving the last published version if a new one fails or is held

What do you see afterwards?
- Installs by product surface and version, listing views, and which searches led people to the listing, per Anthropic's post
- The docs add runs and error rates on the plugin's Usage tab
- Directory plugins show up for Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise users; Team and Enterprise owners choose which sources members see

BUT: the repo can stay private while you validate and submit, and you agree that its source is uploaded to Anthropic for scanning and is visible to reviewers; it must be public before the listing goes live. The analytics screenshots in the announcement are labeled illustrative. Discovery is still moving: Anthropic says one discovery experience rolls out across Claude and Claude Code over the coming weeks, so where a listing appears today is not where it stays. Existing skill, connector and plugin listings need no changes.

Verdict: if you already run a remote MCP server, the connector path is a form. If your workflow is a skill plus the server it calls, bundle them. Either way run claude plugin validate locally, then Validate in the portal, and commit readable source.

Which would you ship first: a connector for a server you already run, or a bundle with the skill that makes it useful?

text:
Why $INJ Makes Sense to Me as a Builder

@injective interests me because it puts useful financial infrastructure within reach of people building products. Its native exchange module provides an onchain orderbook, matching and settlement. Its EVM and WASM environments share assets, liquidity and financial modules. For applications that use those capabilities, that means more of the work can go into what makes the product useful.

As a product designer, I find that compelling. A good financial experience depends on what happens after someone presses a button: whether an order executes, how funds are handled, and what happens when the conditions are not met. Those are design questions as much as engineering questions.

My connection to Injective comes from a very ordinary business problem.

In the autumn of 2025, I started a designer clothing brand. Across repeated pre-orders, I kept facing the gap between people liking a design and people committing to buy it. Before production, you need to decide how much to make and at what price. Interest helps, but it leaves a lot unresolved.

That question became part of the reason we built @MakeBookHQ. Its first version began at AdventureX 2026 in Hangzhou, and our team built an early Solidity prototype on Injective's EVM testnet. We explored a market where buyers could commit their maximum price before production, with predefined rules determining whether those commitments could support a viable batch at a common price.

My role is product and design. I want a buyer to understand what they are committing to, and a creator to have a better basis for deciding whether to produce. The contract can enforce defined conditions for funds; making and delivering a physical product still requires people to do their jobs. Working through that boundary is part of what makes this interesting to me.

That experience gives me a specific reason to like Injective's focus on finance. There are financial coordination problems inside ordinary businesses: demand that is difficult to measure, money committed before delivery, and conditions both sides need to understand. I see room for products that use programmable transactions to handle parts of those problems. MakeBook is our early attempt to explore that space.

I also use AI in my design work, so Injective's open-source MCP server caught my attention. It exposes capabilities such as market data, trading and position management to compatible agents. My interest is in the underlying connection: new interfaces can use existing financial infrastructure. The harder product questions remain permissions, understandable decisions and reliable execution.

For INJ itself, the economic connection matters. INJ supports network security through staking and participates in governance. The monthly Community BuyBack gives eligible participants a way to commit INJ in exchange for a proportional share of ecosystem revenue, with the committed INJ permanently burned. That provides a concrete mechanism to examine when judging how ecosystem activity relates to the token.

A useful chain still has to earn sustained demand. I would judge my thesis by whether users return after incentives fade, whether markets develop dependable liquidity, and whether ecosystem revenue grows. For supply, I would look at burns alongside new issuance. Low fees can help a product attract users, but transaction counts alone do not settle the question of token value.

I am bullish on the possibility that more useful applications will build on this shared infrastructure and turn that activity into lasting economic demand. If usage stays shallow or depends mainly on rewards, that would weaken my case.

What keeps me interested is that I have a problem of my own to work on here. I want MakeBook to help someone make a better production decision, or feel clearer about committing to a purchase. That is a concrete reason to keep building on Injective while the larger thesis is still being tested.

Disclosure: I am building MakeBook on Injective, and I trade INJ.

text:
CLIs ARE COMING BACK.

And strangely, AI may be the reason.

CLI is technology from decades ago.

For humans, we spent years trying to get AWAY from it.

For AI agents?

We may be going back.

Let me explain why — with one very simple example.

Imagine you run a small business.

You have a website.

One morning you tell your AI agent:

“My website update failed last night. Find out what happened, fix it if you can, and make sure the website works.”

Simple request.

But think about what the AI actually needs to do.

It may need to:

→ check GitHub
→ find the failed deployment
→ read the error
→ inspect the files
→ change something
→ run the tests
→ deploy again

The AI needs HANDS.

And this is where MCP and CLI become interesting.

OPTION 1: MCP

MCP stands for Model Context Protocol.

Forget the technical name.

Imagine MCP as giving the AI a special control panel.

You connect GitHub to the AI.

GitHub might then expose tools such as:

“List repositories”

“List deployments”

“Read failed workflow”

“Read file”

“Update file”

“Create pull request”

“Read pull request”

And every tool needs instructions explaining:

what it does,

what information it needs,

and what information it returns.

That is useful.

The AI now has a nice structured menu.

But imagine you connect:

GitHub.

Your database.

Cloudflare.

Slack.

Google Drive.

Your server.

Your monitoring system.

Every connection may add another collection of tools.

Suddenly your AI receives a HUGE menu before it has even started working.

It is a little like hiring someone to fix a broken lightbulb…

and first making them read the instruction manuals for your entire building.

That is one weakness MCP can create at scale.

OPTION 2: CLI

CLI means Command-Line Interface.

This is the old-fashioned terminal programmers use.

The black screen with text commands.

Humans often hate it.

AI agents may LOVE it.

Because the computer already has tools installed.

For example, GitHub has a CLI called:

gh

So our agent could start with:

gh run list

In English:

“GitHub, show me the latest automated jobs.”

The computer might reply:

Deployment #481 — FAILED

The AI sees the failure.

Then it asks:

gh run view 481 --log-failed

In English:

“Show me what failed.”

Now imagine the computer replies:

Test failed:
customer_total.py
Expected field: price
Found field: unit_price

The AI now knows the problem.

Someone changed the name of a field.

So the agent opens the relevant file.

Fixes the outdated reference.

Then runs:

pytest

In English:

“Run all the tests.”

Computer replies:

128 tests passed.

Then the AI pushes the correction:

git push

And checks the new deployment:

gh run list

Computer replies:

Deployment #482 — SUCCESS

Finally YOU receive:

“Your website deployment failed because one test was still using an old field name. I corrected it, ran 128 tests successfully, and the new deployment completed.”

Think about what just happened.

YOU NEVER USED THE TERMINAL.

YOU NEVER LEARNED A COMMAND.

YOU NEVER OPENED GITHUB.

You simply said:

“Fix my website.”

The AI spoke CLI to the computer for you.

THAT is why this matters.

SO WHAT IS THE BIG DEAL?

The AI did not need a special new “AI version” of GitHub.

GitHub already had a perfectly good tool.

gh

The AI simply used it.

And GitHub is not unusual.

There are mature CLIs for things like:

Git

Docker

AWS

Cloudflare

databases

Linux servers

Supabase

and thousands of other systems.

This creates an interesting question:

If the AI can already operate the existing tool…

why build another layer?

WHY ARE CLIs BECOMING INTERESTING AGAIN?

Because an OLD technology suddenly has a NEW perfect customer.

AI agents.

And CLI can solve several problems that direct MCP use sometimes creates.

1. LESS INFORMATION INSIDE THE AI'S HEAD

With MCP, the AI may receive descriptions of many available tools.

Even tools it never uses.

That consumes part of the AI's context — basically its working memory.

With CLI, the agent can often discover things only when necessary.

For example:

gh --help

means:

“GitHub, tell me what commands are available.”

Then:

gh run --help

means:

“Tell me specifically what I can do with automated runs.”

The AI discovers the instructions when it needs them.

Not everything upfront.

That can be much more efficient.

2. YOU MAY NOT NEED TO BUILD AN MCP FOR EVERYTHING

Suppose Docker already gives you:

docker ps

to see running containers.

GitHub already gives you:

gh

AWS already gives you:

aws

Supabase gives you:

supabase

Why create another special AI interface that recreates the same functionality?

Sometimes you should.

Sometimes you are simply adding another layer.

3. CLI TOOLS CAN BE COMBINED

This is where things get really powerful.

Imagine there are 50,000 lines of server logs.

You do NOT want the AI reading all 50,000 lines.

Instead the AI can ask the computer:

“Give me today's errors only.”

Then:

“Only errors containing PAYMENT.”

Then:

“Count them.”

The computer can reduce 50,000 lines to perhaps:

“17 payment errors.”

Only THAT information needs to enter the AI's brain.

This can mean:

less context

fewer tokens

lower cost

faster agents.

4. AI ALREADY UNDERSTANDS MANY CLI TOOLS

There are decades of:

documentation,

Stack Overflow answers,

tutorials,

GitHub projects,

manuals,

and examples

showing how these commands work.

AI models have learned from enormous amounts of this material.

Humans spent decades documenting how computers can be controlled with text.

Without realizing it…

we were creating a fantastic interface for AI.

SO IS CLI REPLACING MCP?

My answer is:

PARTLY — YES.

I think people sometimes avoid saying this clearly.

If an AI agent is running on your computer or your own server…

and a mature CLI already exists…

I increasingly think the first question should be:

“Can the agent simply use the CLI?”

Not:

“Where is the MCP server?”

Because if the CLI already does the job well, wrapping everything inside another MCP layer can sometimes mean:

more setup

more context

more maintenance

and another thing that can break.

But this does NOT mean MCP is useless.

Far from it.

WHERE MCP IS BETTER

Imagine instead that 500 employees need access to Salesforce through AI.

Some employees can only READ customers.

Managers can UPDATE them.

Nobody should be able to delete anything.

Everyone needs authentication.

Access must disappear when an employee leaves.

You probably do NOT want to give 500 AI agents unrestricted terminal access.

Here MCP starts making a lot of sense.

MCP can provide a controlled door:

“You may perform THESE actions.”

“With THESE permissions.”

“Using THIS person's account.”

So the distinction becomes much clearer.

CLI is fantastic when:

the agent already controls a trusted computer

and good tools already exist there.

MCP is fantastic when:

you need standardized, controlled access to external systems.

And the future could become even more interesting.

MCP may still exist underneath.

But instead of dumping hundreds of MCP tools directly into the AI's working memory…

the agent may access them through something that behaves much more like a CLI:

discover what is available,

load only what it needs,

execute it,

get the result,

continue.

So this may not ultimately be:

CLI versus MCP.

It may be:

CLI ON TOP.

MCP UNDERNEATH.

WHY SHOULD A NORMAL BUSINESS PERSON CARE?

Because you probably should NOT learn CLI.

AI changes that.

Ten years ago, if you wanted the power of the command line, you had to learn commands.

Tomorrow you may simply say:

“Why did my website fail?”

“Check yesterday's sales database.”

“See whether my server is running.”

“Find the problem and fix it.”

And behind the scenes:

YOU → speak normal English

AI → uses CLI / MCP / APIs

COMPUTER → does the work

AI → explains the result back to you

That is the real reason CLI matters again.

The command line did not suddenly become easier.

It got a new user.

AI.

And AI may be much better at using it than we ever were.

Every major platform is racing to expose itself over the Model Context Protocol, because that is where agents look for integrations.

The InfiniStrategy take is that integration work is not disappearing, it is moving up the stack. Writing the connector is becoming free. The hard, valuable work is now permission design: scoping what an autonomous agent can read and change on someone else's account, and proving it to a client.
