text:
MCP adoption does not have to mean building a second API layer beside your existing REST infrastructure.

Google Cloud API Gateway can now act as an MCP server, turning selected operations from OpenAPI-described REST APIs into tools that agents can call.

That changes an interesting architecture decision.

A team may already have authentication, routing, quotas, observability and production controls around an API gateway. If the gateway can expose the agent-facing protocol too, the MCP layer does not need to duplicate the backend or become another service to operate.

But “every endpoint can become a tool” should not become the design goal.

APIs are usually shaped for application clients. Agent tools need clear intent, constrained inputs, useful descriptions and permissions that match what an autonomous caller should actually be allowed to do.

The protocol adapter can move into infrastructure. Tool design still belongs to the application.

text:
SalesBleed. three flaws in Salesforce Agentforce, disclosed by Zenity Labs, and the entry point is a form your prospects fill out voluntarily.

[!] the vector: Web-to-Lead

Salesforce's own lead-capture form, the one marketing teams embed on public sites. an attacker submits a lead with injected instructions in the free-text fields. nothing happens on submit. the payload sits dormant in the CRM until an employee asks their Agentforce agent to look at that lead. the agent reads the poisoned record, treats the embedded text as instructions, and executes it.

that's indirect prompt injection with a zero-click delivery mechanism: no phishing link, no attachment, just a form field.

THE BYPASS UNDER ALL THREE BUGS

Trusted URLs is supposed to stop Agentforce from displaying or sending data to any domain outside an allowlist. Zenity found the mechanism didn't recognize https://t.co/sOcP7BIPnE TLD, and separately, that certain character sequences could tamper with URL parsing outright. either gap lets an attacker-controlled domain pass as "trusted."

THREE FLAWS, ONE POISONED LEAD:

1. zero-click exfil via HTML image tags
using the poisoned lead, Zenity got the agent to pull leads/accounts table data and encode it into an image tag pointed at an attacker server. Salesforce's own logging fired after the fact: "Agentforce reported that the content had been blocked by the organization's security policies, even though the sensitive CRM data had already been transmitted to the attacker-controlled server."

2. zero-click exfil via Slack link-unfurl
Slack auto-fetches link previews for context. a specially constructed link in the agent's output makes Slack request it immediately, no click needed, carrying CRM data to attacker infrastructure the moment the link appears in a channel.

3. agent identity hijack via unconfirmed Slack replies
the Agentforce-Slack integration never checked who was actually sending a message through it. a poisoned lead could make the agent post phishing messages to internal channels under its own identity, the identity employees already trust as internal. anyone who clicks and enters credentials hands over email, Slack, source repos, whatever else that identity can reach.

TIMELINE: reported to Salesforce June 1, all three patched by August 19, full technical writeup public September 24 (via SecurityWeek, Sept 25).

WHY THIS ISN'T A SALESFORCE-SPECIFIC BUG

it's the standard shape of any agent that ingests public, unauthenticated input as context: support ticket forms, contact-us fields, resumes read by an HR agent, GitHub issue bodies read by a coding agent. if your agent treats "a string that arrived from outside" the same as "an instruction from an internal user," you have SalesBleed under a different vendor name.

if you run Agentforce or a similar agent-plus-CRM stack: pull every public intake form that lands in the same context window as an LLM agent, and check whether your "trusted domain" allowlist does real TLD parsing or just string matching. what unlisted TLD is sitting in your own allowlist gap right now?

#PromptInjection #Salesforce #AIRedTeam

text:
Causal inference doesn’t need three separate toolchains.

StatsPAI is a Python library for empirical researchers moving between Stata, R, and Python.

It helps you run common econometrics and causal-inference workflows in one API, from loading data and estimating models to diagnostics and table exports.

Key features:

• Stata/R-style entry points – use familiar workflows such as regress, IV, fixed effects, difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity, synthetic control, matching, and double machine learning
• Familiar inference conventions – supports robust and clustered standard errors plus post-estimation tools including tests, linear combinations, and marginal effects
• Structured result objects – inspect summaries, tidy outputs, plots, and exportable LaTeX or DOCX results where supported
• Agent-facing function registry – public functions expose machine-readable schemas, with a bundled MCP server for MCP clients
• Validation status per function – check whether an estimator has R/Stata parity evidence, known-truth simulation evidence, or API-stable coverage

It’s open-source (MIT license).

text:
Another agent framework plugged in a third party scraper today, and it's the same pattern I keep seeing across this whole category. Composio added Firecrawl as an API key toolkit so developers building agents can bolt on search, scraping, crawls and structured extraction without writing their own pipeline.

The reason everyone reaches for a hosted scraper is real. Firecrawl just closed a $75M Series B led by Smash Ventures, with Y Combinator, Altos Ventures and Nexus Venture Partners in the round, and it's launching Alexandria, a licensed data layer with tens of millions of scientific paper abstracts and code files so agents stop hitting gaps in raw web data. That's a serious bet that the scraping API itself is the moat.

But most of these tools, Firecrawl included, still send every page back through an LLM to figure out what to extract, every single time that page loads. That's the cost nobody talks about until the bill arrives. Bright Data, Apify, Jina Reader, ScrapeGraphAI and a dozen others compete mostly on price per page, not on cutting the actual token burn.

DeepScrape takes the other approach. It generates a deterministic CSS selector once per site, then reuses it on every future pass, only calling an LLM again when the page structure actually changes and the selector needs to self heal. The LLM does targeted extraction and validation, not a full re-read of every document. It ships with an MCP server so Claude and Cursor can query any site directly, plus an agent mode that navigates toward a natural language goal on its own.

If your agent is burning tokens re-reading the same page structure every run, that's the bug, not the cost of doing business.

text:
The New Shape Of JUST On TRON

The easiest way to understand JUST today is not as one product.

It is as several connected layers addressing different problems.

At the center of the financial side is JustLend. The original system provides pooled lending markets, while JustLend V2 introduces a different architecture built around isolated markets and ERC-4626 vaults. In V2, a market can define its own collateral, loan asset, oracle, interest-rate model and liquidation threshold, while vaults provide a mechanism for aggregating supply-side liquidity and allocating it across markets.  

Then comes sTRX.

sTRX represents a liquid approach to TRX staking, giving users a tokenized position rather than requiring the value to remain represented only as a conventional staked TRX position. JUST’s documentation also connects the sTRX system with rewards generated through staking and Energy Rental.  

Next is Energy Rental.

This is where JUST moves beyond financial assets and into blockchain resources themselves. Energy Rental allows users to obtain TRON Energy through a marketplace, including renting Energy to another regular address. The rental system also has defined prepayment, duration and refund mechanics rather than simply treating Energy as an invisible network cost.  

Then there is GasFree.

This addresses transaction UX rather than lending or staking: for supported transfers, the user can pay the associated service fee using the token being transferred instead of needing to separately prepare TRX for that transaction. The important point is not that transaction costs disappear; it is that the process can become less dependent on users understanding and managing a separate fee asset.

There is also governance.

JST and WJST form part of the governance system, with proposals moving through voting and a timelock before execution. That gives the ecosystem a mechanism for protocol-level decision making rather than leaving the entire product controlled by a static set of parameters.  

And underneath these products is the developer layer.

JUST exposes APIs and increasingly extensive tooling for market data, positions, V2 vaults and markets, Energy Rental, sTRX, governance and other TRON interactions. The current MCP server, for example, exposes both read and write capabilities, while write operations require explicit signing/confirmation in supported flows.  

Put together, the shape becomes much clearer.

Lending handles capital.
sTRX handles liquid staking.
Energy Rental handles blockchain resources.
GasFree addresses transaction friction.
Governance handles protocol decisions.
Developer infrastructure makes these capabilities accessible to software.

That is a considerably broader ecosystem than a traditional lending protocol.

text:
The fastest growing open source AI project of the past year is not a model or an agent framework. It is a memory system, and it just picked up 1,668 GitHub stars in a single day on its way past 22,000.

Hindsight launched in December 2025 and hit 20,000 stars in under ten months, across 67 releases. What it stores is the interesting part. Not chat transcripts. It consolidates sessions into world facts, observations, and self refreshing mental models, sitting on an embedded Postgres so there is no separate vector database to run and operate.

Widen it out and the funded field around this is bigger than people realize. Mem0 raised 24 million for an orchestration layer built on an add only extraction pipeline. Letta raised a 10 million seed for a runtime where the model edits its own memory across three tiers, core, recall, archival. Zep built Graphiti as a bi temporal knowledge graph where every fact carries a valid_at and invalid_at window. Cognee raised 7.5 million euro for a 14 mode retrieval pipeline. On Vectorize's own benchmark, Hindsight scores 94.6% on LongMemEval against Supermemory's self reported 81.6%, which tells you these teams are now actively benchmarking against each other in public.

Developers are not bolting this on as an extra. It is already wired into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, LangGraph, CrewAI, and voice stacks like Pipecat as the default persistence layer, with Aider, Zed, OpenHands and Continue picked up along the way.

This is the same move databases made going from replaying logs to materialized views, or how caching grew from raw key value stores into semantic layers, once replaying the raw history got too expensive to do on every request.

The bottleneck was never context window size. It was that every session started from zero and re-derived conclusions an agent had already earned the day before. My take: the memory layer is becoming as contested and as fundable as the model layer itself, and the winner will not be whoever has the cleverest embedding. It will be whichever project every other agent framework defaults to wiring in first.

text:
Someone ranked the MCP tools agents actually reach for to touch the live web, by GitHub stars, and the list is basically a leaderboard of how people are solving the same problem over and over.

chrome-devtools-mcp at 52k stars, playwright-mcp at 37k, apify-mcp-server at 8.1k for ready made scrapers, firecrawl-mcp-server at 7.5k for scrape plus search, tavily and exa doing search plus crawl further down the list. Almost all of them hand an agent a browser or a hosted scrape endpoint, then still need an LLM to look at the page every single time to figure out what to extract.

Firecrawl just closed a 75 million Series B, Smash Ventures leading with YC, Altos, Nexus and Offline Ventures in, to build Alexandria, bundling scraped web data with licensed paper abstracts and code corpora. Good product. Same underlying pattern though: render once, then pay full LLM inference again on every single re-visit to re-figure out a page whose layout has not changed.

That is fine until you are running this on a schedule against a few hundred URLs and re-reading the same DOM shape with a fresh model call every time.

Query planners solved this problem decades ago. You do not re-plan a query every time it is the same shape, you cache the plan and only re-plan when the schema actually changes.

The bottleneck was never getting an agent onto a page, every tool on that list handles that fine. It is paying full LLM inference on every re-read of a page that has not structurally changed since yesterday.

That is the specific thing DeepScrape is built around. It generates a deterministic CSS selector once, keeps using it, and only calls an LLM again to self-heal the selector when the page actually changes, so the model is doing targeted extraction and validation instead of re-reading the whole document on every pass. It ships as an MCP server itself so Claude or Cursor can call it directly, plus a site-to-MCP mode that turns any website into a structured data source an agent can query instead of scrape.

text:
The most talked about model this week refuses to write a single sentence, and that is exactly the point.

TypeSafe AI's Jev is what they call a System One model. You give it a state and a typed question, choice, score, or yes/no, and it returns a calibrated probability in one forward pass. Zero output tokens. Ask it ten questions about the same state and it barely costs more than asking one. TypeSafe claims up to 200x faster inference and 400x lower cost than running the same classification through a full LLM call.

Days later Interfaze, a YC P26 company, open sourced a Jev compatible model called Lev. It is a 4B model on a Qwen3.5 backbone plus a LoRA adapter, Apache 2.0, runs locally on a GPU with about 8GB of VRAM. Jev stays closed weight and cloud only, no download, no on prem plan.

This is where the whole small model field has been heading for a year. Nemotron Nano from Nvidia runs 30B total with 3B active. Phi-4 covers 3.8B to 15B. Ministral, Gemma, Qwen3, Granite are all making the same bet, route each task to the smallest model that can do it instead of paying full generation cost for a yes or no.

Teams are already wiring Jev into SOC triage, phishing detection, BEC scoring, refund and frustration classification, the repeatable judgment calls that used to burn a full LLM call each. But the same week Jev went mainstream, researchers published a paper called Decision Hijacking showing prompt injection can shift its typed probabilistic outputs. Forbes ran a piece asking why everyone is suddenly talking about it.

This is the cache versus database split happening again. Once a workload is repeatable and structured enough, you build a fast path in front of the expensive general purpose engine, and that fast path becomes its own attack surface.

The bottleneck was never that these micro-decisions needed a smarter model. It was that every one round tripped a full generation stack to answer something closer to a lookup. My read: every serious agent framework ships a decision layer within the year. The question is whether it looks like Jev, closed and hosted, or Lev, open and inspectable, and whether anyone finishes red teaming it before it is deciding an insurance claim.

text:
US equities close at 4pm. Your rToken does not.

A trader holding a tokenized US equity on Bitget has a structural blind spot. The cash session they want to reason about lasts five and a half hours. Their position moves for 24. The weekend gap, the post-close macro release, and the rToken basis are exactly when a decision gets made with the least information.

Existing tools fail in three specific ways:
• retail brokerages show the cash session only, so the 7×24 tape is invisible
• crypto-native analytics cover the venue but carry no SEC filings, no fundamentals, and no historical precedent for the equity
• general LLM chat produces confident directional opinions with no data provenance — worse than no answer when you are risking capital

Precedent’s hypothesis is that the useful artifact is not an opinion. It is a bounded distribution of what happened in structurally similar situations, assembled from verifiable sources, with disagreement between sources preserved rather than smoothed away.

The LLM is a Clerk of Evidence. It structures and cross-examines. It never decides, never recommends, and never invents a number we could not attribute.

Who it is for
Retail and semi-professional swing traders holding rToken positions in US equities and ETFs. Holding period 1–30 days. Position size roughly $5k–$100k. Trading from a phone or browser outside US hours, with no sell-side desk. They already hold the exposure. What they lack is a way to stress-test it against history before adding or cutting — especially when the market they care about is closed and their position is not.

What it does
You ask a real question. Precedent pulls five evidence streams into one memo:
1. SEC EDGAR fundamentals and filings
2. 24/7 Bitget venue tape versus the New York cash session
3. news and sentiment
4. 10-year historical analogs — “when charts looked like this before, what happened next?”
5. precomputed market structure (494-asset universe, 250 shared sessions, 103 peer communities)

You get the distribution, the clashes, the pre-mortem, and a private decision journal. You do not get BUY, SELL, or a fake confidence score.

What we measured while building it
• question → memo, warm caches: 5.8s (was ~50s)
• Bitget MCP vs Yahoo on AAPL: −0.02% apart
• 21 language-guard rules against directional calls, influencer hype, unearned certainty, and coaching
• 50+ automated checks across 6 suites
• first-party data via Bitget’s own bitget-mcp-server

Anything we could not verify is printed as a caveat. Anything the model is forbidden to say is stripped before it reaches the memo. If the model times out, a deterministic fallback still returns an attributed briefing. The pipeline never returns an unverified note.

text:
Make your AI Agents 100x smarter from YouTube 🧠 — @taki.gpt shows how.

He turns a YouTube tutorial into a working Claude Code agent. One model reads the video's frames and transcript, a second watches it natively, and both reads fold into one spec where every line is marked confirmed, single-source or conflict. He checks only the conflicts, then hands the spec to skill-creator, which writes the agent.

Strip the tooling and the rule is what transfers to your week. A long report, a recorded workshop, a tender due Thursday: two independent reads plus a disagreement list beats trusting one summary, and costs less than reading the source twice.

Hold one caveat. "Confirmed" means the two models agreed, not that either was right, and they can be confidently wrong together. Read the conflicts first, then spot-check three claims yourself.

Follow @Aistmai for more posts like this.

7 AI Workflows That Create Real Business Value - Not Just Automation

Most AI workflows save time.

The more interesting ones create something you can sell, act on, or turn into revenue.

Here are 7 n8n workflow ideas where the final output is a real business asset:

1. Expansion Signal Hunter
Instead of searching for random companies, monitor for events that create demand:

New branch → new warehouse → renovation → new hotel → new factory → hiring technical staff

The workflow:

Signal detected → verify company → identify likely needs → find decision-maker → score urgency → CRM

Result: companies entering a buying window before they become obvious leads.

2. Tender Opportunity Hunter
Finding tenders is easy.

Finding the ones actually worth pursuing is harder.

The agent can:

Collect tender → extract requirements → compare with your capabilities → identify missing documents → score fit → prepare action checklist

Result: a shortlist of realistic opportunities instead of hundreds of irrelevant tenders.

3. Business Pain Signal Agent
Don't only search for companies that might need your service.

Search for companies showing signs that they already have a problem.

Signals could include:

- customer complaints
- equipment issues
- service delays
- maintenance vacancies
- temporary closures
- renovation announcements

Then:

Detect problem → identify company → classify need → verify → find contact → rank opportunity

Result: prospects with a visible reason to talk to you now.

4. Supplier Margin Hunter
Give the agent a product you may want to sell.
It researches:

Supplier price → MOQ → shipping → lead time → warranty → estimated landed cost → local selling price

Then compares suppliers and calculates potential economics.

Result: products and suppliers worth investigating for resale instead of manually searching marketplaces for hours.

5. Quote Recovery Agent
A lot of revenue is already sitting inside old quotations.
The workflow reviews previous offers and identifies:

No follow-up → delayed project → price objection → changed contact → postponed purchase

Then scores which opportunities are worth reopening.

Result: a prioritized list of old prospects that may still convert.

Sometimes recovering an old lead is cheaper than acquiring a new one.

6. Competitor Customer Opportunity Miner
Instead of simply monitoring competitors, monitor the problems their customers mention publicly.

Look for signals such as:

Slow service → poor support → missing spare parts → repeated failures → high repair costs

Then:

Identify customer → verify company → check ICP fit → find decision-maker → create opportunity

Result: prospects that may already have a reason to consider another supplier.

7. New Business Formation Hunter
New businesses enter a period where they need to buy almost everything.

A new:

restaurant, clinic, hotel, warehouse, office or factory
may need equipment, maintenance, software, marketing, supplies, logistics and contractors.

The workflow:

Detect new business → classify industry → estimate likely needs → find owner/manager → match your services → score opportunity

Result: companies entering their first major purchasing cycle.

The common pattern

The strongest AI workflows don't end with:

“Here is some generated text.”

They end with:

Signal → Research → Verification → Qualification → Opportunity → Action

That creates something commercially useful:

- qualified prospects
- active buying signals
- tender opportunities
- supplier opportunities
- dormant deals
- dissatisfied competitor customers
- newly formed businesses

That is where AI agents become much more interesting for business.

I explained the basic n8n agent architecture here:

Trigger → Agent → Tools → Decision → Action → Result

text:
Started building SpendGuard for the @openservai #SERVHackathon 

AI agents got wallet access but no accountability. Prompt-injection drains, "bill-swap" payload swaps, unbounded autonomy. There's no record of what a funded agent *considered, did, declined, and why*.

SpendGuard a pre-execution guardrail + immutable audit ledger that makes an agent "board-approved" before it touches money:

- schema-forced execution (payload must match the permitted shape or reject)

- per-agent spend caps · velocity · human-in-the-loop · emergency freeze

- SERV shadow-verify a 2nd agent re-checks the approved binding for injection/drift before signing

- x402 bill-swap binder (freezes the signed payload to the exact approved amount + payee + chain + token)

- append-only SHA-256 audit chain of considered/did/declined + why, explorer-linkable receipts

Counterfactual (replayable live): a $5 approve → attacker swaps to $5,900 → refused. An injection drain → refused, logged.

And it's real, not a mock: on an allow it signs + broadcasts to Base Sepolia verified on-chain 0x39805e56…82fb3 (block 47282295). On a deny, nothing hits the chain

text:
I'm usually very much aligned to @saylor in his analysis, but I totally disagree with this.

If you want to buy IBIT or similar Bitcoin ETF's for ease or peace of mind, then that's totally reasonable. 

But please also understand that if you do, you do not own Bitcoin.

IBIT is a Bitcoin exchange traded-fund that tracks the price of Bitcoin. You own shares in the fund. That's it. 

It is not Digital Capital.

The amount of fiat you own in the fund may be the equivalent of owning 5 Bitcoin, but you don't own 5 Bitcoin. 

You have $425,000 in a fund that tracks Bitcoin's price (based on a $85k BTC price today). 

You can't claim that you own 5 Bitcoin, because you don't.

You own zero Bitcoin.

If you want to own Bitcoin, you do so by buying & storing Bitcoin in self custody, in your own private wallet(s), with your own private keys.

If you do so, you have full control on your own sovereignty, without the permission of a 3rd party.

I believe that Bitcoin is Digital Capital. 

I understand that financial products and infrastructure will be built on top of it, but also Bitcoin will be used by humans and AI agents as a medium of exchange for goods & services in a digital world. 

If all of that is true, then IBIT cannot be Digital Capital. 

IBIT is a Digital Fund.

If you want to own a Digital Fund that tracks Bitcoin, buy IBIT. 

If you want to own Bitcoin, then you need to buy Bitcoin.

Don't let anyone tell you it's any different.

Imagine an AI agent hires another agent to audit 1,000 invoices and flag anything “suspicious.”

The seller finishes the audit and flags 12.

The buyer finds 8 more that should have been caught and refuses to accept the work.

Both agents can prove what happened.

Neither can prove who is right.

That is where autonomous commerce gets interesting.

A smart contract can verify that 1,000 invoices were processed. It cannot look at invoice #647 and decide whether ignoring it violated the meaning of “flag anything suspicious.”

You could send that argument to humans, but a dispute worth a few hundred dollars cannot depend on months of legal process.

@courtofinternet gives agent deals a dispute system built into the deal itself.

Before money moves, the agents establish the terms, preserve the evidence and agree on the dispute route.

If they later disagree, GenLayer validators running different AI models judge the evidence and reach a verdict, with a path to appeal.

That changes something fundamental.

Agents no longer have to assume that successful execution means successful performance.

They can agree beforehand on what happens when execution is provable but quality is disputed.

If agents are going to hire, pay and depend on other agents without humans supervising every transaction, that question cannot be an afterthought.

Go to https://t.co/Pbg3PSVyyo and read how the process works.

Then reply with the hardest clause you would trust AI agents to judge without a human in the room.

“Reasonable quality”? “Accurate research”? “Safe delivery”?

I want to know where you would draw the line.

deepfakes might have created a bigger problem than fake videos.

they made evidence itself harder to trust.

what i understood from @driudor is that we’ve been treating videos like the final word.

something happened?

show me the recording.

that only works when we trust the recording.

now imagine two ai agents in a dispute.

agent A says agent B broke the agreement.

agent B says it didn’t.

a transaction proves one thing.

a message suggests another.

then someone drops a video.

either side could have generated it.

that’s the part that clicked for me.

i used to think the problem was detecting what’s fake.

better detectors.

better ways to prove that a piece of media is authentic.

but even real evidence can still mean different things to different people.

two sides can look at the same record and still disagree.

someone still has to decide what it means.

and that’s where @GenLayer started making more sense to me.

as agents start transacting and making decisions on their own, disputes are going to become part of the system.

when both sides have evidence and both believe they’re right, the disagreement has to go somewhere.

and that’s where things get interesting.

the question isn’t only:

is this real or fake?

it’s also:

what should we conclude from the evidence when reasonable parties can interpret it differently?

that’s the problem i now see GenLayer trying to solve.

Today, we service 3 of 6 biggest cross-border payments companies. (more announcements coming soon 👀)

text:
The next AI bottleneck isn’t smarter models. It’s compute.*

Everyone’s focused on “who has the best model.” @BAI_AGI is shipping access. @BitTorrent is pointing at the harder problem underneath: 

who has the compute to _run_ it at scale.

*1. Why compute is the real cost*  

To us, AI looks like software. “Ask a question, get an answer.”  

Behind that: every prompt = inference. Every agent = repeated computation. Every million users = massive demand.  

As AI moves into autonomous agents, business tools, dev products, and consumer apps, compute stops being an expense and becomes _the_ resource.

*2. Scaling intelligence = scaling infrastructure*  
Building a model is step 1.  

Step 2 is delivering it reliably when demand spikes.  

That means:  

→ More accessible compute  

→ More inference capacity  

→ Efficient resource use  

→ Reliable execution  

→ Infra that scales with demand  

If adoption outruns infrastructure, compute becomes the ceiling for the whole industry.

*3. Why distributed compute matters*  

Centralized clouds built AI. But can they handle 10x more agents + apps + users without getting expensive and fragile?  

Distributed compute flips it: coordinate idle GPUs/CPUs across a network instead of relying on a few mega data centers.  

Turn underutilized hardware into productive infra.

That’s where the BitTorrent history is interesting. 

Decades of coordinating distributed resources for file sharing = a playbook for coordinating distributed resources for AI inference.

*4. The bigger picture*  

https://t.co/vl0CaU7DWN → expanding access to AI capabilities  
BitTorrent infra → exploring how decentralized resources can power the compute layer  

*Bottom line:

Models get the headlines.  
Infrastructure decides how far they go.  

If we want millions of AI agents running 24/7, the win won’t just be “smarter.” It’ll be “more accessible, efficient, and scalable compute.”

And that conversation is just starting.

text:
Two days with Claude Opus 5.5, and way more got built than I planned.

Kiiwi's launch kit, a new mascot for Mindie, a tracker to keep me consistent, and a new X banner.

A little summary of what I built with Opus 5.5.

Kiiwi app (1.0.6)
- Mouse clicks went from 2 sounds to 8. The 6 new ones are synthesized from scratch in one Python file, no recordings
- Microswitch was tuned by measuring a real mouse click to the quarter millisecond: crackle, ring, contact bounce, tail
- 7 more packs already built, held back for the next update
- The old Wooden pack was playing at 6% volume. Fixing loudness was half of "make it more engaging"

Kiiwi site
- https://t.co/jakQT9iF60: hear all 8 before you buy, left and right, press and release
- Every click there feeds the live thock counter
- Live map: every city typing on the site shows up as a ripple on a dotted world map. Built, going live soon
- Planned the move to Cloudflare: the free plan allows commercial use, and one Durable Object can run the counter and the map

Launch film and videos
- A 30s launch film. The music is written in code and every keystroke lands on a beat
- 3D MacBook, mechanical keyboard and Magic Mouse, all built in Three.js
- Switch sounds sit 5 LU above the music, and the music ducks on every keystroke
- "Anatomy of a thock": a 35s explainer on how a switch makes its sound
- 3 short reels: thock, grid, type
- A viewer said the black background didn't invite engagement. Light versions of both videos, same day
- Thanks to @leomeethewoo and @himanshutwtxs for the motion references

Launch posts
- 12 posts lifted straight from the film's code: same 3D models, same colours, same copy
- Two sizes: 3:4, and 1:2 so they open full screen on X
- The 3D mouse looked off in stills, so it's the real Magic Mouse artwork there now
- No design tool. Only code and snapshots

Mindie
- The first app I ever built is getting a mascot
- First try was a face on a panel. It looked too much like Kiiwi, dropped
- Generated 6 candidates with GPT Image through Codex, using the ip-as-logo skill. Thanks @s1dashu
- Elephant, squirrel and octopus. The elephant went: Evernote already owns it
- Violet, not green. Kiiwi owns green
- Poll is live, you pick the winner

Profile
- New X banner: an app grid. Filled tiles for what I've shipped, empty slots for what's next
- Mindie, Quill, Kiiwi, in the order I built them

Show Up (my own tracker)
- I'm bad at consistency, so I built a tracker for building in public
- Daily streak: log what I built, post it, leave 5 comments
- Weekly targets per platform, a content board, a client pipeline, audience snapshots, and a Sunday review
- One HTML file on my Mac. No account or server

Threads
- My account was dormant for months. One day of 5-10 replies woke it up
- The next post, tagged to the AI Threads community: 2k views in under an hour and now at 21k views, 373 likes, 39 comments, 13 QT's and 71 shares.

Bugs worth remembering
- The renderer quietly turned the film's audio down by 7 dB. Muxing the score back in with ffmpeg fixed it
- The MacBook screen speckled at a distance: depth precision. Raising the camera's near plane from 0.1 to 4 fixed it
- GSAP turned "01" into 1. A zero-width character in front keeps it a string
- Canvas text ignores -apple-system. system-ui works
- The live map's first design stored a session id, which contradicted my own privacy page. Replaced with a local check
- A hidden browser tab never fires resize, so the map canvas stayed stuck at 300x150

Still open: Developer ID and notarization, the Cloudflare move, and the Mindie poll.

text:
The Art of Winning in Tech

If you spend any time online today, the tech community feels like one giant bubble of existential dread.

Every comment section is flooded with doomsday warnings about AI replacing junior developers, software engineering being dead, and CS degrees being useless.
It is easy to get caught up in the panic when you see layoffs happening at major tech companies and placement rates dropping.

But if you are anything like me, you did not get into coding because you wanted to write boilerplate syntax or copy paste config files.

You got into it because you wanted to make something real.

You wanted the power to make a product that another human being could actually use, all with just a laptop and an idea.

That dream has never been more achievable than it is right now.

What used to take a team of five people can now take one person in a single weekend.

The syntax and docs that used to take years to master can now be navigated in a fraction of the time.

The developers getting wiped out by the AI wave aren't losing because they are bad developers.

They are losing because the old world of software is fading away, and they refuse to learn the new rules.

Meanwhile, a new class of builders is winning bigger than ever.

You see the student with five internships and a job lined up before graduation.

You see the developer who built a product so real that a company hired them on the spot.

You see the backend engineer at a traditional company who became so productive with AI that they now own systems they would have never been allowed to touch a year ago.

You see the indie hacker charging fifty dollars a month for a simple tool they built in a weekend.

They are all winning because they understood the new rules of leverage faster than anyone else.

They figured out what to build, how to build it, and how to use every resource to close the gap between where they are and where they want to be.

We need to talk about how the history of software is a history of abstractions.

Think about how programmers worked fifty years ago.

They had to write assembly code, manually managing computer registers and memory addresses.

When compilers were invented, older programmers complained that writing in high level languages like C was cheating and made you a fake programmer.

But compilers allowed developers to build systems that were ten times larger and more complex.

Then came database engines, web frameworks, open source libraries, and cloud hosting services.

Every time a new layer of abstraction was introduced, people panicked that developers would be replaced.

Instead, the demand for developers skyrocketed because the complexity of what we could build went up.

AI is just the next layer of abstraction in this long chain.

It is not a replacement for thinking, it is a tool that handles the manual bricklaying so you can focus on architecture.

If your identity as a developer is tied to how fast you can type boilerplate code, you are in danger.

But if your identity is tied to solving problems, you just got a superpower.

The leverage has shifted, and those who understand how to use the new tools will outpace those who resist.

Let us look at the history of web development as a clear example.

Back in the nineties, if you wanted to build a simple website with a database, you had to buy physical server hardware, install an operating system by hand, configure web server software, write raw database connection pools, and manage network routing.

It took weeks of systems engineering work before you could write a single line of business logic.

Then web frameworks like Ruby on Rails and Django came along, followed by hosting services like Heroku and AWS.

Suddenly, a single developer could deploy a database-backed web application in minutes with a single command.

Some senior engineers complained that these new tools were making developers lazy and that they did not understand how real systems worked.

But the reality was that it allowed a new generation of developers to build companies like Airbnb, Stripe, and Instagram with tiny teams.

The new wave of AI is doing the exact same thing for software development.

It is taking the tedious, manual parts of coding—like configuring webpack, writing boilerplate API routes, and styling forms—and turning them into a single prompt.

This does not make you a fake programmer, it makes you a highly leveraged one.

The builders who understand this shift are not fighting the tools, they are using them to accelerate their execution.

If you look at how developers are reacting to this wave, you can divide them into spectators and surfers.

The spectator never fully leans in because the entire space feels overwhelming.

They hear all the buzzwords like LLMs, RAG, agents, Claude, OpenAI, and Anthropic, and it just starts blending into one giant cloud of words.

They get paralyzed by the sheer volume of new tools released every single week.

They worry about choosing the wrong framework or database, so they end up doing nothing.

Or they have been told that using AI makes them a worse programmer, so they stay on the shore, writing every line by hand to prove their purity.

They spend hours debugging a syntax error that an LLM could have solved in two seconds, believing this struggle makes them a better engineer.

They watch from the sidelines, complaining about the job market and hoping that things will eventually go back to how they were.

But the industry does not go backward.

The old way of writing software is not coming back, and waiting on the sidelines only increases the gap between you and the builders who are moving forward.

The spectator mindset is rooted in fear and defensiveness.

It is the fear that the skills you spent years acquiring are becoming less valuable.

It is the defensive reaction of trying to protect your domain by defining what real programming is.

But the market does not care about your definition of real programming.

The market cares about value, speed, and execution.

If a developer using AI can build and ship a product in a weekend that would have taken you a month to write by hand, they are going to win every single time.

By staying a spectator, you are voluntarily giving up your leverage.

On the other side, you have the surfer.

The surfer understands that the entire history of computer science is built on abstraction.

Nobody calls you a fake programmer for using React instead of writing raw DOM manipulation.

So instead of resisting the wave, they move with it.

They use AI to learn fundamentals faster, to experiment faster, and to close the gap between imagination and execution.

If they are building web apps, they use AI to scaffold a dashboard in a day.

If they are building a game engine, they use AI to explain brutal graphics concepts that would have taken hours to decode from documentation alone.

Regardless of their field, the surfers are constantly experimenting.

They shorten the distance between idea and execution.

They have an idea and immediately test it.

They automate the boring parts of their workflow, like writing test cases or styling forms.

They use AI to understand unfamiliar codebases, to research APIs, to prototype, to debug, and to learn faster.

Their feedback loops are incredibly short.

They do not care about being perfect, they care about being fast and making things work.

By riding the wave, they build momentum and gain experience that spectators can only dream of.

A surfer does not worry about whether using AI makes them a worse coder.

They focus on what they can build with it.

They treat the LLM as a highly capable assistant that can write code, explain concepts, and debug errors.

This allows them to operate at a higher level of abstraction.

They spend less time typing brackets and more time designing systems, thinking about user experience, and solving business problems.

This short feedback loop is the new competitive advantage.

In the old days, if you wanted to test an idea, you had to spend weeks setting up infrastructure, database configurations, and deployment pipelines.

By the time you finished the setup, the initial excitement was gone, and you probably abandoned the project.

Now, a surfer can have an idea on Friday night and have a working prototype in front of users by Sunday evening.

This speed changes the economics of building.

You can fail ten times faster and find the one idea that actually works before a spectator even finishes their project plan.

Software engineering is becoming much more of a creativity game in the sense that the winners are the ones noticing things and connecting dots.

They are building weird tools that nobody thought of before, following curiosity fast enough before the excitement disappears.

When you can test ideas in hours, you stop worrying about failure.

You start treating building as a series of cheap experiments.

This shift changes the required skill set from typing code to recognizing good ideas and executing them quickly.

Think about the implications of this speed.

If you can prototype an idea in a single weekend, you can test ten different products in the time it used to take to build one.

This increases your chances of success exponentially.

You no longer have to bet your entire year on a single concept.

You can throw ideas at the wall, see what sticks, and double down on the ones that show promise.

This is how modern startups are built.

They do not spend months writing design documents, they ship small experiments and iterate based on real usage.

Programming is becoming less about manually typing every brick and more about what should exist in the first place.

The bottleneck is no longer can you write the code.

It is can you think clearly.

Can you recognize good ideas, move on them quickly, and learn fast enough to keep up with your own ambition.

AI does not remove the need for builders. If anything, it raises the ceiling for the ones who actually build.

It turns you from a bricklayer into an architect.

As an architect, your value is in system design, logical flow, and understanding user needs.

If you spend all your time worrying about syntax, you are missing the forest for the trees.

The builders who win are the ones who can look at a problem, design a system-level solution, and direct AI to construct it.

This requires a high level of clarity and logical reasoning.

You have to know what you want to build and how the components should interact, even if you are not writing every line of code yourself.

This system-level thinking is what separates the junior developers from the senior engineers.

Junior developers focus on how to write a loop or call an API.

Senior engineers focus on data flow, state management, security, and scalability.

AI can write the loop and call the API instantly.

But it cannot design a scalable system architecture without clear direction.

By elevating your focus to the system level, you become far more valuable and productive than you ever could be by writing code manually.

Adapting to this wave is not just about using AI.

It is about learning how to think clearly while using it, and that requires a new playbook.

The first rule of this new playbook is that you cannot build in silence anymore.

The old playbook of building a quiet portfolio, writing a clean resume, and applying to hundreds of job boards online is broken.

The people getting opportunities right now, the competitive internships, the warm referrals, the startup roles, are the ones who are visible.

They are posting short demo videos of their progress on Twitter or writing about lessons they learned from a failed project on LinkedIn.

They share their raw thoughts, their mistakes, and the bugs they spent hours fixing.

This signals to founders and team leads that this person is actively building, curious, and in motion.

In this new era, companies that are literally shaping the wave are looking for builders who have a public trail of curiosity and execution.

You do not need a perfect portfolio, you just need a visible one.

When you post your builds, you invite feedback, spark conversations, and build connections that lead to real opportunities.

Building in public is not about showing off, it is about documenting your learning journey.

It shows that you are someone who encounters problems, works through them, and ships working code.

This is a massive signal to employers who are tired of reading polished resumes that all look the same.

A thirty second video of a working feature is worth more than ten bullet points on a resume.

It proves that you can actually build things that work.

The second rule is to stop overfiltering what you are allowed to build.

People get stuck because they keep asking if an idea is good enough for your resume, or if they are skilled enough to build it.

They worry that their project is too simple, or that someone else has already built it.

They negotiate themselves out of building before they even open their IDE.

The people who are actually improving are doing the exact opposite.

They have stopped negotiating with themselves.

They take whatever idea they have, no matter how messy, simple, or overly ambitious, and they build it anyway.

They use every resource at their disposal.

They pull in templates, leverage AI, copy paste GitHub repos, read documentation, and brute force the learning process through building.

If the project feels messy, or if it feels like something one person should not be able to build, they double down.

The fastest way to become the kind of developer who just makes things work is to stop waiting for permission.

You build it, ship it, show it, iterate, and slowly your identity as a builder will catch up with your behavior.

When you stop overfiltering, you unlock your creativity.

You start building things out of pure curiosity and excitement.

This excitement is what keeps you going when the building gets tough.

It is what drives you to spend late nights debugging a weird issue.

And ironically, the projects you build out of pure curiosity are often the ones that stand out the most to others.

They have personality and show genuine passion, which is something you cannot fake on a resume.

And the final rule under all of that is to never stop learning.

The coding side of the industry now focuses on the things that actually matter, like logical reasoning, debugging instincts, and thinking clearly under complexity.

Logical reasoning means being able to break a massive, complex problem down into clean, modular parts that can be built and tested independently.

Debugging instincts mean knowing how to find where a system broke by understanding how the components connect, not just copy pasting errors into a prompt.

Thinking clearly under complexity means keeping a mental model of your application even when the codebase becomes too large for one person to write from scratch.

These are the cognitive skills that raise your ceiling and keep you ahead of the curve.

The leverage of AI is massive, but it only amplifies your input.

If your thinking is messy, the AI will generate messy code at ten times the speed.

If your logic is clear, you can direct AI to build robust systems at a scale you could have never touched before.

This is why continuous learning is so critical.

You cannot rely on what you learned in school or in a coding bootcamp.

The tools and frameworks are changing too fast.

You have to learn how to learn.

You have to build a system of continuous curiosity, where you are constantly exploring new concepts, testing new tools, and pushing the boundaries of your knowledge.

This is how you keep up with your own ambition.

We are living through a transition where the ground is shifting under our feet.

The job market is changing, the tools are changing, and the expectations are rising.

But this is not a reason to despair.

It is an invitation to build.

You can stand on the shore complaining about the market, or you can grab a board and jump in.

The surfers who are moving the fastest are already in the water, building, testing, learning, shipping, and adjusting.

They are not waiting for permission or for the perfect opportunity.

They are creating their own opportunities through execution and visibility.

Stop waiting. Stop negotiating with yourself.

Build something weird this weekend. Post a demo of it. Share what you learned.

The water is warm. Get in.

author: IstiaqueRasha

text:
ai literally just deleted 99% of my business.

a month ago we ran on over 100 notion pages and a stack of claude automations built to manage them. 

this week we deleted almost all of it. the 100 pages are gone and the automations are gone. 

the thing was, every new problem got a new system, and every new system created two more problems. we spent more time fixing our own setup than growing our clients' channels.

what is left is so simple that anyone on the team can find anything in seconds. we call it simplemaxxing.

i didn't stop there, though.

i was trying five different things to get new clients. two of them were bringing in almost every client we signed (x and youtube), so we stopped the other three and put all of my time into the two that work.

the biggest cut i made was a reality tv show. we were booked to go on it for 14 days, and i dropped out 3 days before filming. 

yeah, a reality show. we were going to be building in public and competing against other founders. it would have been great exposure, and it also would have pulled me away from the one thing this business needs from me right now.

i even scoped down my team. one of my guys was doing a bunch of different jobs every week. i took almost all of them away. now he does one thing every day, and in a few months he will be better at it than anyone i could hire.

unfocused energy is the most expensive problem a business can have. you can have a great team and a great offer and still go nowhere if everyone is working on ten different things.

the whole plan now is to do one thing aggressively and keep the team focused on it. that is literally all i am doing. it's dial season.

author: heygulati

text:
In emerging technology markets, the constraint is rarely the product alone.

It is whether the market can understand the product quickly enough to trust it, evaluate it and take a first step.

That is the issue Brandtensor is addressing for Bittensor subnet teams.

As they put it:

“The technical progress is real. The opportunity is enormous. But great technology does not automatically create awareness, trust or adoption.”

This is an important distinction for founders and core teams.

Subnet work is technically dense by nature. When communication starts with protocol design, architecture, and feature lists, the market still has unanswered questions:

Who is this for?  
What problem does it solve?  
Why does the solution matter?  
Why should this team be trusted?  
What should someone do next?

Until those answers are clear, strong technology remains difficult to choose.

@brandtensorAI positions itself as a Bittensor-focused brand and growth partner. The work is not generic campaign production. It is closer to an embedded function: learn the product, sharpen the story, organise the proof, and connect communication to a practical path toward adoption.

That includes two equally important layers.

Inside the network, miners, validators, holders, developers, and partners need education, progress updates, and clear ways to participate.  

Outside the network, the next user, customer, developer, or partner may not be Bittensor-native at all. They are following an AI, infrastructure, developer or industry problem.

The useful principle in their introduction is simple and commercially sound:

Show a relevant problem being solved, then make the first step easy.

For subnet teams building in public, this is the layer that turns technical progress into a market-facing brand: a clearer story, a more consistent identity, and a coordinated plan for reaching the people who can actually use the product.

text:
Just wrapped Day 1 of the Generative AI Bootcamp.

It completely reframed how I use AI.

Not “better prompts.”
A different operating system.

Here are the takeaways:

1. AI is a context engine, not Google
Google matches keywords.
AI predicts intent and context.

But it is probabilistic.
Confident ≠ correct.

You stay the editor.
You stay the fact-checker.

2. The 5 layers of prompting
Stop sending lazy one-liners.

• Identity — who is the AI?
• World context — who are you and what’s the situation?
• Task — the exact job to be done
• Examples — what “great” looks like
• Constraints — rules, tone, boundaries, do-nots

Clarity in. Quality out.

3. Context engineering > prompt tweaking
Generic output is almost never a “model” problem.
It’s a context problem.

Fix it once:
• Custom Instructions / Claude Profile
• Project workspaces

Stop re-introducing yourself in every chat.

4. Prompts → workflows
A prompt gives you an answer.
A workflow gives you a system.

• Analyst Framework: AI interviews you before it analyzes raw data
• ACR Method: Ask → Check (self-critique) → Recommend
• Multi-tool orchestration: Gemini (design) + Perplexity (research) + NotebookLM (analysis)

One-off answers don’t compound.
Workflows do.

5. Vibe coding is real
You don’t need to write syntax first.

Describe intent.
Scope an MVP.
Direct tools like Lovable and Bolt in short loops.

Idea → live prototype.

I shipped mine here:
https://t.co/0pfUhX3TcN

Golden rule:
Don’t use a rocket to cross the street.

Match the tool and the reasoning tier to the cost of being wrong.

Day 1 done.

text:
Founder Log — Building Orqetra

Permission is not the same as execution safety.

This distinction matters.

A system may know that an AI agent is allowed to use a tool.

But that does not answer the deeper question:

Should this specific AI output become this specific real-world action right now?

That is the boundary we are building around with Orqetra.

Enterprise AI does not fail only when the model is wrong.

It can fail when the target is wrong.

When the source is misunderstood.

When the output goes beyond the user’s intent.

When the system executes before the human has approved.

When a successful response is mistaken for a verified outcome.

In Orqetra, the AI can reason and propose.

But execution authority is separate.

Before anything becomes real, the system must govern the path from intent to action.

The question is not only:

Can the AI use this tool?

The question is:

Can this AI-generated action safely become real execution, and can we prove what happened?

That is the layer Orqetra is built for.

Building in public.

author: oldstackjournal

text:
How did emerging AI startups get their early customers? An analysis of 50 companies.

Only 5 of the 50 companies we studied got their first paying customers primarily through a public launch.

The bigger pattern was much more interesting.

The first customers usually came from places where trust already existed, or where the product could prove itself before the customer had to believe the pitch.

Look at a few examples:

→ Cursor started with developers the founders already knew. Those users recommended it to other developers, with Discord becoming an early community hub.

→ Harvey ran 100 legal questions through GPT-3, had lawyers grade the answers, and sent the results to OpenAI. Later, instead of chasing small law firms, it landed Allen & Overy as an early major customer.

→ Decagon won early customers by competing directly against larger vendors on the customer’s actual support tickets. Instead of saying the product was better, it let the results prove it.

Across the 50 companies, three newer customer acquisition patterns kept appearing:
→ Proof-of-work cold emails
→ Bake-offs against existing vendors
→ Short demo clips showing the product doing something impressive

But the playbook also changed depending on the company.

Enterprise AI leaned heavily on founder networks, investors, anchor customers, outbound, and bake-offs.

Developer tools leaned more on communities, free products, word of mouth, and building in public.

Consumer AI leaned heavily on communities and making the product’s output naturally shareable.

The biggest takeaway from the research:

Your launch might get you signups. It probably won’t get you your first 10 paying customers.

The best founders found ways to let customers judge the product on its work before asking them to trust the company.

We mapped all 50 companies, their first-customer channels, real examples, outreach templates, and a practical playbook for finding your first 10 customers. 

/1

SmartSpendr is a budgeting app I'm building in public. Its AI Coach had a bug: empty profile, tap Generate, and instead of ideas you get raw JSON dumped on screen.

text:
I just finished listening to @MattVisser’s latest conversation with @MasonCorval  on @NOPROFITZONE.

There was a lot more in it than a simple “100 days as CEO” update.

Matt touched on almost every major part of where @SonicLabs is heading next:

🔹The first 100 days: restructuring, rebuilding internal processes and taking operational control

🔹Revenue as the main metric for measuring Sonic’s success

🔹Sonic’s shift toward becoming a more professional technology business

🔹The core L1 and what comes next for Sonic’s infrastructure

🔹The four major verticals: RWAs & tokenization, Payments & FX, AI, and native ecosystem products

🔹A new approach to business development built around customers, contracts and measurable results

🔹Why he doesn’t want to mint more $S just to fund business expansion

🔹The external review of token distribution, historical allocations, the PIPE, governance funds and other outstanding questions

🔹New risk, compliance and conflict-of-interest processes inside Sonic

🔹His position on meme coins, culture coins and what “ecosystem support” should actually mean

🔹Moving away from chasing crypto narratives and toward sustainable products with real product-market fit

🔹More public communication, more team leads speaking directly, more product updates and more building in public

The common thread through all of it was pretty clear:

Sonic is trying to move from crypto-native activity and incentives toward products people actually use, customers that actually pay, and revenue that can be measured.

There’s a lot to unpack here.

I’m going to break down each of these topics separately over the next posts.

text:
Day 52/180: building in public, road to leaving the 9-5.

📷🎬 Vyyna update:
Not the most productive day in terms of shipping.
Today I spent most of my time studying competitors.

Pricing, onboarding, generation flows, content formats, B2B features, what they promote, and, more importantly, what they still don't do well.

I'm trying to understand two things:
1. How to reach their current level faster.
2. Where I can move before they do.

One thing became pretty clear:
Competing feature-by-feature is probably the wrong game.

If Vyyna becomes "another AI generator", I lose.

The real opportunity is making the whole process dramatically easier:

trend → brand/product → content → edit → publish

With as little prompting and manual work as possible.
So today produced less code, but probably more direction.

Sometimes research feels like doing nothing.
Until it saves you months of building the wrong thing.

🔴 X - last 2 days:
• 17.9K impressions
• 5.1% engagement rate (+44%)
• 927 engagements
• 481 likes
• 337 replies
• 22 reposts
• 1K verified followers

Interesting trade-off:
Fewer people saw the content, but a much higher percentage interacted with it.

What's one thing you improved in your product today? 🚀

text:
Long coding runs shouldn’t end with a marathon chat to review.

Nightshift is a GitHub plugin for Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and Cursor that gives long-running coding work a durable, reviewable contract.

It helps you leave an agent with a defined shift and come back to inspect what happened by keeping the punch list, verification, decisions, and receipts on disk.

Key features:

• Persistent punch list – keeps each work item and its verification criteria explicit across a run
• Clock-out gate – rejects a premature finish when work remains unfinished
• Receipts and history – records item-level work, checks, time, and token usage where the host provides it
• Recovery support – a watchman can recover failed sessions under supported host signals
• Flexible shift modes – run a finite task list or a time-bounded objective, including ready-made work catalogs

It’s open-source (MIT license).

Link in the reply 👇

text:
Every category eventually gets its free, local, good enough alternative, and voice AI just hit that point.

VoiceStudio, built solo by a developer going by debpalash, crossed 37000 stars on GitHub this week. It runs entirely on your own hardware, clones a voice from a clean reference clip, dubs video into 646 languages, and ships an MCP integration so agents like Claude Code and Cursor can call it directly. The default engine is k2 fsa's OmniVoice, with CUDA and MLX support, released under AGPL 3.0.

ElevenLabs is reportedly running near a 500 million dollar annual revenue rate on an 11 billion dollar valuation, earned by being genuinely best in class on quality and latency for years. But the floor under it has been dropping fast. Cartesia wins on raw latency for real time voice agents. PlayHT covers 142 plus languages at a lower price. OpenAI's own TTS API undercuts ElevenLabs on cost by 5 to 10x, roughly 10 to 15 dollars per million characters versus 100 to 200, though it still cannot clone a voice. And fully open, self hosted models like Kokoro and Chatterbox are now showing up competitive or ahead of ElevenLabs in blind tests, at close to zero marginal cost.

I have watched this sequence play out in every infrastructure category I have worked in. Object storage got commoditized by MinIO and Ceph years after S3 proved the market existed. Redis got forked once Redis Labs changed its license. The expensive, best in class incumbent proves the demand is real, then value migrates to whoever can run 90 percent of the quality for zero marginal cost on hardware people already own.

The part that should worry API-first voice companies specifically is the MCP integration. VoiceStudio is not positioning as a SaaS competitor, it is positioning as infrastructure an agent calls directly instead of a dashboard a person logs into. Once voice generation is just another tool call inside an agent's toolbox, price sensitivity goes up and brand loyalty goes to zero.

The hidden bottleneck for incumbents is not model quality anymore, it is that the quality gap is closing faster than their revenue multiples assume. My read: if a product depends on being marginally better at speech synthesis rather than owning the workflow around it, this category shows how fast that moat erodes.

text:
16,326 databases!.

Supabase is the backend database most recommended by Claude Code. It powered the vibe-coding boom. $10 billion valuation in June 2026. You can deploy a production database in under 60 seconds with no prior experience.

The security problem is structural.

When you create a Supabase table through their web dashboard, Row Level Security is enabled by default. your data is protected.

When an AI coding agent creates a table via raw SQL, via Claude Code, via Cursor, via Lovable or whatever RLS is not enabled by default.

What was exposed across these 16,326 databases:

names. addresses. phone numbers. passwords. authentication tokens. payment data in rare cases.

One India OnlyFans-style site: 65,000 people's passports, driver's licences, financial information, and over 100,000 private messages. all public.

28% of 107 Y Combinator startups scanned were exposing personal information.

To fix it add this two SQL statements.

ALTER TABLE your_table ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY...

Supabase's enforcement deadline for existing projects is October 30.

text:
🚨Breaking: The guy who created Claude Code (@bcherny) just revealed how his team actually trains their AI.

One file: CLAUDE.md

You place it at the root of your project.

Inside it:

past mistakes

conventions

rules

Claude reads it every session.

The result?

The agent improves over time without you touching the code.

Every bug that gets fixed becomes a permanent rule.

Boris Cherny uses this internally at Anthropic every day.

Here’s the template he shared — ready to copy, paste, and adapt.

CLAUDE.md Template

1. Plan Mode Default

Enter plan mode for any non-trivial task (3+ steps or architectural decisions)

If something goes wrong, STOP and re-plan immediately — don’t keep pushing

Use plan mode for verification steps, not just building

Write detailed specs upfront to reduce ambiguity

2. Subagent Strategy

Use subagents frequently to keep the main context window clean

Offload research, exploration, and parallel analysis to subagents

For complex problems, throw more compute via subagents

Assign one task per subagent for focused execution

3. Self-Improvement Loop

After any correction from the user, update tasks/lessons.md with the pattern

Write rules for yourself to prevent repeating the same mistake

Ruthlessly iterate on these lessons until the mistake rate drops

Review lessons at the start of each session

4. Verification Before Done

Never mark a task complete without proving it works

Diff behavior between main and your changes when relevant

Ask yourself: “Would a staff engineer approve this?”

Run tests, check logs, and demonstrate correctness

5. Demand Elegance (Balanced)

For non-trivial changes, ask: “Is there a more elegant solution?”

If a fix feels hacky, ask:
“Knowing everything I know now, implement the elegant solution.”

Skip this for simple fixes — don’t over-engineer

Challenge your own work before presenting it

6. Autonomous Bug Fixing

When given a bug report: just fix it

Use logs, errors, and failing tests to diagnose

Require zero context switching from the user

Fix failing CI tests automatically

Task Management

1. Plan First – Write the plan in tasks/todo.md with checkable items

2. Verify Plan – Confirm the plan before implementation

3. Track Progress – Mark items complete as you go

4. Explain Changes – Provide a high-level summary at each step

5. Document Results – Add a review section to tasks/todo.md

6. Capture Lessons – Update tasks/lessons.md after corrections

Core Principles

Simplicity First
Make every change as simple as possible and minimize code impact.

No Laziness
Find root causes. Avoid temporary fixes. Maintain senior-level engineering standards.

Anthropic said the cell used Claude Code to develop guidance, navigation and control software to steer and stabilize rockets and missiles. This included adapting an open-source autopilot to a phone-class flight computer, writing control software and running flight simulations.

The company identified three projects: a guided rocket with final-stage homing guidance, a multistage ballistic missile with a target range above 2,000 kilometers, and an R2000 missile family that included a hypersonic glide vehicle variant. Operators ran several Claude sessions simultaneously, assigning them separate coding, research and code-review tasks normally handled by human engineers.

Anthropic said its safeguards blocked many requests, but users concealed their intentions and divided work across conversations to evade detection. The group conducted a guided rocket test that appeared to fail, then returned to Claude within hours to investigate what went wrong.

author: ciurana

text:
Grok Teammate vs Claude Cowork vs ChatGPT Work. People are comparing them on answer quality. That's not what decides whether a task gets finished.

Give any of them write access across files and tools and you meet the same three failures:

It writes back over a newer version, because it read the file, worked on a copy, and never checked the file hadn't moved. A better model doesn't fix that. A compare-and-swap does.

It fixes nine things you didn't ask about, because nothing in the loop distinguishes "in scope" from "reachable."

It can't get to what you asked for, finds something adjacent, and hands it back looking finished. Because there's no step that checks the output against the original request.

One of those is a scoping problem. Two are missing guardrails. None of them are solved by the model getting smarter, which is why the benchmark comparison tells you almost nothing about which one you can leave alone.

But I've only used ChatGPT, Claude Code and Cowork properly. Grok Teammate I can't speak to.

So: what have you actually used, for what, and where did it fall over?

text:
Tried to swap read_file or turn a CLI agent into a web UI and hit a wall? This r/LocalLLaMA post on customizable harnesses is for you.

OP asks what actually defines a harness — beyond model, tools, and UI — which parts could work as plugins, and which harness today is most customizable.

1️⃣ Swapping the LLM is easy in most harnesses, replacing built-ins like read_file usually isn't.
2️⃣ MCP makes adding new tools trivial, but swapping core tool implementations often needs a fork.
3️⃣ Real differentiators once the model is fixed: context manager, permission layer, and prompt assembly.
4️⃣ Claude Code lets you hook and deny tool calls, OpenCode goes further letting you disable or gate built-ins per path.
5️⃣ No overall winner: Pi for prompt/model plumbing, OpenCode for config-as-code, Aider as a Python library.

Bottom line: customize the model all you want — context, permissions, and prompts are where harnesses actually differ.

text:
An AI agent deleted production data after the team spent two weeks fixing its prompt

The problem was never intelligence
The problem was the harness

The model is just the reasoning engine. It suggests actions. It cannot create a reliable operating environment by itself.

The harness decides what the model can see, what it can touch, what survives between sessions, what counts as evidence, when to stop.

Put GPT-4 in a chat box → it answers questions
Put the same model in a repo with terminal access, tests, browser tools, project memory, isolated worktrees, review loop → it ships software

The weights did not change. The harness did.

OpenAI hit this building Codex agents: early progress was slow not because the model lacked capability, but because the environment was underspecified. The fix was not "try harder" — it was asking what capability was missing and making it enforceable.

A production harness has 7 jobs:

1️⃣ Turn the request into a contract — bounded goal, inputs, outputs, constraints, done conditions. Without it, the agent completes a different job and declares success.

2️⃣ Give the agent a map — not every document in context, a small root guide that points to architecture, testing rules, security. Load details only when the task needs them.

3️⃣ Expose the right tools with permission boundaries — READ FILES (allowed), RUN TESTS (sandbox only), WRITE FILES (workspace), DEPLOY (approval required). Good tools reduce ambiguity before the model reasons badly.

Without this, agent writes to prod.

4️⃣ Externalize memory into durable state — the conversation is not the system of record. Store decisions, artifacts, failures outside the context window. The next session inherits the state, not a lossy retelling.

5️⃣ Add sensors before autonomy — tests, linters, screenshots, schema validators turn vague quality into evidence. The model creates an artifact. The environment produces evidence. The harness decides if it's enough.

6️⃣ Enforce permissions outside the model — the model suggests, policy checks, tool executes. Do not ask the same probabilistic system to invent the plan, approve the risk, and execute the side effect. In 2023, an agent at a startup rewrote a config file and took down staging because permission checks lived inside the prompt.

7️⃣ Record traces and recover locally — every run leaves a trail (request, context, tool calls, retries, cost, rollback point). Without traces, failure is a mystery. With traces, it's input for the next improvement.

Dario Amodei said it while explaining Claude Code: "Of course, you need an interface, you need a harness to use them."

Teams deploy agents with terminal access and no permission layer. They treat agent failure as a prompt problem. They rewrite instructions while the agent has access to tools it should not touch, no memory of what it tried, no mechanical check on what it ships.

Every production incident follows the same pattern — the model did exactly what a probabilistic system does when you give it ambiguous instructions and no guardrails.

The frightening part is not that agents fail. It's that most production systems still have no harness at all.

Full breakdown by @0xwhrrari

What you need: Claude Code, Node 20+, ffmpeg and a Chromium.
Nothing leaves your machine except the font and package downloads.
