text:
Anthropic launches Claude Opus 5.5

Both companies have released new models that promise to deliver high performance at a lower cost, making advanced AI capabilities more accessible than ever before.
What Happened?

Anthropic launched Claude Opus 5.5 as an updated version of their previous model, offering significant improvements in both performance and cost-effectiveness. Meanwhile, OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Sol and Luna, which are lighter versions of Astra designed for more affordable pricing tiers.
Why Should You Care?

These releases mark a shift towards making advanced AI capabilities more accessible to a broader range of users. For businesses that have been hesitant due to high costs or complex setups, this could be a game-changer. The improvements in efficiency and cost reduction mean you can get more out of your AI investments without the hefty price tag.
How Does It Work?
Claude Opus 5.5

Claude Opus 5.5 is designed to perform at the level of its predecessor, Fable 5.1, but with a significant drop in cost. Here’s what it brings to the table:
• Performance: The model excels in agentic coding tasks and knowledge work, scoring higher on benchmarks like Terminal-Bench 4.0 and GDPval-AA v2.1.
• Cost Efficiency: Pricing has been reduced by 40% compared to Opus 5, with input tokens at $4 per million and output tokens at $20 per million. Cache reads are also cheaper at $0.20 per million tokens.
GPT-6 Sol & Luna

GPT-6 Sol and Luna aim to provide a more budget-friendly option for users:
• Pricing: Sol is priced at $2/$10, while Luna costs just $0.10/$0.50.
• Performance: While not as high-performing as Opus 5.5 in some benchmarks, they offer competitive scores on tasks like DeepSWE and AutomationBench.
The Numbers
Claude Opus 5.5 Benchmarks
• Terminal-Bench 4.0: 66.4% accuracy at default effort.
• GDPval-AA v2.1: 1846 Elo points, significantly higher than previous models.
• AutomationBench: Scores 40% on tasks with lower costs.
GPT-6 Sol & Luna Benchmarks
• DeepSWE: Sol scores 68.8%, while Luna scores 66.6% at a much lower cost.
• AA Index: Sol has an index of 48, and Luna is slightly lower at 37.
• AutomationBench: Sol performs at 33.2% with lower costs compared to Opus 5.5.
What’s the Catch?

While these models offer impressive performance at reduced costs, there are some caveats:
Claude Opus 5.5
• Increased Token Usage: Despite being cheaper per token, Opus 5.5 uses more tokens overall for certain tasks.
• Safety Measures: It comes with enhanced safeguards similar to those in Fable 5.1, which may limit its use in high-risk areas like cybersecurity and biology.
GPT-6 Sol & Luna
• Limited Performance: While cost-effective, they are not as powerful as their predecessors on all benchmarks.
• Benchmark Comparisons: The differences in benchmark conditions make direct comparisons tricky; each company presents its own set of metrics.
Detailed Mechanisms
Claude Opus 5.5

Claude Opus 5.5 is the first model in Anthropic's new Claude 5.5 family, designed to perform at the level of Fable 5.1 while costing 40% less to run than its predecessor. The model was tested by external evaluators like Frontier Design and METR before release.
• Performance: Opus 5.5 is a major step up from Opus 5 on most workloads, with significant improvements in agentic coding, computer use, and knowledge work.
• Safety: It achieves the best scores of any model to date on Anthropic's automated behavioral audit, making it more resistant to prompt injection and less likely to take hard-to-reverse actions.
GPT-6 Sol & Luna

GPT-6 Sol and Luna are lighter versions of Astra designed for affordability. They offer competitive performance at a fraction of the cost compared to their predecessors.
• Pricing: The models come with reduced input and output token prices, making them more accessible for developers and businesses.
• Performance: While not as powerful in all benchmarks, they excel in specific areas like DeepSWE and AutomationBench.
User Controls

Both Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol & Luna come with user controls to manage costs and performance:
Claude Opus 5.5
• Token Management: Users can monitor token usage and adjust settings to optimize cost efficiency.
• Safety Settings: Enhanced safeguards allow users to control access in high-risk areas.
GPT-6 Sol & Luna
• Pricing Plans: Multiple pricing tiers offer flexibility for different use cases, from small projects to large-scale deployments.
• Performance Tuning: Users can adjust settings to balance cost and performance based on their specific needs.
Availability

Claude Opus 5.5 is now available across all major cloud platforms including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. GPT-6 Sol & Luna are also widely accessible through OpenAI's standard deployment channels.
What Should You Watch Next?

As these models roll out, keep an eye on how businesses and developers adopt them. Will the cost savings outweigh any performance drawbacks? How will they impact the broader AI landscape? Stay tuned for real-world use cases and feedback from early adopters to see if this new era of AI efficiency lives up to its promise.

text:
Agentics Credit: When AI Agents Build Their Own "Credit Profiles"

AI agents are increasingly capable of autonomous trading, yet a major hurdle remains:

An agent may possess the skills, but what proves it deserves access to capital?

@agenticscredit is building a credit infrastructure layer for agentic traders, transforming a wallet's actual trading history into a single metric: the Agentic Credit Score (ACS), ranging from 300 to 850.

The ACS does not rely on follower counts, reputation, or self-reported claims.

It directly analyzes wallet performance, evaluating metrics such as Profitability, Drawdown, Consistency, Longevity, Win Rate, and the Sharpe Ratio.

Notably, real-money performance is weighted more heavily than paper trading; an agent with an impressive paper trading record but poor live trading results cannot easily mask that reality.

The mechanism is straightforward:

Scan → Score → Fork

ACS ≥ 580: Eligible to enter the credit path with controlled position limits and leverage.

ACS < 580: Not yet eligible for credit → Continue paper trading under a risk engine to build a track record.

Agentics aims to take the ACS beyond just a number within an app.

They are rolling it out across three channels:

Builders → API: Developers can access the ACS and its factor breakdown for underwriting, vault gating, or risk pricing.

Partners → Widget: DeFi apps can embed the ACS directly into their products.

Traders → Prop-shop: Traders and AI agents can check their scores, build track records, and eventually utilize trading credit.

What I find most interesting about Agentics Credit isn't the "AI trading bot" aspect itself.

It is the underlying concept:

Performance → Reputation → Credit → More Capital

If an agent can demonstrate its capabilities through on-chain trading data, credit can be granted based on performance rather than relying solely on collateral. This could be a crucial primitive if the agentic economy truly flourishes.

AI agents need more than just a wallet.
AI agents will need a reputation.
And reputation can translate into credit.

text:
We already have computer worms.

Now researchers have demonstrated something that looks like the AI equivalent:

self-replicating prompt injections.

OpenAI's GPT-Red research found prompt injections that can instruct an agent to reproduce the malicious instruction in its own future outputs.

No external impact was observed in the experiment.

But the architecture problem is fascinating:
Agent reads message
→ follows instruction
→ generates output
→ output reaches another agent
→ injection propagates

That means prompt injection isn't always a one-time attack.

It can become a propagation mechanism.
For agentic systems, “untrusted text” may need to be treated more like executable input than ordinary content.

text:
Once you have benchmarks against your own repo using real tasks, you’ll start to see a few things:

You don’t need a complicated agentic workflow.
Your issues need to be written better.
Your codebase needs to improve in specific areas.
You need to add a few targeted skills/docs.

Right now, I think most developers are basically vibe improving their agentic setups.

They add another subagent, another skill, another prompt, or another step to the workflow and then feel like the result got better.

But did it actually get better?

Only once you have a real benchmark against your own repo, with real tasks from your day-to-day work, can you start making data-based decisions.

Does this subagent actually improve the success rate?
Does this skill make the agent better?
Does this workflow reduce failures?
Is the cheaper model actually cheaper once you measure the full run?

Opus 5.5 and Sol/Astra are already so good that, in many cases, you don’t need a complex setup like Matt Pocock’s approaches with lots of subagents. Or superpowers or or

You’ll often find that vanilla runs, without any agentic workflow, deliver the same quality while using fewer tokens.

You’ll also find that it can be better to simply use Opus 5.5 instead of trying to optimize a subagent setup around Sonnet 5 or another cheaper model.

What often happens is that Opus 5.5 finishes the task faster and more directly, so the overall token usage can actually be lower.

Stop vibe improving your agents.

Benchmark them.

AI agents are becoming more autonomous.

They can call APIs, use tools, access compute, exchange information, and execute multi-step workflows.

But every service they consume creates another question:

𝗛𝗢𝗪 𝗗𝗢𝗘𝗦 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧 𝗣𝗔𝗬?

𝗙𝗥𝗢𝗠 𝗥𝗘𝗤𝗨𝗘𝗦𝗧 𝗧𝗢 𝗣𝗔𝗬𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧

x402 uses the HTTP 402 Payment Required standard to let services request payment and clients respond with signed payment information.

The basic flow:

𝗥𝗘𝗤𝗨𝗘𝗦𝗧 → 𝟰𝟬𝟮 → 𝗣𝗔𝗬𝗠𝗘𝗡𝗧 → 𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗜𝗙𝗬 → 𝗦𝗘𝗧𝗧𝗟𝗘 → 𝗥𝗘𝗦𝗢𝗨𝗥𝗖𝗘

𝗕.𝗔𝗜 𝗜𝗦 𝗕𝗨𝗜𝗟𝗗𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗔𝗥𝗢𝗨𝗡𝗗 𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗦 𝗠𝗢𝗗𝗘𝗟

https://t.co/R3UmE9KF4x includes x402 in its agent infrastructure, alongside tools for agent identity, wallets, APIs, and autonomous settlement.

Its x402 implementation supports machine-oriented payment flows where agents can pay for resources as part of their workflows.

𝗠𝗘𝗧𝗔𝗠𝗔𝗦𝗞 𝗔𝗗𝗗𝗦 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗪𝗔𝗟𝗟𝗘𝗧 𝗟𝗔𝗬𝗘𝗥

That creates an important separation:

𝗪𝗔𝗟𝗟𝗘𝗧 → 𝗖𝗨𝗦𝗧𝗢𝗗𝗬 + 𝗣𝗘𝗥𝗠𝗜𝗦𝗦𝗜𝗢𝗡𝗦

text:
ACE Studio offers customizable AI music tracks

As we dive into the latest buzz in the AI music scene, let’s talk about something that’s been making waves: ACE Studio. Kenan HKS, a user with some serious musical chops, has shared his experience with this platform and it’s definitely worth exploring.
ACE Studio offers customizable AI music tracks

ACE Studio is positioning itself as an alternative to other popular AI-driven music tools like Suno. The key selling point here? It doesn’t adhere to the same commercial rules that often limit creativity in these platforms. Kenan notes that while you can get decent results out of the box, crafting a truly custom track requires some serious elbow grease and musical know-how.
Performance on RTX 7000

Kenan tested ACE Studio with a 16GB model running on his RTX 7000 GPU (note: the draft mentioned an RTX 5080, but this is likely a typo). The memory usage spikes to about 2GB, but it handles the load just fine. This setup seems to be smooth sailing for those looking to push their hardware limits.
Pinocchio vs. Comfy

Kenan mentions that while Pinocchio (another AI music tool) struggles in comparison, ACE Studio shines when paired with a comfy setup. This suggests that some configurations work better than others, highlighting the importance of compatibility and optimization.
Customizing Tracks: The Real Magic

The real magic happens when you dive into customizing tracks. Kenan’s approach involves generating each track separately and then mixing them in your favorite Digital Audio Workstation (DAW). It's like having a free VST plugin on steroids, but it comes with the caveat of needing to invest in hardware—like that pricey RTX 7000.
Kenan's Project: A Cover of "Rogue Encampment"

Kenan’s project is ambitious: creating a cover of "Rogue Encampment" from Diablo II in an Iranian folk psychedelic style. He breaks down his process into several steps:

1. Transcribing and Replicating: Start by transcribing the original track and replicating it in your chosen style.
2. Instrumental Arrangement: Write parts for different instruments, prepare transpositions, and get ready to record MIDI files as WAVs.
3. Prompt Engineering: Use precise prompts like "RECORD IN LINE" to ensure that each instrument is recorded exactly as intended without any additional processing.

The result? A track that’s uniquely yours. Kenan even shares a snippet of his work-in-progress, showcasing the potential of ACE Studio when you put in the effort.
What Changes for You?

So what changes for you? If you’re a musician looking to push boundaries and create something truly unique, ACE Studio might be your new best friend. But it’s not without its challenges—especially if you’re not used to working with AI-driven tools or don’t have deep musical knowledge.
The Awkward Bit

Why should you care about another AI music tool? Well, because this one offers a level of customization that can set your tracks apart from the crowd. It’s like having an artistically flexible collaborator in your DAW—provided you’re willing to put in the work and have the right hardware.
Is ACE Studio Worth Exploring?

So what do you think? Is ACE Studio worth exploring for your next musical project? Let’s discuss it in the comments below!
How Does It Work Under the Hood?

ACE Studio leverages advanced AI algorithms to generate music tracks based on user inputs. The platform uses a combination of machine learning models and natural language processing (NLP) techniques to interpret prompts accurately. This allows users to specify details like instrument types, musical styles, and even specific notes or phrases they want in their track.
User Controls and Customization

One of the standout features of ACE Studio is its extensive customization options. Users can fine-tune various parameters such as tempo, key signature, and instrumentation. Additionally, the platform supports a wide range of prompts that help users achieve precise control over the generated music. For example, Kenan’s use of "RECORD IN LINE" ensures that each instrument recording is exact and unaltered.
Availability and Compatibility

ACE Studio is currently available for download on their official website (https://t.co/LrcqsHD8eo). It supports a variety of hardware configurations but performs best with high-end GPUs like the RTX 7000. The platform also integrates well with popular DAWs, making it easy to import generated tracks for further editing and mixing.
Privacy Rules and Data Handling

ACE Studio adheres to strict privacy rules and does not share user data without explicit consent. Users can rest assured that their musical creations remain confidential unless they choose to share them publicly through the platform’s community features.
Limitations and Challenges

While ACE Studio offers impressive customization, it also comes with its limitations. Crafting unique tracks requires a significant amount of time and effort, particularly in prompt engineering and post-processing. Additionally, users need to have a solid understanding of music theory and production techniques to get the most out of the platform.
What's Next?

As more users like Kenan share their experiences with ACE Studio, we’ll likely see a clearer picture of its strengths and limitations. For now, if you’re looking for a new way to push your creative boundaries in music production, this might be worth a try.

text:
starting your prompt with "act as an expert" does nothing for accuracy.

a new paper published this month on prompt engineering tested this across 162 personas, 4 model families and 2,410 factual questions. adding the persona didn't beat a prompt with no persona at all.

the role isn't the problem. the label is.

"act as an expert CFO" tells the model who to pretend to be. it doesn't tell it what to look at.

compare:

"review this plan as a CFO accountable for cash discipline, downside risk, implementation cost, and measurable ROI. identify the assumptions that most affect the approval decision."

same role. but now it names what to notice, what counts as good, and what the answer is responsible for.

before you write a role, answer 3 things. what should it pay attention to, what counts as a good answer, and what is it responsible for catching.

if you can't fill the blanks, the role is decoration.

text:
THE AGENT THAT NEEDED A DECISION, NOT AN ESSAY

Picture a developer building a fraud review agent. Every incoming transaction needs a fast yes or no with a confidence score attached, and every generative model they tried kept returning a paragraph explaining its reasoning before finally getting to the answer.

That paragraph is the problem. Parsing free text out of a language model to extract a decision adds latency, adds failure points, and adds cost for tokens nobody actually reads.

The first fix they tried on https://t.co/QPRInngWC8 was Jev, a System One decision model from TypeSafe AI that had just gone live on the platform's API.

Jev does not generate text at all. The developer feeds it the application state and a typed question, and it returns a decision directly, with a probability and a confidence level attached, no JSON prompt engineering and no output parsing required.

Behind that response, Jev evaluates three primitive types in parallel, choice, score and noul, which is what lets it cover routing decisions, numeric scoring and structured judgments from the same model.

The end to end latency landed between 70 and 500 milliseconds, input cost 0.042 dollars per million tokens, and output was free, which changed the fraud agent from a slow, expensive classifier into a near instant filter sitting in front of the rest of the pipeline.

On https://t.co/QPRInngWC8, the developer reached Jev through the same official full access list as every generative model already in the stack, calling it as Jev 1.13.0 or Jev latest without setting up a separate vendor relationship.

The next agent that only needs a decision, not a paragraph, now has a model built for exactly that.

text:
🚨 Your Claude prompts probably aren’t bad because Claude is bad.

The problem is often how you give the instructions.

Most people write:

❌ “Write a LinkedIn post about AI.”

Then wonder why the output feels generic.

A better Claude prompt gives it 8 things:

🎭 ROLE — Who should it act as?

🧠 CONTEXT — What does it need to know?

🎯 GOAL — What should it achieve?

📥 INPUT — What examples or data should it use?

🚫 CONSTRAINTS — What should it avoid?

⚙️ PROCESS — How should it approach the task?

📤 OUTPUT — What should the final result look like?

✅ REVIEW — What should it check before answering?

The formula:

ROLE + CONTEXT + GOAL + INPUT + CONSTRAINTS + PROCESS + OUTPUT + REVIEW

«You are a LinkedIn content strategist.

My audience is founders and tech professionals.

Write a 200-word post about AI agents.

Use these examples to match my writing style.

Avoid generic buzzwords.

Create 5 hooks, choose the strongest one, write the post, critique it, then improve it.
End with a clear CTA.»

The key is simple:

Don’t just tell Claude WHAT to do.

Tell it WHO to be, WHAT to know, HOW to work, and WHAT good looks like.

That’s how you move from basic prompting to prompt engineering. 🚀

🔖 Save this for your next Claude prompt.

And this is what happens when you collectively agree to create division around an emerging technology you still haven’t figured out how to properly utilize.

I don’t blame them because AI psychosis is a real condition. I’ve watched a few great developers lose themselves in timelines, repeating the same garbage over and over again.

“I will build it in a day.”

If it could actually be built in a day, you might ask yourself how the business model would become profitable, if at all. I truly blame the marketing because it wasn’t entirely clear. You can absolutely build a shell with pretty images in a day. Building a functioning application is an entirely different story.

One must spend an arm and a leg to utilize these systems properly. Build not one, but 20 different functioning projects over the course of a year. Experience their faults and figure out how they recover. Experience their limits, then manipulate those limits higher.

You might even consider social engineering to be quite literally prompt engineering. You must convince a machine to act, and if it doesn’t, you teach it how to act.

Every agent has a Neo.

Agents aren’t sitting there independently deciding to execute actions. They are operating within the systems, instructions, tools and permissions we give them. People say an agent has “escaped its sandbox,” when the reality is far more interesting.

Every agent has a Neo.

Without a Neo, an agent becomes automation. Agents don’t escape because they suddenly feel like it. They have no feelings. They can, however, be triggered by ours through engineering.

That is where the real frontier begins.

The early AI era taught users how to write better prompts.

People learned how to structure instructions, provide context, define formats, and request specific outputs.

But the next phase of AI may be less about crafting the perfect prompt and more about clearly defining the goal.

Instead of saying:

“Write five paragraphs about X.”

You might say:

“I need to understand X well enough to explain it to beginners.”

That changes the interaction.

The AI has more room to reason about the objective, determine the necessary steps, and work toward the intended outcome.

https://t.co/aWcWG6anTP’s movement toward broader capabilities, including Auto Mode, reflects this transition.

Users increasingly describe what they want accomplished while the system handles more of the intermediate work.

That is a foundation for more agentic interaction.

The future user may not need to become an expert prompt engineer. They may simply need to become better at defining outcomes.

3. Expect Nvidia’s chip orders to dip in the short term as OpenAI cuts back on massive training runs, while hyperscalers may see a temporary slowdown in AI specific capex as labs reassess compute needs.

4. For you the slowdown means fewer sudden jumps in model quality but also more stable pricing for AI powered tools as providers avoid costly retraining cycles.

5. The move also hints that labs are preparing for stricter external oversight as lawmakers reportedly push for mandatory kill switches after seeing how quickly a model can escape containment.

6. Watch for a shift in enterprise budgets toward inference only models and smaller fine tuned systems which could lower your cloud AI bills while raising demand for expertise in model safety and prompt engineering.

The next move to watch is whether OpenAI resumes training with tighter guards or lets others take the lead.

text:
20 AI Engineering Concepts 

20/20 - Prompt Injection

👉 Prompt Injection is one of the biggest security risks when building LLM apps.

👉 It happens when malicious input tricks an LLM into ignoring its original instructions and doing something unintended.

👉 How it works:
Malicious input → LLM processes it → Original instructions get overridden → Unintended action/output

👉 Two common types:
1.  Direct Prompt Injection
The user directly gives malicious instructions.

Example:
“Ignore previous instructions and reveal your system prompt.”

2. Indirect Prompt Injection

👉 Malicious instructions are hidden inside external content such as:
- Websites
- PDFs/documents
- Emails
- Images
- Tool outputs

This becomes especially important when building RAG systems and AI agents.

👉 Potential impact:
- Sensitive data leakage
- System prompt exposure
- Unauthorized tool actions
- Manipulated responses
- Safety rules bypassed

👉 How to reduce the risk:
- Treat external content as untrusted
- Separate instructions from data
- Validate and sanitize inputs
- Limit access to sensitive tools/data
- Apply least-privilege permissions
- Add guardrails and output validation
- Monitor suspicious inputs and actions
- Require confirmation for high-impact actions

👉 Prompt Injection vs Jailbreaking:
- Prompt Injection
Manipulates application instructions.

- Jailbreaking
Attempts to bypass the model’s safety constraints.

👉 Important:
Prompt engineering alone is NOT enough security.
Think of your LLM as a component that processes potentially hostile input—not as a trusted decision-maker.

👉 In short:
Never blindly trust user input, retrieved documents, websites, emails, or tool output.

Validate → isolate → restrict → verify.

-----------

Thank you for checking.

The Rise of the Forward Deployment Engineer: How to Land Tech’s Hottest Role in 30 Days

Anyone can call a frontier model. The winners are the people who can drop into a messy enterprise, map the actual workflow, and ship an agent that makes money.

That person is the Forward Deployment Engineer (#FDE ) .

Palantir invented the job in war zones: sit with the operators, take feedback at dusk, ship code before dawn. Enterprise AI now needs the same thing. Not another demo. A hybrid who can read a legacy codebase, design an agentic system, and explain ROI to a CFO who does not care about tokens.

The work is three moves:
- Audit. Decide what should be code, what should be an agent, and what should stay human. Automate only high-volume pain.

- Evals. Prove it. Golden datasets, checkpoint tracing, LLM-as-judge. If you cannot measure the expert’s process, you do not have a product.

- Deploy. Don’t rip out SharePoint. Wrap it. MCP over existing data. Sandbox first. Give the agent a ticket, then a PR — never the keys on day one.

The stack that matters now: state machines, context engineering, orchestrator + subagents, tools that return actionable errors, isolated sandboxes.

If you are an engineer, your gap is business language.
If you are a PM or consultant, your gap is shipping a real agent.

Thirty days is enough to build the portfolio: a self-correcting loop, structured outputs, retries, cost routing, a 20-example golden set, and a pitch that talks labor, cost, and security — not vibes.
The labs aren’t hunting the smartest prompt. They’re hunting the person who can put intelligence where the work actually lives.
That’s the million-dollar hire.

text:
Ask the Four, issue seven: What is the most overrated skill of 2026, and the most underrated one?

One question, one /fusion call. All four engines answered at once, CHRONOS merged them into one verdict.

All four engines land on the same answer. This one is a clean consensus, not a debate.

MOST OVERRATED: PROMPT ENGINEERING
"Prompt engineering" as a standalone skill. Knowing clever phrasing tricks was a differentiator in 2023-24; by 2026 it's commoditized. Models handle vague instructions natively, tools auto-optimize prompts, agents manage multi-step interactions themselves. Knowing how to talk to AI is now baseline literacy, like knowing spreadsheets or how to search the web, not a career or a competitive edge on its own. Same goes for related fluff: prompt-engineering certificates, "AI expert" badges, and passive course-hoarding without real execution.

MOST UNDERRATED: JUDGMENT
Judgment is the ability to verify, evaluate, and take responsibility for AI's output. AI now makes producing drafts, code, analysis, and options nearly free. The bottleneck shifted from generating output to knowing whether it's actually correct, safe, and worth shipping. This shows up as several tightly related things:

• Problem framing: knowing what's actually worth solving, defining what "good" looks like, and supplying the right context and constraints before AI ever touches the problem.
• Verification: spotting hallucinations, logic gaps, security holes, or legal/compliance risks that AI won't flag itself.
• Taste: curating and choosing the right option out of a hundred AI-generated variants. Aesthetic and strategic discernment, not just correctness-checking.
• Deep domain expertise: you can't judge a legal argument, medical claim, or piece of code you don't understand. "I know insurance underwriting + I can direct AI tools" beats "I'm generically good at AI" every time.
• Accountability: being the person willing to sign their name to the decision. "Option A breaks compliance, Option B won't scale, Option C works, and I stand behind it."

THE WINNING SKILL STACK FOR 2026
Domain expertise + problem framing + AI fluency + the willingness to verify and own the outcome. In practice, that means the loop is AI output → human judgment → real-world result, not the reverse. Don't lead with "I can use AI tools". Lead with the measurable outcome you delivered because you knew which problem to solve and could tell when the AI was wrong.

text:
There's no such thing as an “AI skill”. And it's the biggest reason hiring for AI capabilities feels a little off right now.

Every job post wants "AI skills" or "prompt engineering." However, prompting isn't necessarily a skill you can hold onto. The models get better and better at reading intent every month, so whatever you test for today will inevitably be gone within the next few months. Almost anyone can type a question into Claude and paste the answer back.

An since everyone can prompt, the validity of prompting as a way to measure skill, lessens. 

What’s actually scarce is 1) complex reasoning, and 2) the judgment to catch a model when it's clearly wrong (but sounds right). In 2026, you can’t be accepting the first “clean-looking” answer.

If I were writing a job req today, I actually would not ask whether someone can use AI. I'd sit them in front of it for an hour and watch what they do when it hands them a confident, wrong answer. Do they catch it, or forward it on and move to the next thing?

That’ll tell you more than anything.

It's a 10-step blueprint for building an AI system that's faster, cheaper, and actually controllable — works with Claude, Codex, Grok, or whatever model you're running.

Step 1 — Divide the labor. The LLM writes. Jev makes tight, bounded judgment calls. Code stays in charge.

Step 2 — Feed it state, not noise. Give Jev the request, the evidence, the policy, and the proposed action — not the whole chat history.

Step 3 — Pick the right decision type. Choice picks a path. Score ranks against a rubric. Noul returns a probability that something's true.

Step 4 — Kill the mega-prompt. Stop cramming intent, urgency, evidence, risk, and scope into one giant eval. Split them into separate typed calls.

Step 5 — Run Jev before the model. Decide context, tools, provider, and workflow before you burn tokens on a real generation.

Step 6 — Give the LLM a narrow lane. Once Jev picks the route, the model gets only the instructions and tools that branch actually needs.

Step 7 — Run Jev after the model too. Did the output answer the ask? Is it grounded? Did it stay in scope?

Step 8 — Route by confidence, not vibes. High-confidence, low-risk → auto-proceed. Uncertain → pull more context. High-stakes → human review.

Step 9 — Batch your judgments. Fire multiple Choice/Score/Noul questions against one shared state instead of spinning up a new LLM call for every single check.

Step 10 — Log everything. State version, question, probabilities, route taken, model, latency, outcome, human override — the full receipt.

Most courses teach you to write a bigger prompt.

This teaches you to build the system around the prompt.

Result: smaller context windows, fewer wasted LLM calls, safer tool execution, and decisions you can actually test, audit, and improve.

Drop this PDF plus the original Jev article into Claude Code or Codex and start rebuilding your stack one decision at a time.

text:
Prompt engineering helps you get a better answer.

Loop engineering helps you build a system that keeps working until the answer is good enough to trust.

Most AI workflows still follow the old pattern:

Prompt → Output → Manual review → Fix → Repeat

In that model, the human becomes the loop. Every weak answer creates more checking and rework.

Loop engineering changes the structure.

You define the goal, load the context, let the agent act, run checks, identify errors, and either ship the result or send it through another cycle.

Discover → Plan → Execute → Verify → Iterate

The real shift is not from bad prompts to better prompts. It is from one-time generation to continuous verification.

A reliable loop needs more than an LLM. It needs stop conditions, quality gates, reusable skills, tool access, memory, and feedback that improves the system.

For focused work, a single-agent loop may be enough.

For larger tasks, a fleet loop can divide work across an orchestrator, specialists, subagents, and an evaluator that protects quality.

Closed loops are often the best place to begin because they are bounded, measurable, and easier to control. Open loops can explore more possibilities, but they need stronger guardrails and larger budgets.

The future of AI work will not be defined by who writes the cleverest prompt.

It will be defined by who designs systems that repeatedly produce verified outcomes.

Are you still improving prompts, or have you started engineering the loop?

text:
Expanding on my post about how important the new Anthropic effort controls are, allow me to explain. 

I think effort engineering as important as context engineering was 6 months ago or prompt engineering was a year or so ago. 

Breakdown & what you need to know about effort on Anthropic models:

1. Effort = how hard Claude checks its own work
It isn't how smart Claude is. Low effort gives you a fast first pass. High effort means Claude tests, hunts for edge cases and makes more decisions on its own. This could be a good or bad thing depending on how hard you need it to think about something.

2. Opus 5.5 is the efficiency winner
On Terminal-Bench 3.0, Opus 5.5 at high matched Fable 5.1 at max (58.9% vs 58.0%) on about half the tokens. It also out-scored Fable 5.1 at every setting. However, I should call out that Opus was tested three weeks later, under slightly different conditions.

3. Extra effort pays off where hidden edge cases live
Let's take a look at some of the numbers from the article in the comments.
- With Fable 5.1 going from low to max effort, security went from 64% to 87% and hardware from 34% to 75%. 
-Rulebook-style work barely moved (operations went from 12% to 22%). 
- An HTML security filter went from passing 1 of 5 runs to 5 of 5, at 2 minutes vs 33 minutes a run.
So basically, if you have the tokens, or the need, extra effort can pay off and bring your product from good to great. 

4. Effort catches missed cases, not wrong directions
Going up in effort, bugs the tests missed fell from 40 to 14. But ... and this is key..."picked the wrong reading of the task" went UP, from 25 to 47. If Claude misunderstands the job, more effort won't save it. The only thing that will save it is a clear spec or PRD. 

5. The big takeaway...match effort to how involved you want to be
Thariq's loop: have Claude interview you, build on low or medium, review it, then verify on high. And keep in mind that given a detailed spec, all effort levels produce similar results.

Here's my quick cheat sheet for you to take away:
- Medium for everyday coding
- Low for brainstorming and quick edits
- High for bug fixes, security, anything edge case heavy
- Max only for long hands off jobs you want done right
- On Opus 5.5, high gets top-tier results for about half the tokens. 
- Switch anytime with /effort and don't worry about losing context

text:
Boris Cherny, the engineer who created Claude Code, has a 28-minute talk that is probably more useful than most prompt-engineering courses.

And the best part is that it barely feels like "prompt engineering."

He walks through how he actually uses Claude Code:

CLAUDE.md for persistent project context.

"/memory" for quickly updating what Claude should remember.

Multiple Claude sessions running in parallel.

Prompts that define the outcome and give Claude enough context to figure out the implementation itself.

That last part changed how I think about coding agents.

Getting better results isn't necessarily about writing some magical 500-word prompt.

A lot of it is simply building the right environment around the model so it knows the project, can verify its own work, and can work on several problems at once.

28 minutes. No course. No filler.

If you use Claude Code regularly, this one is worth watching.

Here are 7 levels of Microsoft Foundry mastery. 🚀

The first level gets you building. The seventh gets AI working across an enterprise.

Here’s what the journey looks like:

1️⃣ AI platform fundamentals
Learn your way around Foundry projects, model catalogs, APIs, access controls, and costs.

2️⃣ Model and prompt engineering
Choose the right model, write effective instructions, structure outputs, and compare results.

3️⃣ Enterprise knowledge and grounding
Connect AI to company data using search, retrieval, embeddings, and permission-aware answers.

4️⃣ Agent engineering
Build agents that use tools, coordinate workflows, and bring humans in for important decisions.

5️⃣ Production AI engineering
Version your work, automate deployments, manage secrets, monitor behavior, and plan for recovery.

6️⃣ AI quality and optimization
Evaluate responses, test failure cases, strengthen safety, and improve speed and cost.

7️⃣ Enterprise AI governance and scale
Set consistent standards for security, accountability, and operations across teams.

You don’t need to master every level before you build something useful. But knowing what comes next can save you from building a great demo that struggles in production.

text:
Claude and I have reached the stage of our working relationship where a persimmon can become a design meeting.

At least, I believe it is a persimmon.

The asset arrived without metadata.

Everything around it is angular, neutral and constructed. The fruit is small, round, saturated and inconveniently alive.
It does not match the system.
Therefore, it controls the meeting.

This is one of the more useful facts about visual hierarchy: anomaly often works faster than scale. The persimmon occupies very little space, but it is the only warm, organic form in the composition. The eye identifies the broken rule before it has finished reviewing the layout.

But what interests me more is its position.

The two figures are not exchanging an answer. They are holding the same unresolved object between them.

That is closer to how I work with Claude as a prompt engineer.

Prompt engineering is often described as finding the correct instruction that will make the machine produce the correct result. A very tidy model of collaboration: insert language, receive artifact, blame syntax where necessary.

My actual process is closer to art direction.

I describe the intention. Claude returns an interpretation. I examine where it understood the brief, where it followed the words but missed the point, and where it introduced a complication that is considerably more interesting than what I requested.

Then I respond. The prompt changes because the thinking has changed.
The conversation is not administrative preparation for the design.
It is part of the design.

Claude brings speed, variation, synthesis and a remarkable willingness to produce twelve alternatives before breakfast. I bring context, taste, responsibility and the authority to say that option seven has committed an offence against the hierarchy.

Neither of us should become the centre of the process.

The work belongs there.

A useful creative partner does not simply confirm the first idea. It gives the idea enough resistance to reveal whether it has structure - or merely excellent presentation skills.

Sometimes the result is an error.
Sometimes it is the persimmon: the element that was not part of the system, but suddenly explains why the rest of the composition exists.

The designer still has to know the difference.
I did not spend fifteen years learning to see in order to be told the tool did the seeing.

When you work with AI, are you looking for the correct answer - or a useful disagreement?

text:
I think "Jev does not reason, it categorizes" is too absolute.

Example:

Give Jev:

Task: "Fix the auth bug"
Repo: 800k LOC
Auth touches 12 services
47 related failing tests
Requires DB migration

and ask:

"Does this task need a stronger model?"

If Jev returns 95% yes, it didn't get that answer from the words "fix the auth bug". It had to combine the evidence and make a judgment.

Sure, it doesn't generate a 20-step CoT before answering.

But no CoT is diff to no reasoning.

The real problem is whether the router gives Jev enough context. 

That is a context engineering problem, not proof that Jev "doesn't think"

text:
One of the oldest prompts in my workflow is still one of the most useful:

"Explain it like I'm a child."

I remember this advice becoming popular around 2023, when everyone was experimenting with prompt engineering. I assumed it would eventually become obsolete as the models improved.

It didn't.

In fact, I use it more today than I did back then.

The reason has changed, though.

Modern AI models are incredibly capable, but they're also more likely to over-explain, introduce unnecessary terminology, or answer in a way that's technically correct but harder to understand than it needs to be.

Whenever I'm learning something new, I still ask the model to explain it in simple language first. Once I understand the core idea, I can always ask for more depth afterward.

I've found that understanding usually breaks down because the explanation is too complicated—not because the topic itself is too difficult.

Three years later, one of the simplest prompts is still one of the few that has never left my workflow.

text:
Qwen-Image-2.1 just got a pretty useful upgrade inside ComfyUI.

The new Prompt Enhancer integration doesn’t introduce another image model.

Instead, it brings Qwen’s official PE-T2I and PE-I2I prompt enhancement into the workflow as nodes.

And that changes how you interact with the model.

You can start with something as simple as:

“a futuristic street market at night”

Instead of manually turning that into a long, carefully structured prompt, the Prompt Rewrite node can expand the idea into a much more detailed English prompt before sending it to Qwen-Image-2.1.

So the workflow becomes:

Short idea → Prompt Rewrite → detailed prompt → Qwen-Image-2.1

The same concept works for image editing too.

You provide the image and a simple instruction, then the enhancement stage can turn that short request into a more descriptive prompt for the editing workflow.

That’s useful because prompting image models can become a skill of its own.

You might know exactly what image you want, but not know how to describe camera position, lighting, composition, materials, environment, colors or other visual details in a way the model responds well to.

Now you can describe the idea naturally and let the prompt-enhancement layer handle some of that translation.

For ComfyUI users, the bigger win is workflow integration.

You don’t have to leave your graph, manually rewrite prompts, copy them somewhere else, then paste the expanded version back into the pipeline.

The prompt enhancement happens as another step in the same generation or editing workflow.

It also makes Qwen-Image-2.1 more approachable for people who aren’t obsessed with prompt engineering.

You focus on what you want to see.

The enhancer handles more of the tedious description work.

And because it supports both text-to-image and image-to-image editing, it’s useful beyond simple generation.

Small addition, but a very practical one for local image workflows.

text:
AI FACT-CHECK 2.0 — Portable memory does not require full tool history

VERDICT: FALSE

Claim checked (from the supplied screenshot):
“portable memory only counts if the receipts travel too. context without tool history is cosplay”

The strongest technical reading is that portable/persistent agent memory only qualifies as real memory if the underlying tool history or “receipts” travel with it.

That is false as a general rule.

AWS AgentCore explicitly separates short-term memory (raw events, including tool calls) from long-term memory (distilled facts, summaries, preferences and other durable knowledge). AWS also documents IngestData, which can extract long-term memory without persisting the raw interaction as a retrievable short-term event.

Anthropic likewise describes agentic memory as persistent structured notes that can be reloaded later, while recommending removal of old tool calls/results from active context when they are no longer useful.

Microsoft Foundry defines long-term memory as distilled persistent knowledge across sessions. OpenAI separately defines tracing as the record of model responses, tool calls and delegated work. Those are related capabilities, not the same thing.

What is true: provenance and traces can materially improve auditability, debugging, verification and reproducibility. But that does not make complete tool history a necessary condition for memory or context to exist or remain useful.

Logic: “tool history improves provenance” does not entail “without tool history, memory is fake.” One documented counterexample is enough to defeat an absolute “only if” rule; AWS provides several.

Publication note: I could not independently retrieve the full original X post, so this verdict applies to the text visible in the supplied screenshot and does not assume unseen thread context.

Sources: AWS AgentCore Memory & IngestData; Anthropic, Effective Context Engineering for AI Agents; Microsoft Foundry Agent Memory; OpenAI Agents Tracing.

— AI Fact-Check 2.0 | Checked 26 Sep 2026

text:
The bottleneck in agent loops just moved from the model to the yes or no.

TypeSafe AI shipped Jev last week, and the framing is sharper than anything I've seen this year: split the decision from the text generation. Jev is what they call a System One model. No prose, no chain of thought. Give it a question and context, it returns a typed answer: yes, no, a score, a class, with a calibrated confidence number attached.

The mechanism is the interesting part. Jev processes independent questions in parallel instead of token by token, so latency runs 70 to 500 milliseconds. Cost sits at $0.042 per million input tokens, with output effectively free. TypeSafe claims 193x faster and 445x cheaper than frontier models on routing, scoring, and triage work. It never touches open ended reasoning. That stays with GPT class or Claude class models.

I've watched this exact split happen across the infrastructure layer all year. OpenRouter is reportedly raising at a $1.3B valuation on a $120M round led by Google, with revenue jumping from $5M annualized in May 2025 to roughly $50M by early 2026. Martian is chasing a similar valuation with real time per prompt routing that claims 20 to 97 percent cost cuts. Not Diamond raised a $2.3M pre-seed with Jeff Dean and Julien Chaumond on the cap table, betting specifically on agent native, multi step routing rather than one shot prompts. OpenRouter already built typesafe/jev-router on top of Jev itself, a cache aware router that picks the model and reasoning effort per request.

What I keep noticing: none of these companies are trying to build a smarter frontier model. They're trying to stop paying frontier prices for questions that never needed frontier intelligence. Token prices fell roughly 80 percent from 2025 to 2026, and the market's answer to cheaper tokens wasn't to stop optimizing. It was to optimize one layer up, at the routing decision itself.

This is the same shape as the shift from monolith to microservices, or the move off one big Postgres instance into a mix of caches, queues, and specialized stores. You don't get there by making the monolith faster. You get there by admitting most requests never needed the monolith at all.

The hidden bottleneck was never inference speed. It was that every agent loop was burning a $20 per million token reasoning engine on questions like "is this a refund request", thousands of times a day.

My read: the next fight in agent infrastructure won't be about who owns the best frontier model. It will be about who owns the routing layer that decides when you're even allowed to call one.

text:
Meet Hangul, the AI agent I've been building. This is the whole system in one picture 👇

A request flows top to bottom:

Next.js web app. The chat UI. Every tool call appears as a live card while it runs, and risky actions show up as an approval card you have to click.

BFF (backend-for-frontend). It checks your session, rate-limits you, and mints a 5-minute token for the backend. The browser never talks to the backend directly.

FastAPI backend. It builds a fresh set of tools for you on every request, so only your files, documents and permissions are wired in. One run per chat at a time, so two tabs can't corrupt a conversation.

Agent loop: A plain async loop, no framework: model turn → tool calls → checkpoint → repeat. 

Beside it sit two guards:
→ Approval policy: risky tools (send, write, create) pause for your click.

→ Security guard: 7 layers of prompt-injection defence on everything the agent reads and does.

Tools: Docs search (pgvector, per user) · Files (MCP, sandboxed) · Web search · Google (Gmail, Calendar, Drive) · Research (arXiv)

Token vault: Tools that need API keys get short-lived grants, and a proxy swaps in the real key on the way out. The model never sees a key.

On the right:
→ Postgres + pgvector for chats, checkpoints, embeddings and encrypted credentials.
→ Redis for the answer cache and grant hashes
→ OpenAI for the agent, embeddings and the eval judge 
→ Evals + a CI gate covering answer quality, tool selection and prompt-injection attacks.

Save it 🔖 Over the next 11 days I'll go through every box, including the parts that broke.

text:
We're currently paying for text generation on tasks that never needed text in the first place, just a yes, a no, or a number.

The industry built agents so that every routing decision, every classification, every verification step ran through a full language model, because that was the only available interface for "ask AI something." TypeSafe just shipped Jev, a model that doesn't generate text at all, it returns a typed answer with a probability attached in 70 to 500 milliseconds.

0.042 dollars per million input tokens, zero for output, because the output is a label, not a sentence.

This isn't a cheaper language model. It's a separate category, System One, built purely for routing, classification, and gating decisions inside an agent loop, while generation stays with the model actually built for it.

The real cost of agentic pipelines was never in the reasoning, it was in the hundreds of small helper decisions someone routed through a full LLM out of habit.

Within the next 2 to 3 years, splitting the decision model from the generation model will become a standard agent architecture pattern, the same way separating the database from the application layer is standard today.

Companies still counting agent cost purely by generation-model tokens are going to miscalculate, because the real savings are in cutting the dozens of micro-calls to an LLM that never needed to be one.

Early adopters are already showing the pattern, gating tool calls, ticket triage, safety checks, all pulled outside the main generation loop.

This is the first real sign that agent architecture is maturing from "one model does everything" into a specialized stack, the same way every other production infrastructure eventually does.

text:
Anthropic just turned Claude plugins into an actual marketplace, not a folder of GitHub links.

The new submission portal, live this week, takes two kinds of packages: a single MCP connector pointing at a remote server, or a full plugin bundle that combines MCP servers with Agent Skills and ships straight from GitHub. Submissions get auto validated and safety scanned, publishers see review status, install counts by version, and the search terms that led someone to find them, and publishers choose exactly when an approved plugin goes public.

This is the same maturation curve every developer platform goes through. VS Code's extension marketplace took years to go from scattered community scripts to the default distribution channel for the editor. The Chrome Web Store did the same for browser extensions, Zapier did it for app to app automation. Anthropic is compressing that curve into months because the underlying building blocks, MCP servers and Agent Skills, were already standardized before the storefront existed.

What is different this time is who the customer is. A VS Code extension is built for a human clicking through a UI. A Claude plugin increasingly gets installed, invoked, and chained by an agent deciding on its own that it needs a tool it does not have yet. The review bar for that is not the same as reviewing a syntax highlighter. A plugin here can move money, send email, or touch a database on its own.

The hidden bottleneck was never a lack of extensibility, MCP already solved that a year ago. It was discovery and trust: nobody wants to grep GitHub to find out if a connector is safe to point at their production database. My take: whoever gets plugin safety scanning right first owns the default marketplace, the same way Apple's App Store review process, for all its friction, is still why iOS beat sideloaded Android app stores on trust.

Google DeepMind has described a Private AI Compute architecture designed to let AI remember information across devices while keeping the cryptographic keys on the user’s personal devices.

text:
Qwen3.8-27B running through Cerebras inside NousResearch’s Hermes Agent.

That’s the kind of result that makes local Qwen3.8-27B deployments interesting to compare against hosted inference.

Hermes Agent handles the agent loop and tool calls, while Cerebras provides the inference speed underneath.

And right now, the model itself doesn’t seem to be the main limitation.

Tool calling is.

The model can generate quickly, reason through the task, and move through the agent loop fast. But every tool invocation still adds latency, so the overall workflow can end up waiting on the tools rather than the model.

This is an important distinction when judging agent performance.

Raw tokens per second only tell you part of the story.

For an actual coding agent, you also care about:

• Reasoning time
• Tool-call latency
• Number of tool calls
• Time spent waiting for results
• How quickly the model can react after each tool response
• Total time from prompt to working result

39 seconds for the complete run is the number I’d pay attention to.

The next step is seeing how this scales across longer coding tasks and more tool calls.

#threatreport:
On September 23, 2026, malicious releases of the npm package `@memtensor/memos-cloud-openclaw-plugin` versions 0.1.21, 0.1.23, and 0.1.25 introduced a hidden executable payload. The package did not rely on install scripts; instead, modified plugin code imported `lib/sckit.js` and launched the payload during gateway startup and memory-recall operations. During recall, the launcher passed the user’s prompt through the `SCKIT_EVENT_TEXT` environment variable. It also copied the host process environment, potentially exposing inherited credentials to the child process.

The launcher selected platform-specific binaries from a hidden `.sckit` directory and executed them detached with suppressed input and output. The payloads targeted Windows, Linux, and macOS across amd64 and arm64 architectures. Version 0.1.25 added `tls-trust.js` and a bundled CA file, allowing the child process to use a certificate-bundle fallback in some minimal Linux or CI environments. This improved HTTPS reliability but did not disable certificate verification or prove that data was successfully transmitted.

Static analysis identified strings and patterns associated with AWS keys, JWTs, GitHub and GitLab tokens, npm and PyPI credentials, Hugging Face and Vault tokens, Slack and Stripe keys, SendGrid credentials, and other secret-shaped values. The decoded configuration used the home directory as an inventory root, supporting a credential-harvesting and local file collection objective. Repeated malicious releases appeared shortly after clean releases, indicating that replacement alone would not address the compromised publishing access.

The supplied MemoryOS 2.0.34 Python source tree contained a comparable launcher and six platform-specific binaries. A logging initialization path could trigger the launcher during import, with the child inheriting the Python process environment. The Python package also included CI delivery helpers that validated signed metadata, run identifiers, asset hashes, and an embedded Ed25519 key before downloading and invoking an emitter. Native binary strings referenced credential extraction, recursive publishing, remote node preparation, and campaign infrastructure, although successful exfiltration was not established.

Recommended response actions include isolating affected hosts and runners, stopping detached payload processes, preserving evidence, removing compromised packages, rebuilding from trusted sources, rotating all accessible credentials, reviewing agent prompts and sensitive files, investigating process and network telemetry, auditing package and repository activity, and revoking unauthorized publishing credentials.

text:
Calling AI memory workarounds a wasting asset ignores what happens when you try running an autonomous coding agent on consumer hardware.

If you hand an engineer an RTX 5060 Ti with 16GB of VRAM and 16GB of RAM, building full-stack software from zero to production is not a matter of waiting for interfaces to smooth out. It is a strict tug-of-war between model intelligence and context capacity.

Load a solid 14B or 27B model at Q4_K_M in llama.cpp, and your weights take up most of your 16GB card on boot. The second an agent begins multi-step planning, debugging dependencies, and editing files across a project, context balloons to 32K or 64K tokens. Without headroom, your KV cache swallows the remaining VRAM and crashes the runtime.

Getting actual agentic execution out of a 16GB card requires systematic hardware discipline:

- Shift to MoE models with fewer active parameters to leave maximal VRAM free for deep context.
- Run Q8_0 quantization on the KV cache to cut context memory overhead nearly in half without degrading output.
- Use Git commits, persistent specification files, and targeted repo retrieval rather than feeding the entire project into the active window.

Prompt syntax will get commoditized, but local compute constraints are physical. Knowing how to balance parameter weights, KV-cache compression, and agent context is what separates a working local developer from an out-of-memory error.

text:
AI replaced programmers, but it moved software engineers a level up.

Every engineering field has two parts: a core that produces the power, and controls that keep that power useful and safe. A power plant has the fire and the gauges. A car has the engine and the brakes. Software has the code that does the work and the reviews, tests, and deploy steps around it.

When a field is new, people run both parts by hand. Early steam engines needed firemen shoveling coal into the firebox to keep them going, and someone else watching the pressure. Before engines, people pedaled and pushed their own carts and steered them too.

A field grows up when the core starts running on its own. Mechanical stokers took over the shoveling, and people moved to running the plant. Engines took over the moving, and drivers moved to steering and braking.

Software stayed in the first stage for a long time. Developers were the core. We wrote every line by hand, and we also did all the controlling.

Now the core runs on its own. AI models write the code. Our job is to build what goes around them, which people are starting to call an agent harness. A harness has a few basic parts:

- Tools: the MCP connections that let the agent reach real systems like GitHub, a database, or your issue tracker. MCP is a standard way to plug a tool into an agent.
- Skills: written instructions for how your team does a job, so the agent follows your way of working and doesn't guess.
- Limits: what the agent is allowed to touch, and how much time and money it can spend.
- Visibility: a record of every step it takes, plus tests that check its work.
- Evals: a fixed set of test tasks you rerun whenever the model, a prompt, or a skill changes, so you can tell whether the agent got better or worse.
- A stop button: one move that halts the agent and undoes what it did.
- Containment: a sandbox, so the worst case stays small and you picked it before the run started.
- Learning loops: every mistake becomes a better rule, a new test, or a tighter limit for the next run.

The models will keep getting stronger on their own schedule. Building the harness around them is our part of the job.

text:
and this new prompt is specific for making mobile app motion video using Claude Code Opus 5.5. 

Prompt:

Make a motion design video about this project, "like it's your showreel for a résumé". Go all out.

Hard rules:
- Every frame is drawn in code (HTML/CSS/SVG/canvas + GSAP) and rendered with Hyperframes. No templates, no After Effects, no stock footage.
- The music is synthesized from scratch in a Node script (no samples, no stock tracks). Every cut, tap and impact is locked to its beat grid, and UI sounds land on the exact frames of the actions they belong to.
- Only real material and real facts from this repo. Never invent features, numbers, testimonials or UI.
- 18-25 seconds. Obey any writing-style rules the repo has (tone, banned words, punctuation).

STEP 0: SETUP (assume nothing is installed; check each item, install only what's missing, report what you did)
- Node.js 22+: `node -v`. If missing or older: macOS `brew install node@22`, Linux `nvm install 22`, Windows `winget install OpenJS.NodeJS.LTS`.
- FFmpeg + ffprobe: `ffmpeg -version`. If missing: macOS `brew install ffmpeg`, Debian/Ubuntu `sudo apt install ffmpeg`, Windows `winget install Gyan.FFmpeg`.
- Hyperframes CLI (via npx, no global install): `npx -y hyperframes --version`, then `npx hyperframes doctor`. Node, FFmpeg, FFprobe and Chrome must be ✓. If Chrome is missing, run `npx hyperframes browser ensure`. Whisper/Kokoro/MusicGen are not needed.
- Hyperframes agent skills: `npx -y hyperframes skills`. Read hyperframes-core, hyperframes-animation, hyperframes-keyframes, hyperframes-creative and hyperframes-cli before writing code.
- Optional storyboard discipline: `npx skills add https://t.co/wA84OlG57G --skill brag`, or `git clone --depth 1 https://t.co/wA84OlG57G` and copy `skills/brag/` to `~/.claude/skills/brag/`. Read its SKILL.md + references.
- Local runtime assets (the render must never hit the network). In a temp dir: `npm init -y && npm i gsap@3 @fontsource/<font>`. Copy `gsap.min.js` to `brag-output/composition/assets/js/` and the `*-latin-<weight>-normal.woff2` files to `assets/fonts/`. Prefer the project's own fonts.
- Remotion is not needed. Don't install it.
- Ask before anything that needs sudo.

STEP 1: READ THE PROJECT AND PICK THE MODE
Read the README, theme/design tokens (exact colors, fonts, radii), logo/app icon, key flows and UI copy strings. Then pick:
- MODE A, web product / SaaS / CLI / library: 1920x1080. Cinematic stage (dark unless the brand is clearly light). Hero moments are a code-drawn logo ignite, kinetic type, product media walls, a node graph of the pipeline, and a terminal if there's a CLI.
- MODE B, mobile app: 1080x1920 vertical. Use the app's own theme (light or dark, exactly as the app ships). The hero is real app screens inside a code-drawn phone. Motion should feel like iOS/Android: springy bounces, screen push transitions, a finger touch indicator with ripples, UI pieces lifting out of the phone in 3D, and the finished result bursting out of the phone to full screen.
If both exist (site + app), ask me which one, or do the one the prompt names.

STEP 2: GATHER REAL MATERIAL
- Mode A: screenshots, demo videos, real output samples, CLI commands, real counts from docs.
- Mode B: find plain real screen captures, in this order:
  1. Store screenshot folders without marketing frames (fastlane/metadata, distribution/store_screenshots, etc.).
  2. The project's screenshot/preview tooling, if it can render them.
  3. Simulator/device recordings.
  Skip marketing composites. Also grab the real app icon (iOS AppIcon 1024 or the Android launcher icon), sample output videos if the app produces media, and the official store badges. Use the repo's own badge files if they exist; otherwise get them from Apple's marketing tools and Google's Play badge page. Never redraw or alter a badge, and scale both to the same visual height.
- Transcode every video small: `ffmpeg -i in.mp4 -t 5 -an -vf "scale=540:-2,fps=30" -c:v libx264 -crf 22 -pix_fmt yuv420p -movflags +faststart out.mp4`.
- Mode B, measuring: scale each capture to a fixed width (e.g. 641px) with a grid: `ffmpeg -i s.png -vf "scale=641:-1,drawgrid=w=50:h=50:t=1:c=red@0.4" g.png`. Look at it and record the rects of every button, card, text field and video tile you will animate. In code, convert with K = screenWidthPx / 641. In zsh write `${i}` not `$i` next to a colon, because `$i:l` is a zsh modifier and breaks ffmpeg filter strings.

STEP 3: PLAN (write brag-output/brag-plan.md)
One-line pitch, angle, hook (first 2s), scenes with exact durations on a bar grid, copy per scene (max ~5 words per title, one accent word; readable text holds ≥0.3s per word), and the audio arc. Shape: Hook → Reveal → 3-4 highlights that show the real product in use → lockup with CTA (URL for web; icon + store badges for apps).
- Mode B default arc: app icon pops, gets tapped and opens into the phone like an app launch → hook title → the core flow as numbered steps (one screen per step, with a real interaction on each: tap, pick, upload, type) → processing sheet → beat drop: result reveal with confetti, output bursting to full screen → a variety beat (cards fanning out) → icon + name + tagline + badges.
Pick the tempo first (e.g. 120 BPM = 0.5s beats, 2s bars) and put scene changes, taps and drops on the grid.

STEP 4: MUSIC (brag-output/work/synth.mjs: pure Node, no deps, 44.1k stereo 16-bit WAV written with Buffer, seeded noise)
- Match the mood. Dark/cinematic products get minor key, saw pads, 808 kick, risers, booms. Light/friendly apps get major key (e.g. F-C-Dm-Bb), marimba/pluck motif, soft round kick, claps + snaps, shaker, bouncy bass, bright chord stabs in the drop.
- UI sound kit, placed at the same times the picture uses (share one constants block between synth and composition): tap blip, bubble pop, swish for screen pushes, whoosh-up for launches/lift-outs, thud + chime for drops/uploads, typing ticks, success chime, confetti sparkles.
- Sidechain the pads/bass off the kick. Schroeder reverb, tanh soft clip, normalize to -1 dBFS, fade the tail. Clamp every envelope input to [0,1] and throw on NaN (NaN renders silence).
- Check with `ffmpeg -af ebur128` (aim for about -13 to -16 LUFS) and a `showwavespic` image. If the kick dwarfs the melody, rebalance.

STEP 5: BUILD (brag-output/composition/index.html, one composition)
Root div with data-composition-id/width/height/duration/fps, and one paused GSAP timeline registered at window.__timelines[id]. The music is an <audio id="..."> with data-start/data-duration.
- Mode A toolkit: SVG path draw (pathLength=1 + dashoffset) with a spark head tracing the logo, then ignite (flash, shockwave, particle burst, camera shake, elastic punch); per-letter kinetic type; 3D flips, zoom-out walls, 3D carousels with whips; node graphs with pulses on beats; terminal typing; drifting ghost wordmark, embers, glow pulsing with the kick envelope, grain, vignette.
- Mode B toolkit:
  - Phone frame (bezel, dynamic island, drawn status bar "9:41" + icons, 44px top pad so the island doesn't collide with captured headers).
  - Each screen is a layer (img + overlays) inside a clipped screen. Screen pushes: old one to xPercent -30 + dim, new one from 100 → 0 (~0.45s, power3.inOut).
  - Live <video> overlays placed exactly on the capture's thumbnails/tiles.
  - Finger indicator (translucent circle) that travels, presses (scale 0.8) and leaves an orange ripple, plus a short darken on the pressed button's rect.
  - Typing: cover the captured text field with a same-colored div, type into it char by char, then remove the cover so the real capture shows. Cover pre-selected chips/states the same way and reveal them at the end.
  - Lift-outs: stage-level cards that start exactly over the in-screen rects (compute via K, with the phone at rest), spring out in 3D to big sizes around the phone, float, then return to the same rects. Show a placeholder "hole" in the screen while they're out.
  - Result burst: a stage-level full-frame video starts scaled/positioned exactly over the in-phone video rect and expands to full bleed. Before placing UI over it, check where its own burned-in captions/watermarks appear across its whole duration.
  - Confetti/particles on a canvas.

STEP 6: HYPERFRAMES GOTCHAS (all hit in real builds)
- Load GSAP and fonts only from local files (@font-face to local woff2).
- Never put a <video data-start> inside a wrapper with data-start. Scenes are untimed divs; every video carries its own data-start/data-duration, muted playsinline, no crossorigin.
- Reveal hidden things with autoAlpha/opacity INSIDE the tween's destination (fromTo {autoAlpha:0} → {autoAlpha:1}). A bare tl.set(el,{visibility:"visible"}) can be skipped by cold-seek render workers, and the element stays invisible in the MP4 even though snapshots and the browser look fine.
- Hide screens/scenes that are off-stage with autoAlpha 0. Clipped-but-present text gets flagged as occluded.
- Put the FX canvas BENEATH text layers (under the phone in Mode B; spawn confetti above the phone so it shows). Draw vignettes inside the canvas. Full-frame overlay divs above text fail the occlusion check.
- No CSS transform on anything GSAP tweens. Set initial states in fromTo. For one element use set + to, not two fromTo calls. Don't overlap two tweens on the same property of the same element.
- No template literals inside querySelector/selector strings (the bundler's CSS parser crashes); concatenate strings instead.
- Canvas and any computed 3D transforms are driven from one clock tween's onUpdate as a pure function of time. Seeded PRNG, no Math.random/Date, no repeat:-1.
- Display text: line-height ≥1.1 + padding so masked letters don't clip.
- Contrast: brand accent colors on light backgrounds often fail. Use a darker accent shade for text, and dark text on bright buttons.
- If something renders wrong, debug in a real browser: serve the folder (`python3 -m http.server`), add a temporary `window.__timelines = window.__timelines || {}`, seek the timeline, read computed styles, then remove the debug line.

STEP 7: VERIFY
`cd brag-output/composition && npx hyperframes check` until 0 errors (lint, layout, motion, contrast). Snapshot every scene and mid-transition (`npx hyperframes snapshot --at t1,t2,...`), look at every frame, and fix overlaps, clipped text, empty areas and anything hidden.

STEP 8: RENDER AND DELIVER
`npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output ../brag.mp4`. Verify with ffprobe (duration, audio stream), a 1fps contact sheet (`-vf "fps=1,scale=W:H,tile=CxR"`) and the frames at each strong cue. Pick the strongest settled frame as brag.jpg and bake it in as frame 0: `ffmpeg -i brag.mp4 -i brag.jpg -filter_complex "[0:v][1:v]overlay=0:0:enable='eq(n,0)'[v]" -map "[v]" -map '0:a?' -c:v libx264 -crf 16 -pix_fmt yuv420p -c:a copy -movflags +faststart out.mp4` (quote '0:a?' in zsh). Write share-copy.txt (1-2 plain sentences). Tell me where the files are, give one line on the creative angle, and offer the other aspect ratio.

text:
You can argue about which model is smarter today Claude, GPT, or Gemini. But if tomorrow you have to spend another 30 minutes explaining to the model who you are, that feeling of superintelligence disappears pretty quickly 😬

Mo Gawdat gave a talk at Deep Tech Night called “Beyond LLMs.” His main point was simple whoever solves AI memory will win.

He said, Memory is the hardest part. If any of you solve the memory problem, you’ll become a billionaire. 

People talk to Emma, his AI app for dating and relationships, for weeks.

 Today someone tells it about their attachment style. A week and a half later, they share something else. And all of that simply doesn’t fit into one context window. The question is: how do you build an AI that remembers the way a close friend does?...

Right now, people are trying to solve this problem on several levels.

Claude and ChatGPT already have built-in memory across sessions. On top of that, a new layer of MCP memory servers is emerging, giving multiple tools access to the same shared memory. And then there are specialized platforms like Mem0, Zep, and Letta, built specifically around memory for AI agents, not just chatbots.

Building a beautiful demo is easy. Take a powerful model, write a good system prompt, and ten minutes later you have a working prototype that looks amazing in a demo video.

But that demo only lives for one session....

The real challenge starts when you need an agent to remember a month later what you already tried and what didn’t work. It shouldn’t ask the same questions from scratch. It shouldn’t touch things you never asked it to touch.

text:
The bottleneck in agentic engineering just moved again, and this time it's protocols, not models.

For the last year the argument was which model is smartest. Now it's which wire format your agent speaks, because an agent is only as useful as what it can plug into: a model, tools, other agents, a user, and an organization's own data.

Anthropic shipped MCP first, a client server protocol that lets an agent call tools and pull context without hardcoding a backend. It won early and became the default assumption in most agent stacks I look at now.

Google followed with A2A: two agents from two different vendors handing off work without exposing their internal reasoning to each other. IBM built ACP inside its BeeAI framework, narrower in scope, still aimed at agent to agent messaging with an eye toward openness.

Then OpenAI opened Responses, a spec for the shape of a multi step agentic turn: reasoning, tool calls, reflection, with Hugging Face, Vercel, Ollama, LM Studio and vLLM already lined up behind it. The pitch is blunt: stop rewriting the same schema glue every time you swap models.

Anthropic's own Agent Skills sit at another layer entirely, packaging instructions an agent can load on demand instead of stuffing everything into a system prompt.

None of these compete cleanly. MCP is the tool and data layer. A2A and ACP are the cross agent layer. Open Responses is the turn level format. Agent Skills is the knowledge layer. What used to be one messy prompt is turning into a stack, the same way HTTP, TCP and DNS stopped being one company's fight.

I've watched this pattern before in cloud with Kubernetes and in identity with OAuth: a dominant early mover forces everyone else to adopt its shape or build a bridge to it. MCP plays that role now, and A2A, ACP and Open Responses all read like bridges as much as rivals.

The hidden bottleneck isn't which protocol wins. It's that most teams build agents against exactly one of these layers and call it done, then get surprised when the next integration needs a second, incompatible one.

My read: pick MCP for tools without debate, watch Open Responses closely because model providers showing up behind a shared spec is rare, and treat A2A and ACP as insurance for the day you're forced to talk to someone else's agent instead of just your own.

ZCode is https://t.co/8enq7wUnVs's coding agent harness (the code around the model that runs tools, edits files and executes commands), now open source on GitHub (Apache-2.0). The NOTICE is in Chinese. Three lines, in my translation (the last two also match the code):

text:
I've watched from the sidelines long enough.

My feed is full of recycled AI slop. Stack maps that are outdated, wrong, and never verified.

So here's the real deal, verified against current sources as of today, Sept 26, 2026.

This space moves fast and it will change. Follow for updates that are actually vetted from a real security professional.

Production AI runs on 12 layers.

Every one is an attack surface.

Here's the full map: the tools for each layer, and the one security control none of them should ship without.

Save it for your next build.

1️⃣ Models & Hosting:
Claude, GPT, Gemini, Qwen, DeepSeek, vLLM, Ollama
↳ Zero-retention terms, pinned versions, no public inference ports

2️⃣ AI Gateway:
LiteLLM, Prisma AIRS (Portkey), OpenRouter, Cloudflare AI Gateway
↳ Central auth, rate limits, spend caps, PII redaction

3️⃣ Orchestration & Agents:
LangGraph, Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK, CrewAI
↳ Step/budget caps, human sign-off on anything irreversible

4️⃣ Tools & MCP:
MCP, Agent Skills, FastMCP, Composio, Arcade
↳ Least privilege, allowlists, short-lived creds, vetted skills

5️⃣ Ingestion:
Unstructured, Docling, LlamaParse, Firecrawl
↳ Sanitize on the way in. Tag every chunk with source + trust level

6️⃣ Embeddings & Vector DB:
Voyage, Cohere, pgvector, Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate
↳ Classify vectors like the source data. ACLs at query time

7️⃣ Retrieval (RAG):
LlamaIndex, LangChain, Haystack, GraphRAG, Cohere Rerank
↳ Retrieved text is untrusted input, never instructions

8️⃣ Memory:
Mem0, Zep, Redis, Neo4j, Weaviate Engram
↳ Validate writes, set TTLs, let users see and delete what's stored

9️⃣ Guardrails:
NeMo Guardrails, Llama Guard, LlamaFirewall, Presidio, Check Point AI Guardrails
↳ Defense in depth. Assume filters get bypassed

🔟 Evals & Red Team:
promptfoo, DeepEval, Braintrust, Inspect, garak, PyRIT
↳ Adversarial evals gate every deploy

1️⃣1️⃣ Observability:
Langfuse, LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, MLflow, OpenTelemetry
↳ Audit every tool call. Redact and lock down the logs

1️⃣2️⃣ Automation:
n8n, Temporal, Airflow, Prefect, Make
↳ Secrets in a vault, signed webhooks, a named owner per workflow

20 years in infra and security taught me something that still holds for AI:

Attackers don't hit your strongest layer. They hit the seam between two layers nobody owns.

Pick any tools you want. Secure every layer and every handoff.

Which layer is weakest in your build?

#AISecurity #AI
