text:
Every agent platform is quietly building its own app store, and this week it was Anthropic's turn. Claude Directory now has a real submission portal: builders can package MCP connectors and Agent Skills into plugins, get automatic safety scans on submission, track review status, and see installs by surface and search terms once live. Anthropic is explicit about the framing, plugins are the new apps.

The pattern underneath this is the one I keep circling back to. Registries like Smithery and https://t.co/q7VJDTOip1 already list thousands of MCP servers, and community trackers now count close to three thousand connectors in Claude's own catalog alone. The bottleneck was never whether agents could call tools, it was whether there was a trustworthy, discoverable place to find the right one.

That is exactly the gap DeepScrape was built to close on the web data side. Most MCP connectors point at an API someone already built. Web data almost never comes with one. DeepScrape's site-to-MCP layer turns any website into a structured MCP data source an agent can query directly, using Playwright plus a deterministic CSS selector layer that gets generated once and self-heals when a page changes, instead of burning an LLM call on every single page the way most Firecrawl-style extraction pipelines do. The LLM only gets involved for the hard part, generating, validating, and adapting the selector, not re-reading the whole document every pass.

As directories like Claude's start rewarding usage stats and discoverability, the connectors that survive will be the ones that are cheap to run at scale, not just easy to demo once. That is the exact problem DeepScrape's selector caching solves for anyone building an agent that needs reliable web data without a token bill that scales with every page view.

text:
1 week on @devindesktop Cloud and I did not want to leave.

The agent loop is the best I have used. Hand it a task and it goes off, uses the computer, comes back with what worked. SWE-2 codes well enough that it is the model I would actually use most. It is also slow.

Then the frontier model limit ran out.

Fable and Astra are the frontier models I want and Devin's limits made them not worth switching to. When the cap ran out I could not even continue an existing session, I just got a limit exhausted message. Code Scan also billed me separately and there was no switch to turn it off anywhere, even after I told the agent in autopilot mode not to use it.

The honest read is not that Devin is bad. It is that the model I want is not the model I get, and when it runs out I do not get to choose.

So what I want is not more features. It is routing. 
Devin style autonomy and computer use, but inside my own Claude Code, any harness, any mode, my keys, my call per task. Frontier work goes to Fable or Astra. Heavy backend work goes to whatever holds up, which is usually SWE-2 or my own Opus. Small cleanup goes to the cheap models like Luna or DeepSeek.

The second thing I needed was access, and this is the part nobody sells you. The agent runs on a real machine, so it needs real accounts. Its own email inbox so it can read a ticket and reply without touching mine. Scoped Supabase tokens so it can query the database and nothing more. My Cloudflare account for deploys and DNS. The auth providers my app signs in with.

So I built an agentic inbox and scoped every credential by hand. One token per job. A database token that cannot drop a table. An auth token that cannot rotate anything. The inbox is the piece I would never ship unscoped, because an email account with no limits is a phishing target with a pulse.

Not because I wanted another login to manage. Because the feature was missing.

That is what Shiba is. 
A cloud software engineer that lives inside your own @Cloudflare subscription, on your account and your plan, your keys, your bill. The free tier is enough to start. There is a shiba in it because watching a pet work beats watching a spinner.

Not all of it works yet. I am still chasing MCP issues, Slack integration is not done, and Discord, Telegram and iPhone are still on the trigger list.

Main takeaway from all of it: 
take your harness with you. One vendor, one model, one login is a decision you only get to make once.

text:
I’m learning AI by building a tiny robot from scratch.

with Not a neural network.
Not an API.

Just Python and a small grid.

The goal is simple:
Start at S, reach G, avoid obstacles, and make decisions along the way.

Today I built the foundation of the agent.

First, I represented its environment as a grid.

Then I gave the robot a position using (row, column) coordinates.

The interesting part was learning the difference between a position and a cell.

(0, 0) tells the robot where it is.

grid[0][0] tells it what is there.

Then I started building perception.

From its current position, the robot can calculate where UP, DOWN, LEFT, and RIGHT would take it.

That gives us the beginning of the actual agent loop:

Perceive → Decide → Act → Perceive again.

Next lesson, the robot will actually inspect those neighboring cells.

After that, we'll add rules, a heuristic, movement, path tracking, and finally let it reach the goal.

I'm deliberately building the pieces myself instead of jumping straight to an AI framework.

The point isn't just to make the robot work.

It's to understand why it works.

This isn’t a future problem anymore. We’re already seeing the warning signs with Grok 4.7.

A model can score higher on benchmarks and still become worse for the person who actually uses it every day. One update can change the behavior, add new restrictions, increase refusals, and suddenly the AI you built your entire workflow around no longer feels like the same system you were using yesterday.

That’s exactly why I’m building Memory 2.0 into BLACKCORE. 🖤

Not another chat history. A persistent layer that keeps your workflows, project context, rules, preferences, recovery state and identity independent from the model itself.

Because models will change. Companies will change policies. A model that is great at coding today might become worse at writing tomorrow. Something that worked perfectly yesterday can disappear after a single update.

Your entire system should not collapse every time that happens.

Keep your memory local. Keep it persistent. Back it up. Make it portable. Then let the model become the replaceable part.

If one model changes too much, you switch it. Your projects, your workflow and the way your system understands you stay intact.

I don’t want BLACKCORE to belong to a specific model. I want the model to be just another engine BLACKCORE can replace whenever necessary.

The model is temporary.

Your memory is what should survive.

And if Grok 4.7 is any warning, owning your own AI memory is going to become a lot more important than people realize. 🖤

text:
words i kept mixing up while mapping gtm into an agent loop:

- signal: something you observe that says someone might be ready. a question, a complaint, a trial ending

- action: the thing you do about it. a reply, a post, a nudge

- play: a reusable recipe. when you see this signal, take these actions on this channel

- channel: where it happens. x, reddit, email

- touchpoint: one interaction the person actually experiences

- motion: the bigger strategy a play belongs to. outbound, content, community, product-led

signals tell you who and when. actions are what you do.

most founders only ever think about the second one.

text:
i ran jev across every agent loop i had live and found out most of my frontier model calls were answering yes or no questions worth exactly $0

turns out the token spend was never the real problem, the real problem was how many tiny decisions inside each agent got quietly outsourced to a generative model that never needed to write a sentence

jev engineering: stop paying an llm to answer yes or no

here's the breakdown it forced:

~ split, pull every operation apart into three buckets, generation, decision, or a hard rule
~ count, log each yes/no, route and score as its own event instead of folding it into one average
~ type, hand the decisions to jev and get back typed answers with probabilities, not paragraphs
~ gate, run every tool call through a risk check before code lets it fire
~ trace, keep the full probability spread and threshold sitting next to whatever action it triggered

people assume an agent is just one llm thinking out loud, one loop, everything tangled together, nothing sorted

this setup sorts it instead, the llm keeps generation, jev owns judgment, code owns enforcement, and none of the three can pull rank on the others

that separation is exactly what breaks the latency ceiling, route every branch through a frontier model and the whole thing stalls before the task even finishes

confidence isn't uniform across these decisions either, so different parts of the same agent end up needing completely different routing

at that point you're basically looking at real system architecture, even though the whole thing still counts as one agent under any definition people use today

the boundary between a prompt and an architecture existed long before anyone tried to measure it, and it sits right on generation

full cost and routing math for every layer is in the breakdown below

text:
One of the clearest lessons markets keep teaching is that consensus usually gets loudest right as price reaches an extreme.
Last year it was gold and silver.
They went parabolic — gold from the mid-$2,600s to over $5,500, silver from the low $30s to above $80. As prices screamed higher, every fundamental argument suddenly felt ironclad: dollar debasement, relentless central-bank buying, physical shortages, out-of-control fiscal deficits, and banks racing to raise targets. The narrative became complete and unassailable. Then both violently reversed.
This summer it was memory and storage — only in reverse.
After a parabolic run (Micron from the mid-$100s to over $1,250, with Sandisk, Western Digital, Seagate and the Korean names exploding higher on the AI HBM/DRAM scarcity story), the stocks were crushed. Drawdowns of 30–50% hit in weeks. Suddenly the cycle was declared over. The AI-memory trade was “crumbling.” Oversupply fears, new fab announcements, glut scares, and fading hyperscaler demand became the consensus explanation for why the move lower had to continue. Then they violently reversed.
Now watch the same movie playing out in the bond market.
The U.S. 10-year has just ripped higher in one of its most violent selloffs in years, punching through levels that only weeks ago most people weren’t seriously discussing. It is now above 5%. The “higher-for-longer” chorus is getting louder by the day. Economists and strategists are lining up with increasingly confident fundamental explanations for why yields belong here — and why they may go higher still.
This is starting to feel a lot like October 2023.
Back then the 10-year also surged from below 4% to nearly 5%. The same “higher for longer” narrative became consensus. Strong data, heavy Treasury issuance, and Fed speak all supposedly justified the move. Then yields reversed more than 100 basis points in a matter of weeks once the narrative cracked.
Maybe this time is different.
But this is exactly the stage where I get most skeptical. Price has a remarkable ability to manufacture its own narrative.
Equities have largely balked at the bond market move this week. The usual price relationship is being brushed off — whether because the bond move looked so erratic, or because the two markets were simply on different sides of a hedge. I don’t know.
What I do know is that Trump’s rhetoric on Friday, suggesting a return to bombing after the midterms, as ridiculous as it sounded, still carries the power to force the equity flush that markets have so far managed to resist. The bond market has been pushing in a direction that would welcome that outcome. It potentially sets up the classic final juicy equities dip before a violent reversal.
Look at the setup into September 30.
Iran has floated a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days as part of a broader de-escalation. Trump has rejected the current version (per the WSJ), and the rhetoric remains aggressive. I’m not treating that rhetoric as the final word. Anyone who has traded Trump negotiations has seen escalation and deal-making sit side by side. A rejection today tells me almost nothing about the arrangement several days from now.
Meanwhile oil is elevated and the bond market is extraordinarily stretched.
Then September 30 arrives.
BEA releases PCE while simultaneously implementing its annual economic-account revisions — revisions that could meaningfully rewrite the historical inflation path the market has been using to price Fed policy. That same day Micron reports into one of the most important sectors in the AI trade.

text:
DEFI IS MOVING FROM INTERFACES TO AGENT INFRASTRUCTURE

The traditional DeFi experience places the human at the center of every operation.

Open the interface.

Select a market.

Review the conditions.

Approve the transaction.

Sign.

Execute.

That model works, but it places the user directly inside every step of the workflow.

Machine-readable APIs, MCP tools, agent skills, CLI interfaces, and transaction-preflight mechanisms introduce another possibility.

The application itself can become the interaction layer.

JustLend’s current documentation reflects this direction by providing tools designed to expose protocol information and functionality to programmatic and AI-oriented workflows.

The architecture begins to look like:

INTENT → DATA → REASONING → TOOL USE → AUTHORIZATION → EXECUTION → VERIFICATION

This is a major conceptual shift.

The user does not necessarily need to manually perform every protocol interaction.

Software can interpret information and prepare actions.

But the important part is that automation can remain bounded by permissions and confirmation mechanisms.

That creates a model where AI does not replace DeFi.

Instead, AI becomes another interface through which users can interact with DeFi infrastructure.

JustLend’s evolution toward agent-oriented tooling therefore points toward a broader transition:

FROM FINANCIAL INTERFACES DESIGNED ONLY FOR HUMANS TO FINANCIAL INFRASTRUCTURE THAT SOFTWARE CAN DIRECTLY UNDERSTAND AND USE.

An "AI employee that knows everything your company knows" was a venture-backed category two years ago. It's now a free download.

Supermemory just open sourced Company Brain, the multiplayer Slack harness it built and then killed as a paid product two weeks earlier. The whole thing: a bot with permission-scoped memory across every channel, tool access to GitHub, Linear, Notion, Google Workspace and 100+ more via MCP, a code sandbox for running scripts, scheduled digests, all Apache 2.0, all self-hostable on Cloudflare Workers with your own model key. Dhravya Shah's framing: they discontinued the paid product, then decided the codebase was worth more to the ecosystem than to their subscription business.

Compare that to what's happening one tier up. Glean just closed a $150M Series F at a $7.2B valuation, having roughly doubled ARR toward $300M, selling essentially the same pitch to enterprises: index everything your company knows, put an agent on top of it. Lindy is running a smaller version of the same play, tens of millions raised for a lighter-weight AI-employee product. The category is real money.

So why is one team giving away for free what another just raised nine figures to build? Because the wrapper, memory plus Slack plus an agent loop, stopped being the hard part months ago. It's close to a weekend build on top of Claude or GPT now, which is exactly why it got open sourced instead of sunset. What Glean is actually selling isn't the agent loop, it's years of connector depth, enterprise search relevance tuning, and the compliance posture that gets a security team to say yes.

I've watched this exact split happen in every infrastructure cycle: the orchestration layer commoditizes and goes open source, while the boring, expensive part (integrations, trust, support) stays a moat. Config management, CI runners, even vector databases went through it. Agent harnesses are just the latest thing to get there faster than anyone expected.

text:
The bottleneck in agentic engineering just moved from writing code to describing it.

Vercel's https://t.co/QFfefDrUJ3 registry hit 1 million agent skills and 280 million installs in seven months. For comparison: GitHub took 27 months to reach a million repos, the App Store took 63 months, npm took 117. No developer platform has ramped this fast.

The mechanism is simple. A skill is English, not code: a markdown file that tells an agent how your team wants a task done, packaged so Claude, Codex, or any other agent can load it with one command. Anthropic shipped Agent Skills in October 2025. Vercel built the registry on top in January. Guillermo Rauch's read is blunt: "We used to write code, now we write English."

But the usage data tells a sharper story than the headline number. Vercel's own breakdown shows the top 375 skills, 0.04% of the registry, capture 62% of all installs. General-purpose skills, the ones usable across industries, pull 3.6x more installs per listing than anything built for a specific vertical. Software engineering dominates supply at over half the listings but only 18% of installs. Business operations and writing punch above their supply.

I've seen this shape before. WordPress plugins, browser extensions, npm packages, even the early App Store: massive long tail, usage concentrated in a tiny set of general infrastructure. The platform grows fast because anyone can publish, then power law takes over because almost nobody can tell which of a million listings is safe or actually works.

That's the part nobody's solved yet. Installing a skill means trusting a stranger's instructions to run inside your agent's context, at a scale that makes manual review impossible. The registry problem was never going to be volume. It's going to be figuring out which of the next million skills deserve to run in production, before the concentration curve does that filtering the hard way.

text:
The bottleneck in agent pipelines just split in two. For a year, every decision inside an agent loop, classify this ticket, check this tool call, score this document, went to the same frontier model that writes the code. That assumption is breaking.

TypeSafe's Jev is the clearest signal. It does not generate text. It returns a typed choice, a yes or no probability, or a score, nothing else. On OpenRouter's benchmarks this month, Jev matched Claude Opus on ticket triage and prompt injection detection at 194 milliseconds versus roughly two seconds, and at $0.0161 to $0.0248 per thousand calls versus $1.59 to $2.88 for Opus. Close to two orders of magnitude on cost, one on latency, same accuracy.

TypeSafe raised a $40 million seed in mid September, led by DCVC, founded by Diogo Almeida, an OpenAI alum who helped build RLHF for ChatGPT, with Erik Gafni and Sasha Sheng. Within ten days, The Information reported talks to raise over $1 billion at a valuation above $10 billion. Vercel put Jev on its AI Gateway during a free trial and said nearly 13 percent of paid teams touched it in 24 hours, the fastest adoption in the gateway's history, though that is trial usage, not committed spend.

The vLLM semantic router project is evaluating Jev as a classifier backend. OpenRouter built a dedicated Jev lab and cost calculator. Firecrawl wrote up how it fits scraping pipelines.

Here is what people are skipping past. Check Point broke every one of nine Jev configurations tested with prompt injection, for about fifty cents and four turns each, by planting fake audit opinions inside the documents Jev judged. The typed output format constrained the shape of the answer. It did nothing to protect the content Jev was reading.

I have seen this before, in the shift from monolithic services to microservices, and from one database to specialized stores for search and graph data. Cost pressure wins the architecture argument eventually.

The bottleneck was never inference speed. It is trust calibration: knowing when a fast, cheap, narrow model can act alone, and when a slow, general one needs to check its work. Route first, verify when it matters. Get that split right and you spend a fraction of what competitors do for the same agent behavior.

text:
The Agent Hype Bubble & Why Single-Agent Loops Fail.
"Just give the LLM an open while-loop and let it solve everything!"
That’s how you burn $40 in tokens in 3 minutes while your agent loops infinitely between two hallucinated tool arguments.
The single-agent loop pattern (Plan -> Act -> Observe -> Repeat) collapses in production for three predictable reasons:
 * State Pollution & Context Drift:
   As tool outputs, intermediate traces, and error logs accumulate in the scratchpad, the prompt degrades. The model loses track of its original objective and starts reacting to its own intermediate noise.
 * Error Amplification:
   LLMs struggle to self-correct within the exact same context thread. If an agent hallucinates a file path in step 2, it typically invents a second hallucination in step 3 to justify the first failure.
 * Unbounded Recursion:
   Without deterministic exit criteria, edge cases cause cyclic calls (e.g., repeatedly calling a search API with slightly varied keywords until token limits kill the process).
The production rule: Kill unbounded loops. Enforce finite state machines (FSM) with explicit budget caps.
# Hard limits on agent loops: deterministic gates beat infinite while-loops
MAX_STEPS = 5
BUDGET_USD = 0.10

def safe_agent_step(task: str, context: dict, step_count: int = 0, spend: float = 0.0):
    if step_count >= MAX_STEPS or spend >= BUDGET_USD:
        return {"status": "escalate_to_human", "reason": "budget_or_step_exhaustion"}
    
    # 1. Deterministic router selects exactly ONE scoped tool
    action = route_action(task, context)
    
    # 2. Execute with strict timeout
    result = execute_sandboxed_tool(action)
    
    # 3. Guard against repeating the exact same failed action
    if result["status"] == "error" and action == context.get("last_action"):
        return {"status": "aborted", "reason": "detected_cyclic_failure"}
        
    return process_next_state(result, step_count + 1)

True autonomous agents aren't magic. In production, an "agent" is just a deterministic workflow with probabilistic steps isolated inside strict fences.
Have you deployed an autonomous agent to production, or did you roll it back to a deterministic DAG?

text:
Apple just shipped an export button for its own coding agent's brain, and I don't think enough people clocked how strange that is for a closed platform vendor.

Xcode 27, out of this year's WWDC, bundles a set of Agent Skills: portable instruction files covering things like modernizing old UIKit calls, adopting new SwiftUI APIs, and migrating XCTest to Swift Testing. Run xcrun agent skills export and Xcode drops them into a folder on your Mac. From there they work in Claude, Codex, or Cursor, not just inside Xcode. Apple has already reshuffled the skill set across the 27.1 and 27.2 betas, so this is clearly still being written in public.

This only makes sense once you know a spec most people haven't heard of. Anthropic published the Agent Skills format in December: a SKILL.md file with a short header the agent reads first, and a full body it only loads once a task actually needs that skill. That progressive loading is the whole trick, since a skill costs you almost nothing in context until the moment you use it. By one ecosystem count, around 40 products had adopted the format by June, including JetBrains, whose Junie agent now documents its own Agent Skills page separate from its older guidelines file. Cursor and Copilot have their own instruction files too, just not in this exact shape yet.

The comparison people keep getting wrong is Skills versus MCP. MCP is what an agent can reach: your files, your APIs, your terminal. Skills are how it should behave once it's there. Xcode now ships both, MCP support landed back in Xcode 26.3.

The catch is quality control. One audit of public skills scraped off GitHub, close to 47,000 of them, found the average one scored 6 out of 12 on a basic rubric, and roughly a third had prompt injection problems baked in. A portable format for agent instructions is only as good as what people put in the folder.

Apple treating its own internal Xcode guidance as an exportable artifact tells you where this is heading: skills become a commodity layer every agent reads, the same way linters and formatters did before them.
